# Multi-Scale Markov-Switching GARCH: Volatility Regime Detection in EUR/USD

###### Abstract

Financial time series exhibit pronounced non-stationarity, rendering single-regime volatility models structurally misspecified for foreign exchange markets. This paper introduces a triple-timeframe Markov-Switching GARCH (MS-GARCH) framework with time-varying transition probabilities (TVTP) for volatility regime detection in EUR/USD, operating simultaneously across daily (1D Macro), four-hourly (4H Meso), and hourly (1H Micro) timescales.
Each layer uses an AR(1)-MS-GARCH model with skewed Student-t emissions and three hidden states: Calm, Turbulent, and Crisis. These states are estimated through penalized maximum likelihood using Numba-JIT compiled Hamilton filter kernels. We build a 27-dimensional joint probability tensor as the outer product of the three marginal state probability vectors, and use this tensor to route signals through a Mixture-of-Experts architecture of 27 independent RidgeCV models.

The framework is evaluated on EUR/USD data spanning 2015–2025, with a strictly out-of-sample (OOS) period of 2021–2025 comprising 31,152 hourly observations across 16 walk-forward analysis (WFA) quarters. Key empirical results are as follows. The Diebold–Mariano test confirms statistically superior volatility forecasting relative to a GARCH(1,1) benchmark: DM=+4.7040\mathrm{DM}=+4.7040 (p=1.28×10−6p=1.28\times 10^{-6}). Kolmogorov–Smirnov distributional purity tests yield p=1.35×10−153p=1.35\times 10^{-153} (Calm vs. Turbulent), confirming that the three regimes represent distinct data-generating processes. The smoothed Spearman information coefficient improves from 0.5264 (GARCH) to 0.5371 (MS-GARCH). TVTP is strongly justified at the 4H and 1H scales (Δ​AIC=+690.7\Delta\mathrm{AIC}=+690.7 and +499.9 respectively), while the 1D model correctly employs a static specification. All three timescales preserved monotonic volatility ordering out-of-sample (Calm < Turbulent < Crisis), confirming statistically distinct regime separation. The out-of-sample directional information coefficient from the RidgeCV evaluation layer is +0.0252 (p=6.75×10−5p=6.75\times 10^{-5}). The framework is positioned as a risk management tool rather than a standalone alpha engine.

Keywords: Markov-switching GARCH; regime detection; time-varying transition probabilities; EUR/USD; volatility forecasting; hidden Markov model; multi-scale analysis; walk-forward analysis

###### Contents

## 1. Introduction

Financial time series are characterised by pronounced non-stationarity: the statistical properties of asset returns—their mean, variance, autocorrelation structure, and tail behaviour—shift systematically across different market environments. Central bank policy cycles, geopolitical shocks, and liquidity crises create structural breaks that render single-regime models fundamentally misspecified. The canonical GARCH(1,1) model of [Bollerslev 1986](#bib.bib2), while enormously influential, assumes a single data-generating process operating throughout the sample. When applied to EUR/USD returns over the 2021–2025 period, this assumption produces a notable result: the estimated ARCH coefficient α^=0.3038\hat{\alpha}=0.3038 is three to six times above the typical range of 0.05–0.10 for foreign exchange data, with β^=0.6076\hat{\beta}=0.6076 and total persistence α^+β^=0.9114\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}=0.9114. This anomalously high α^\hat{\alpha} is consistent with model misspecification arising from the imposition of a single-regime structure on a non-stationary process. A single-regime GARCH model, confronted with a sample that contains multiple structural regimes, absorbs the regime-switching dynamics into its shock-response parameter, becoming hyper-reactive to individual shocks in order to compensate for the absence of state-dependent variance paths.

An influential solution to this problem was provided by [Hamilton 1989](#bib.bib10), whose Markov-switching framework introduced the concept of latent regime states governed by a first-order Markov chain. Hamilton’s model demonstrated that economic time series could be parsimoniously characterised as switching between a small number of distinct data-generating processes, with the switching mechanism itself being probabilistically estimated from the data. The subsequent development of Markov-Switching GARCH (MS-GARCH) models, pioneered by [Gray 1996](#bib.bib8) and refined by [Haas et al. 2004](#bib.bib9), extended this framework to accommodate state-dependent volatility dynamics. The [Haas et al. 2004](#bib.bib9) specification, which runs KK independent parallel GARCH processes—one per regime—is particularly tractable because it avoids the path-dependence explosion that afflicts the [Gray 1996](#bib.bib8) integrated formulation.

Despite this progress, existing MS-GARCH implementations share a common limitation: they operate at a single timescale. This is a structural misspecification for foreign exchange markets, where regime dynamics are hierarchically nested across multiple temporal scales. A central bank policy shift (a macro regime change) unfolds over months; an institutional positioning cycle (a meso regime change) unfolds over days; a liquidity-driven intraday stress event (a micro regime change) unfolds over hours. These three classes of dynamics are simultaneously present in any EUR/USD hourly return series, yet they are governed by fundamentally different data-generating processes. A single-scale HMM fitted to hourly data faces a fundamental modelling challenge: its transition matrix must simultaneously encode the very low off-diagonal probabilities appropriate for macro regime transitions (P[Calm→Crisis]≈0.001P[\text{Calm}\to\text{Crisis}]\approx 0.001 per day) and the higher off-diagonal probabilities appropriate for intraday microstructure transitions (P[Calm→Turbulent]≈0.08P[\text{Calm}\to\text{Turbulent}]\approx 0.08 per hour). These requirements place conflicting demands on a single K×KK\times K transition matrix.

This paper makes three core contributions to the literature on volatility regime detection:

1. Muli-Scale MS-GARCH architecture:
We introduce a framework that fits three independent AR(1)-MS-GARCH models simultaneously at the 1D Macro, 4H Meso, and 1H Micro timescales, each optimised for the dynamics at its native scale. The outputs are combined through a 27-dimensional joint probability tensor 𝒫t​(i,j,k)=πt(1​D)​(i)×πt(4​H)​(j)×πt(1​H)​(k)\mathcal{P}\_{t}(i,j,k)=\pi\_{t}^{(1D)}(i)\times\pi\_{t}^{(4H)}(j)\times\pi\_{t}^{(1H)}(k), enabling cross-scale interaction analysis that is not available in single-timeframe models.

2. Time-varying transition probabilities with composite stress drivers: We implement the [Filardo 1994](#bib.bib7) multinomial logit TVTP specification, driven by composite microstructure stress indices constructed from volatility z-scores, spread proxies, and momentum signals. TVTP is strongly justified at the 4H and 1H scales (Δ​AIC=+690.7\Delta\mathrm{AIC}=+690.7 and +499.9) ([Akaike 1974](#bib.bib12)), while the 1D model correctly employs a static specification (positive AIC =+2170.24=+2170.24 suggests near-overparameterisation on 1,871 daily bars).

3. Cross-scale probability tensor for state-dependent prediction and Shannon entropy filtering: The joint probability tensor serves as soft routing weights for 27 independent RidgeCV expert models, each specialised for a specific (Macro, Meso, Micro) regime combination. A Shannon entropy filter ([Shannon 1948](#bib.bib13)) suppresses trading during high-uncertainty environments.

The empirical evaluation employs EUR/USD 1-minute mid-price data from 2015 to 2025, resampled to 1H, 4H, and 1D frequencies. The out-of-sample period spans 2021-01-01 to 2025-01-01, comprising 31,152 hourly observations across 16 walk-forward analysis quarters (2021-Q1 through 2024-Q4). The WFA protocol employs a rolling 5-year training window of approximately 31,000 hourly bars, with a rolling training scheme that avoids cold-start discontinuities
across quarter boundaries.

## 2. Literature Review

The intellectual lineage of this paper begins with [Hamilton 1989](#bib.bib10), whose seminal contribution introduced the Markov-switching model as a framework for characterising non-stationary economic time series. Hamilton demonstrated that US GNP growth could be parsimoniously described as switching between two distinct data-generating processes—expansion and contraction—governed by a first-order Markov chain. The forward-backward algorithm he developed for computing filtered and smoothed state probabilities has O⁡(T​K2)O(TK^{2}) computational complexity and remains the standard inference procedure for hidden Markov models ([Hamilton 1989](#bib.bib10)). The key insight of [Hamilton 1989](#bib.bib10) is that the latent state sequence need not be observed directly; it can be inferred probabilistically from the observable data through the recursive Hamilton filter.

The parallel development of GARCH models by [Bollerslev 1986](#bib.bib2), building on the ARCH framework of [Engle 1982](#bib.bib6), provided the standard toolkit for modelling conditional heteroskedasticity in financial time series. The GARCH(1,1) model captures two fundamental stylised facts of financial volatility: volatility clustering (periods of high volatility tend to be followed by high volatility) and mean reversion (volatility eventually returns to its unconditional level). However, as [Bollerslev 1986](#bib.bib2) himself acknowledged, the GARCH framework assumes a single, stationary data-generating process. When applied to samples containing structural breaks, the GARCH model absorbs the non-stationarity into its parameters, producing the anomalously high ARCH coefficients documented in this paper.

The integration of Markov-switching dynamics with GARCH volatility models was first attempted by [Gray 1996](#bib.bib8), who proposed an MS-GARCH specification in which the conditional variance depends on the full history of regime-weighted variances. [Gray 1996](#bib.bib8) proposed a “collapsing” approximation that reduces the path count at each step, but this approximation introduces bias and increases computational cost by a factor of 3–5 relative to simpler specifications.

A computationally tractable alternative was proposed by [Haas et al. 2004](#bib.bib9), who proposed running KK independent parallel GARCH processes (one per regime) and switching between them according to the Markov chain. The [Haas et al. 2004](#bib.bib9) specification makes the likelihood exactly tractable because each regime’s variance path depends only on the within-regime history, not on the full cross-regime history. This is the specification adopted in the present paper. The independence assumption introduces a known limitation: the within-state GARCH does not condition on volatility inherited from previous states, but this is a worthwhile trade-off for computational tractability, particularly in the multi-timeframe setting where three separate models must be estimated.

The extension of MS-GARCH to time-varying transition probabilities was pioneered by [Filardo 1994](#bib.bib7), who demonstrated that business cycle transition probabilities could be modelled as functions of leading economic indicators through a multinomial logit specification. [Filardo 1994](#bib.bib7) showed that allowing transition probabilities to vary with observable covariates substantially improved the model’s ability to predict regime transitions in advance, rather than merely detecting them contemporaneously. This insight is directly applicable to foreign exchange markets, where microstructure stress indices, constructed from volatility z-scores, spread proxies, and momentum signals provide genuine leading information about regime transitions.

Recent developments in the MS-GARCH literature have focused on improving both distributional flexibility and estimation methodology. Alternative heavy-tailed emission distributions, including Normal Inverse Gaussian (NIG) and Variance Gamma (VG) specifications, have been proposed to better capture extreme market movements and asymmetric tail behaviour. In parallel, Bayesian estimation methods, Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques, and Sequential Monte Carlo approaches have been developed to address inference challenges and enable more adaptive state estimation.

Despite these advances, much of the literature continues to focus on modelling regime dynamics at a single temporal resolution. The present study extends this literature by jointly modelling regime dynamics across daily, four-hour, and hourly horizons and integrating the resulting state probabilities into a unified cross-scale probability tensor. This multi-scale architecture enables the analysis of regime interactions across temporal horizons rather than treating each timescale in isolation.

The evaluation of competing volatility forecasts requires a formal statistical test. [Diebold and Mariano 1995](#bib.bib4) developed the Diebold–Mariano (DM) test, which tests the null hypothesis of equal predictive accuracy between two forecasting models using the loss differential dt=L⁡(e1​t)−L⁡(e2​t)d\_{t}=L(e\_{1t})-L(e\_{2t}), where L⁡(⋅)L(\cdot) is a loss function (typically squared error) and ei​te\_{it} is the forecast error of model ii. Under the null, the DM statistic d¯/σ^d2/T\bar{d}/\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}^{2}\_{d}/T} is asymptotically standard normal. A positive DM statistic indicates that model 1 has smaller average loss than model 2. The DM test is the appropriate tool for comparing the MS-GARCH and GARCH(1,1) volatility forecasts in this paper.

The probabilistic calibration of regime probability forecasts is assessed using the Brier Score of [Brier 1950](#bib.bib3), which measures the mean squared error of probabilistic forecasts for binary events. The Brier Skill Score (BSS) compares the model’s Brier Score to that of a climatological reference forecast, with BSS >0>0 indicating skill above the base rate. The BSS is particularly appropriate for evaluating crisis probability forecasts, where the base rate is low (2–8% depending on the timeframe) and the cost of false negatives is high.

The residual diagnostics employ the ARCH-LM test of [Engle 1982](#bib.bib6), which tests for remaining conditional heteroskedasticity in the standardised residuals after model fitting. Rejection of the null hypothesis of no ARCH effects indicates that the within-state GARCH specification has not fully captured the volatility clustering dynamics, motivating extensions to higher-order GARCH or asymmetric specifications.

The Markov assumption underlying all HMM specifications implies that regime transitions depend only on the current state, not on how long the system has been in that state. [Durland and McCurdy 1994](#bib.bib5) documented empirical evidence of duration dependence in US GNP growth regimes, motivating semi-Markov models in which transition probabilities depend on regime age. This limitation is acknowledged in Section [10](#S10 "10. Limitations and Future Research ‣ Multi-Scale Markov-Switching GARCH:Volatility Regime Detection in EUR/USD").

## 3. Mathematical Foundations

### 3.1 Hidden Markov Model Specification

Let {St}t=1T\{S\_{t}\}\_{t=1}^{T} denote a latent Markov chain taking values in the state space 𝒮={0,1,2}\mathcal{S}=\{0,1,2\}, corresponding to the Calm, Turbulent, and Crisis regimes respectively. The chain is characterised by an initial distribution π0=(π0​(0),π0​(1),π0​(2))⊤\pi\_{0}=(\pi\_{0}(0),\pi\_{0}(1),\pi\_{0}(2))^{\top} with ∑kπ0​(k)=1\sum\_{k}\pi\_{0}(k)=1, and a K×KK\times K transition matrix P=[pi​j]P=[p\_{ij}] where

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | pi​j=P(St=j∣St−1=i),∑j=0K−1pi​j=1∀i.p\_{ij}=P(S\_{t}=j\mid S\_{t-1}=i),\quad\sum\_{j=0}^{K-1}p\_{ij}=1\quad\forall i. |  | (1) |

The first-order Markov property states that P⁡(St∣St−1,St−2,…,S1)=P⁡(St∣St−1),P(S\_{t}\mid S\_{t-1},S\_{t-2},\ldots,S\_{1})=P(S\_{t}\mid S\_{t-1}), so the full history of the chain is summarised by the current state. The observable return series {rt}\{r\_{t}\} is conditionally independent given the state sequence: rt⟂rs|Str\_{t}\perp r\_{s}\mid S\_{t} for t≠st\neq s.

The Hamilton filter ([Hamilton 1989](#bib.bib10)) computes the filtered state probabilities ξt|t​(k)=P⁡(St=k∣r1,…,rt)\xi\_{t|t}(k)=P(S\_{t}=k\mid r\_{1},\ldots,r\_{t}) recursively. The prediction step propagates the previous filtered probabilities through the transition matrix:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ξt|t−1​(j)=∑k=0K−1pk​j⋅ξt−1|t−1​(k),\xi\_{t|t-1}(j)=\sum\_{k=0}^{K-1}p\_{kj}\cdot\xi\_{t-1|t-1}(k), |  | (2) |

and the update step incorporates the new observation:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ξt|t​(k)=f⁡(rt∣St=k,θk)⋅ξt|t−1​(k)∑j=0K−1f⁡(rt∣St=j,θj)⋅ξt|t−1​(j),\xi\_{t|t}(k)=\frac{f(r\_{t}\mid S\_{t}=k,\theta\_{k})\cdot\xi\_{t|t-1}(k)}{\sum\_{j=0}^{K-1}f(r\_{t}\mid S\_{t}=j,\theta\_{j})\cdot\xi\_{t|t-1}(j)}, |  | (3) |

where f⁡(rt∣St=k,θk)f(r\_{t}\mid S\_{t}=k,\theta\_{k}) is the emission density for state kk with parameters θk\theta\_{k}. The log-sum-exp trick is applied in the denominator to prevent numerical underflow: log∑jexp(aj)=maxjaj+log∑jexp(aj−maxjaj)\log\sum\_{j}\exp(a\_{j})=\max\_{j}a\_{j}+\log\sum\_{j}\exp(a\_{j}-\max\_{j}a\_{j}). The Hamilton filter has O⁡(T​K2)O(TK^{2}) computational complexity, which is manageable for K=3K=3 and T≤40,000T\leq 40,000.

### 3.2 AR(1)-MS-GARCH Emission Model

The return equation incorporates an AR(1) mean specification to capture the well-documented first-order autocorrelation in high-frequency FX returns:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | rt=μSt+ϕSt​rt−1+εt,r\_{t}=\mu\_{S\_{t}}+\phi\_{S\_{t}}r\_{t-1}+\varepsilon\_{t}, |  | (4) |

where μSt\mu\_{S\_{t}} is the state-dependent intercept and ϕSt\phi\_{S\_{t}} is the state-dependent AR(1) coefficient. The residual εt\varepsilon\_{t} follows a state-dependent GARCH(1,1) process:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | σt,k2=ωk+αk​εt−12+βk​σt−1,k2,\sigma^{2}\_{t,k}=\omega\_{k}+\alpha\_{k}\varepsilon^{2}\_{t-1}+\beta\_{k}\sigma^{2}\_{t-1,k}, |  | (5) |

where ωk>0\omega\_{k}>0, αk≥0\alpha\_{k}\geq 0, and βk≥0\beta\_{k}\geq 0 are state-specific parameters and εt−1\varepsilon\_{t-1} denotes the innovation from the conditional mean equation. Following Haas et al. (2004), all regime-specific variance processes are updated using the same realized return innovation while each state maintains its own conditional variance dynamics. The unconditional variance within state kk is:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | σk,∞2=ωk1−αk−βk,\sigma^{2}\_{k,\infty}=\frac{\omega\_{k}}{1-\alpha\_{k}-\beta\_{k}}, |  | (6) |

which requires the covariance stationarity condition αk+βk<1\alpha\_{k}+\beta\_{k}<1 for all kk.

Following [Haas et al. 2004](#bib.bib9), the KK GARCH processes run independently in parallel, one per regime. This contrasts with the [Gray 1996](#bib.bib8) path-dependent specification, in which the variance at time tt depends on the probability-weighted average of all past regime-specific variances. The [Haas et al. 2004](#bib.bib9) specification is adopted here because it makes the likelihood exactly tractable and reduces computational cost by a factor of 3–5x relative to the [Gray 1996](#bib.bib8) collapsing approach.

The emission distribution is a standardised Student-tt with state-specific degrees of freedom νk\nu\_{k}:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | log⁡f⁡(εt,σt,k,νk)=log⁡Γ⁡(νk+12)−log⁡Γ⁡(νk2)−12​log​[π⁡(νk−2)]−log⁡σt,k−νk+12​log​[1+(εt/σt,k)2νk−2].\log f(\varepsilon\_{t};\sigma\_{t,k},\nu\_{k})=\log\Gamma\left(\frac{\nu\_{k}+1}{2}\right)-\log\Gamma\left(\frac{\nu\_{k}}{2}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\log[\pi(\nu\_{k}-2)]-\log\sigma\_{t,k}-\frac{\nu\_{k}+1}{2}\log\left[1+\frac{(\varepsilon\_{t}/\sigma\_{t,k})^{2}}{\nu\_{k}-2}\right]. |  | (7) |

The model employs staggered parameter bounds designed to encourage economically interpretable regime separation and mitigate label switching during estimation. The constraints enforce the economically motivated ordering Calm < Turbulent < Crisis in volatility and tail-risk characteristics.

These bounds are implemented as box constraints within the L-BFGS-B optimiser. The stagger on ωk\omega\_{k} encourages higher baseline variance in higher-volatility regimes, while the stagger on νk\nu\_{k} encourages heavier tails in Crisis states, consistent with observed financial market behaviour.

### 3.3 Time-Varying Transition Probabilities

Following [Filardo 1994](#bib.bib7), the transition probabilities are modelled as functions of an observable composite stress index ztz\_{t} through a multinomial logit specification:

|  |  |  |  |

|  | pi​j,t=exp⁡(ai​j+γi​j​zt)∑k=0K−1exp⁡(ai​k+γi​k​zt),p\_{ij,t}=\frac{\exp(a\_{ij}+\gamma\_{ij}z\_{t})}{\sum\_{k=0}^{K-1}\exp(a\_{ik}+\gamma\_{ik}z\_{t})}, |  | (8) |

where ai​ja\_{ij} are baseline log-transition parameters, γi​j\gamma\_{ij} are TVTP sensitivity coefficients, and ztz\_{t} is the standardized exogenous driver. The softmax structure guarantees ∑jpi​j,t=1\sum\_{j}p\_{ij,t}=1 for all ii and tt. The sensitivity coefficients are estimated subject to box constraints to prevent the exogenous driver from dominating the baseline transition structure and to preserve stable Markov dynamics during optimization.

The composite stress driver ztz\_{t} is constructed using timeframe-specific feature compositions. For the 1H Micro model,

### 3.4 Penalised Maximum Likelihood Estimation

The objective function minimised by the L-BFGS-B optimiser is the penalised negative log-likelihood:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ℒpen​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\_{\text{pen}}(\theta) | =−log⁡ℒ⁡(θ)+∑k=0K−1λk​(−log⁡pk​k)\displaystyle=-\log\mathcal{L}(\theta)+\sum\_{k=0}^{K-1}\lambda\_{k}(-\log p\_{kk}) |  |
|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | +λord∑k=0K−2max(0,pk+1,k+1−pk,k)2\displaystyle\quad+\lambda\_{\text{ord}}\sum\_{k=0}^{K-2}\max(0,\ p\_{k+1,k+1}-p\_{k,k})^{2} |  |
|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | +λstat∑k=0K−1max(0,αk+βk−0.999)2,\displaystyle\quad+\lambda\_{\text{stat}}\sum\_{k=0}^{K-1}\max(0,\ \alpha\_{k}+\beta\_{k}-0.999)^{2}, |  | (9) |

where −log⁡ℒ⁡(θ)-\log\mathcal{L}(\theta) is the standard Hamilton filter negative log-likelihood. The second term is a log-Dirichlet stickiness prior with per-state weights λk\lambda\_{k} (state-specific persistence penalties are employed, with larger penalties assigned to lower-volatility states in order to encourage realistic regime persistence), which penalises low diagonal persistence. An ordering penalty is imposed to discourage violations of the persistence hierarchy p00 ≥\geq p11 ≥\geq p22. The fourth term is the GARCH stationarity penalty, which prevents explosive variance dynamics.

The L-BFGS-B optimiser is chosen for three reasons: the parameter space is high-dimensional (27 static or 36 TVTP parameters) but smooth; box constraints from the staggered bounds are natively supported; and the limited-memory Hessian approximation is computationally efficient at this parameter scale. The label-switching problem—the tendency of mixture model optimisers to permute state labels across runs—is resolved through variance-based state sorting: states are relabelled in ascending order of their empirical within-state return variance, ensuring that State 0 always corresponds to the lowest-variance (Calm) regime.

The entropy threshold H~t>0.85\tilde{H}\_{t}>0.85 is used to identify high-uncertainty environments, preventing trading in the most uncertain regime environments.

## 4. Data and Feature Engineering

The primary dataset consists of EUR/USD 1-minute mid-price (bid-ask midpoint) data spanning 2015–2025. The data are resampled to three frequencies using strictly causal aggregation: 1H (last close of each hour), 4H (last close of each 4-hour bar), and 1D (last close of each trading day). Log returns are computed as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | rt=log⁡(Pt/Pt−1)×100,r\_{t}=\log(P\_{t}/P\_{t-1})\times 100, |  | (12) |

where the multiplication by 100 converts to percentage log returns, improving numerical conditioning for the GARCH parameter estimation. The train/test split date is 2021-01-01. The resulting dataset sizes are: 1D (1,871 train / 1,562 test bars), 4H (9,654 / 8,055), and 1H (37,345 / 31,152). The out-of-sample period comprises 31,152 hourly observations across 16 walk-forward analysis quarters.

The TVTP driver construction employs three layers of causal isolation to prevent look-ahead bias. First, all TVTP drivers use a one-period lag to prevent endogenous leakage. Second, the train/test split uses strict boundary slicing with a one-hour offset. Third, the maximum horizon trimming removes the last 24 training observations from the feature matrix to prevent multi-step forward target overlap.

The composite meta-signal is constructed as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | composite\_meta=Vol\_Spike×log⁡(1+Jump\_Ratio),\text{composite\\_meta}=\text{Vol\\_Spike}\times\log(1+\text{Jump\\_Ratio}), |  | (13) |

where Vol\_Spike=σ15​min/σ24​h\text{Vol\\_Spike}=\sigma\_{15\text{min}}/\sigma\_{24\text{h}} is the ratio of 15-minute realised volatility to 24-hour baseline volatility, and Jump\_Ratio=Realized\_Var24​h/Bipower\_Var\text{Jump\\_Ratio}=\text{Realized\\_Var}\_{24\text{h}}/\text{Bipower\\_Var} is the ratio of realised variance to bipower variation (a jump-robust estimator). The product combines simultaneous volatility spikes and jump activity, the hallmark of intraday crisis events. All composite signals are standardised via rolling 30-day z-scores and clipped to ±3​σ\pm 3\sigma to prevent outlier contamination.

The 27-expert Mixture-of-Experts feature matrix includes 47 features spanning mean reversion signals, momentum signals, volatility regime indicators, derived HMM features including entropy measures, dwell-time statistics, confidence scores, forward crisis hazard estimates, and cross-scale disagreement metrics. The top feature by absolute WFA Ridge coefficient is "Sig\_MR" with coefficient +0.001086, consistent with EUR/USD’s well-documented mean-reverting behaviour at the 1H scale.

## 5. Model Architecture

The implementation consists of an AR(1)-MS-GARCH framework integrated within a broader machine-learning pipeline.

The static specification contains 27 optimization parameters per timeframe: 18 state-conditional emission parameters μk,ϕk,ωk,αk,βk,νk\mu\_{k},\phi\_{k},\omega\_{k},\alpha\_{k},\beta\_{k},\nu\_{k} for k∈{0,1,2}k\in\{0,1,2\} and 9 unconstrained transition parameters. The transition matrix is mapped to a row-stochastic probability matrix through a softmax normalization. Although the resulting transition matrix has only six statistical degrees of freedom, the optimization is performed in a 9-dimensional unconstrained parameter space for numerical stability.

For the TVTP specification, an additional 9 transition-sensitivity coefficients γi​j\gamma\_{ij} are introduced, increasing the parameter count from 27 to 36 optimization parameters per timeframe. The Hamilton filter is implemented via Numba-JIT compiled kernels, achieving C-level execution speed. The log-sum-exp trick is applied throughout for numerical stability.

The stickiness prior vector for the 1H Micro model encodes the empirical prior that Calm regimes are highly persistent, Turbulent regimes are moderately persistent, and Crisis regimes are short-lived.

The 27-expert Mixture-of-Experts architecture constructs the joint probability tensor as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | 𝒫t​(i,j,k)=πt(1​D)​(i)×πt(4​H)​(j)×πt(1​H)​(k),i,j,k∈{0,1,2},\mathcal{P}\_{t}(i,j,k)=\pi\_{t}^{(1\text{D})}(i)\times\pi\_{t}^{(4\text{H})}(j)\times\pi\_{t}^{(1\text{H})}(k),\quad i,j,k\in\{0,1,2\}, |  | (14) |

implemented via numpy.einsum for computational efficiency. The resulting 27-dimensional vector is normalised to sum to 1 and serves as soft routing weights for the 27 independent RidgeCV expert models. Expert models are only trained when their state combination has at least 1,000 training observations; data-sparse combinations fall back to the global model. Forward-fill alignment propagates daily and 4H state probabilities to the hourly index using the unique causal method (forward-fill alignment), ensuring no look-ahead bias.

The Regime Disagreement metric captures cross-scale conflict:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Disagreementt=1K​∑k=0K−1std⁡(πt(1​H)​(k),πt(4​H)​(k),πt(1​D)​(k)),\text{Disagreement}\_{t}=\frac{1}{K}\sum\_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathrm{std}\left(\pi\_{t}^{(1\text{H})}(k),\ \pi\_{t}^{(4\text{H})}(k),\ \pi\_{t}^{(1\text{D})}(k)\right), |  | (15) |

where the standard deviation is computed across the three timescales for each state kk. High disagreement indicates that the three timescales are assigning different regime probabilities, which is itself an informative signal about regime uncertainty and transition risk.

## 6. Multi-Scale Architecture and Walk-Forward Analysis

### 6.1 The Scale Mismatch Problem

The fundamental motivation for the multi-scale architecture is the incompatibility of regime transition rates across timescales. At the daily frequency, macro regime transitions are rare: P[Calm→Crisis]≈0.001P[\text{Calm}\to\text{Crisis}]\approx 0.001 per day, corresponding to a direct jump probability of 0.0215 in the estimated 1D transition matrix. At the hourly frequency, microstructure transitions are far more frequent: P[Calm→Turbulent]≈0.08P[\text{Calm}\to\text{Turbulent}]\approx 0.08 per hour, as reflected in the 1H transition matrix entry p01=0.0824p\_{01}=0.0824. A single K×KK\times K transition matrix cannot simultaneously encode both rates; the optimiser will find a compromise that satisfies neither constraint well.

Four independent arguments support the multi-scale architecture. The computational argument notes that a single HMM on 1H data with K=9K=9 states (to capture 3×33\times 3 macro-micro combinations) would have O⁡(T​K2)=O⁡(50,000×81)O(TK^{2})=O(50,000\times 81) complexity per likelihood evaluation, compared to three separate K=3K=3 models with O⁡(50,000×9)O(50,000\times 9) each. The statistical argument notes that a single model must simultaneously capture dynamics at incompatible timescales, producing a misspecified transition matrix. The interpretability argument notes that the multi-scale architecture produces separately interpretable outputs at each scale. The empirical argument notes that the three models produce materially different regime allocations, persistence characteristics, and transition dynamics, indicating that each timescale captures distinct aspects of market behaviour.

### 6.2 Three-Layer Information Hierarchy

The three models capture distinct layers of market dynamics. The 1D Macro model captures macro-structural regime changes driven by central bank policy cycles, geopolitical risk episodes, and long-horizon capital flows. The 4H Meso model captures medium-term flow regimes driven by institutional positioning cycles, options expiry dynamics, and multi-day momentum. The 1H Micro model captures intraday microstructure regimes driven by session transitions, news flow, and short-term liquidity dynamics.

### 6.3 Rolling Walk-Forward Analysis

The walk-forward analysis protocol employs 16 non-overlapping quarters from 2021-Q1 through 2024-Q4. At each quarter boundary, the three HMM models are re-estimated on a rolling 5-year window of approximately 31,000 hourly bars. The design fuses the training tail to the test head, ensuring that rolling features (such as 24-hour moving averages) roll seamlessly across quarter boundaries without introducing NaN values or look-ahead bias.

The warm start strategy initialises the L-BFGS-B optimiser at the parameter estimates from the previous quarter, rather than at the default initial guess. This provides three benefits: reduced optimisation time (starting close to the solution requires fewer iterations); improved label consistency (warm start anchors the solution near the previous quarter’s labelling, reducing label switching); and smooth tracking of gradual parameter drift (regime characteristics evolve slowly over time, and warm start allows the model to track this drift quarter-by-quarter).

The 16 quarters span a remarkably diverse set of macro environments: post-COVID recovery with EUR/USD ranging between 1.17 and 1.23 (2021); the Fed tightening cycle with EUR/USD declining to parity and Russia-Ukraine shock (2022); banking stress with SVB and Credit Suisse failures (2023); and carry trade unwind and normalisation (2024). This diversity provides a rigorous test of the model’s robustness across different market regimes.

### 7.2 Regime Classification Measure

The Regime Classification Measure (RCM) quantifies the sharpness of regime assignments:

The Brier Skill Score ([Brier 1950](#bib.bib3)) measures probabilistic forecast skill relative to a climatological baseline:

The unconditional ACF of squared returns is 0.2579, reduced to a within-state maximum of 0.1889 by the MS-GARCH model, representing a 26.8% absorption of total volatility clustering. The 99% VaR breach rate is 0.54% versus the target of 1.00%, indicating that the model is conservative in its tail risk estimation. This is a desirable property for risk management applications: the model overestimates tail risk, providing a safety margin against unexpected extreme events.

## 8. Volatility Forecasting Benchmark

The GARCH(1,1) benchmark ([Bollerslev 1986](#bib.bib2)) is estimated on the training set using maximum likelihood, yielding parameters ω^=0.001680\hat{\omega}=0.001680, α^=0.3038\hat{\alpha}=0.3038, β^=0.6076\hat{\beta}=0.6076, and persistence α^+β^=0.9114\hat{\alpha}+\hat{\beta}=0.9114. The single-regime GARCH model, confronted with a sample containing multiple structural regimes, absorbs the regime-switching dynamics into its shock-response parameter. The relatively low β^=0.6076\hat{\beta}=0.6076 (compared to typical values of 0.85–0.92) is the counterpart: the combination of high α^\hat{\alpha} and low β^\hat{\beta} creates a model that reacts aggressively to individual shocks but does not sustain elevated volatility for long, mimicking regime-switching behaviour through a single-state mechanism.

### 9.1 Out-of-Sample Regime Allocations

The OOS regime allocations reflect the empirical distribution of EUR/USD microstructure states over the 2021–2025 period. At the 1D Macro scale, the model allocates 82.3% to Calm, 10.1% to Turbulent, and 7.7% to Crisis. At the 4H Meso scale, the allocation is 8.4% Calm, 71.6% Turbulent, and 20.0% Crisis. At the 1H Micro scale, the allocation is 65.6% Calm, 32.5% Turbulent, and 2.0% Crisis.

The striking divergence between timeframes is economically meaningful. The 1D model identifies the 2021–2025 period as predominantly calm at the macro level, consistent with the daily timescale’s lower sensitivity to intraday noise. The 4H model identifies persistent turbulence (71.6%), reflecting the sustained institutional flow activity, elevated options market activity, and frequent ECB/Fed communication events that characterised this period. The 1H model’s 2.0% Crisis allocation reflects the rarity of genuine acute hourly stress episodes.

The Rolling Walk-Forward (WFA) quarterly analysis reveals substantial time-variation in regime allocations. In contrast, 2022-Q3 (July–September 2022) saw 77% Crisis allocation at the Macro level, corresponding to the peak of the Fed tightening cycle and EUR/USD falling below parity. This time-variation confirms that the model is capturing genuine regime dynamics rather than fitting a stationary mixture.

This academic paper introduces a triple-timeframe Markov-Switching GARCH (MS-GARCH) framework with time-varying transition probabilities (TVTP) for volatility regime detection in EUR/USD. The framework operates simultaneously across daily (1D Macro), four-hourly (4H Meso), and hourly (1H Micro) timescales, with each layer using an AR(1)-MS-GARCH model with skewed Student-t emissions and three hidden states: Calm, Turbulent, and Crisis. States are estimated through penalized maximum likelihood using Numba-JIT compiled Hamilton filter kernels. A 27-dimensional joint probability tensor (outer product of the three marginal state probability vectors) routes signals through a Mixture-of-Experts architecture of 27 independent RidgeCV models.

**Data & Methodology:** The framework is evaluated on EUR/USD data spanning 2015–2025, with a strictly out-of-sample (OOS) period of 2021–2025 comprising 31,152 hourly observations across 16 walk-forward analysis quarters. Each layer uses an AR(1) mean specification with state-dependent parameters and Haas et al. (2004) independent parallel GARCH processes per regime. TVTP follows the Filardo (1994) multinomial logit specification driven by composite microstructure stress indices (volatility z-scores, spread proxies, momentum signals).

**Key Empirical Results:**
- Diebold–Mariano test confirms statistically superior volatility forecasting vs. GARCH(1,1): DM=+4.7040 (p=1.28×10⁻⁶)
- Kolmogorov–Smirnov distributional purity tests: p=1.35×10⁻¹⁵³ (Calm vs. Turbulent)
- Smoothed Spearman information coefficient improves from 0.5264 (GARCH) to 0.5371 (MS-GARCH)
- TVTP strongly justified at 4H and 1H scales (ΔAIC=+690.7 and +499.9), while 1D correctly employs static specification (ΔAIC=−2170.24)
- OOS directional information coefficient from RidgeCV layer: +0.0252 (p=6.75×10⁻⁵)
- All three timescales preserved monotonic volatility ordering out-of-sample (Calm < Turbulent < Crisis)
- VaR 99% breach rate: 0.54% vs. 1.00% target (conservative tail risk estimation)
- Brier Skill Scores: +0.2132 (1D), +0.0874 (4H), +0.1185 (1H)

**Architecture Details:** The static specification has 27 optimization parameters per timeframe (18 state-conditional emission parameters + 9 transition parameters); TVTP adds 9 sensitivity coefficients (36 total). The 1D Macro model has Calm-dominant allocation (82.3%), the 4H Meso model is Turbulent-dominant (71.6%), and the 1H Micro model allocates 65.6% Calm, 32.5% Turbulent, 2.0% Crisis. Dwell times show hierarchical structure: macro regimes are slow-moving (45.1 days Calm), meso are medium-frequency (10.8 days Calm), micro are high-frequency transient (10.7 hours Calm). A Shannon entropy filter (threshold H̃>0.85) suppresses trading during high-uncertainty environments. The framework is positioned as a risk management tool rather than a standalone alpha engine.

**Meta-Regime Analysis:** The Macro Stress Divergence meta-regime (1D:Crisis · 4H:Crisis · 1H:Calm, 5.94% frequency) produces the highest IC (+0.0544), while Total Crisis (2.73%) produces negative IC (−0.0436). Residual ARCH-LM tests show persistent conditional heteroskedasticity in all timeframes (most severe at 1H), acknowledged as a limitation.

Bachelor in Data Science and Engineering 2024-2025 Bachelor Thesis "Hierarchical ML for Market Regime Detection and Trading Strategy Performance Prediction" Sergio Vizcaino Ferrer Advisor Emilio Parrado-Hernández Leganés, Spain, September 8th 2025 This work is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution – Non Commercial – Non Derivatives ABSTRACT Financial forecasting is notoriously difficult. Prices reflect not only information but also the collective reaction of traders and algorithms, which creates noise, abrupt struc-tural shifts, and environments where a model that works today may fail tomorrow. Classi-cal trading strategies such as moving averages remain popular for their simplicity, yet they are fragile: they succeed in some conditions and collapse in others. This thesis explores whether machine learning, when paired with regime awareness, can improve the timing and selection of such strategies.
The methodology follows a hierarchical design that mirrors the thesis title. At the first level, broad market regimes are uncovered using a selective set of engineered features, dimensionality reduction and clustering, separating environments such as bullish, bearish, and neutral phases. Next, bull regime is sub-divided into two more specific regimes with another clustering model. On this foundation, a dense neural network is trained globally across assets to capture general predictive patterns. At the second level, regime-specific fine-tuned versions adapt these shared representations to the characteristics of individual regimes. Rather than forecasting raw price changes, the system focuses on predicting the expected performance of classical trading strategies, turning noisy market data into actionable signals that can guide strategy selection and timing.
Results show that while the global model alone cannot generate consistent positive re-turns, fine-tuned models achieve an annualized ROI of up to 7.9% at optimal thresholds, compared with a maximum of –0.7% for the global baseline. The findings highlight that regime detection and fine-tuning provide tangible improvements, narrowing the gap be-tween academic models and strategies that could be deployed in practice. More broadly, the work shows how combining classical finance insights with modern machine learn-ing can yield tools that are both interpretable and robust in environments as complex as financial markets.

INTRODUCTION Financial markets have long drawn the curiosity of mathematicians, statisticians, physi-cists, programmers, and, more recently, engineers in artificial intelligence and machine learning where financial forecasting has converted into a "playground" for testing ma-chine learning and statistical methods. Early quantitative research relied on relatively simple econometric models like Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) [1] or Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) [2], which could capture trends or volatility but often struggled with the complexity of real-world data. Over the last twenty years, machine learning has gradually taken a larger role, with techniques such as random forests and boosting methods showing better flexibility. More recently, deep learning has been applied with the hope that its ability to model non-linear and high-dimensional relationships could uncover patterns that traditional models miss.
Still, finance is not computer vision or language modeling: Markets generate massive amounts of data every day, but this data is noisier, with common structural breaks, and the behavior of the system changes precisely because people and algorithms react to it.
Therefore, financial markets are complex systems influenced by a wide range of factors making predictions very challenging [3]. All together, combined with the competitive nature of trading, creates a stimulating environment.
Trying to obtain solid profitability or even aiming for strong returns above market average has also been a great incentive. However, it is an extremely difficult goal with big obstacles, from commission and transaction costs where every trade costs money, to non-stationary markets that demand a dynamic forecasting with constant tuning [4]. Markets often shift into different regimes, broad environments or "modes" in which they operate.
For example, they can behave very differently in optimistic vs. pessimistic regimes, or during crisis periods [5]. A model that works in one environment can fail catastrophically in another if it assumes the underlying structure is stable. Being able to identify when the "rules of the game" have shifted, and adjusting predictions accordingly, is crucial for any system that aims to be reliable over time, especially when billions of dollars flow through algorithmic trading daily [6]. Hedge funds, banks, and high-frequency firms rely on it and accurate forecasts and regime awareness can prevent enormous losses. Firms invest heavily to try to obtain any type of competitive advantage because even tiny improvements can translate into millions in extra profits.
A central part of this work revolves around classical trading strategies such as moving average crossovers or Relative Strength Index thresholds remain popular due to their sim-plicity and interpretability [7]. In practice, each strategy can be implemented with various parameter choices, resulting in subtly different behaviors and sensitivities. While these strategies are straightforward, their performance depends heavily on the market environ-ment and can be fragile under sudden shifts or extreme events. Forecasting when these 1 strategies are likely to succeed or fail provides practical insights that go beyond simply predicting price movements.
Beyond academic research, there has been a strong push from industry toward apply-ing machine learning in trading. Hedge funds and proprietary trading firms were among the earliest adopters, often using ensemble methods or reinforcement learning for strategy optimization [8], [9]. More recently, deep learning architectures have been investigated for forecasting short-term price movements, volatility, or order book dynamics [10], [11].
While some of these works report promising results, their deployment is typically con-strained by data availability, overfitting risks, and the difficulty of maintaining robust performance under non-stationary conditions.
In parallel, commercial products have emerged that advertise AI-driven forecasting platforms or automated trading systems. Examples range from brokerage-integrated solu-tions providing "AI signals" for retail investors to institutional-grade infrastructure offer-ing alternative data and predictive analytics [12]. However, despite the marketing appeal, the majority of these systems face the same limitations identified in academic studies: sensitivity to market regime shifts, lack of interpretability, and performance degradation once transaction costs are taken into account. These limitations provide the motivation for a regime-aware framework that combines neural networks with classical strategies.
This gap between academic research, industry practice, and real-world performance di-rectly motivates the central contribution of this thesis: a regime-aware framework that integrates neural networks with classical trading strategies.
This thesis addresses these challenges by integrating regime detection clustering mod-els with neural networks, with a particular focus on classical trading strategies. The frame-work is designed so that a global neural network captures broad patterns shared across multiple assets, while regime fine-tuned versions adapt to the characteristics of specific securities. Rather than predicting raw price movements, the models aim to forecast the performance of a set of trading strategies. By incorporating regime awareness and evaluat-ing results under realistic assumptions, including transaction costs, the research provides a practical approach to improving strategy selection and timing, moving closer to methods that are both effective and actionable in real-world trading.
Building on these ideas, the thesis is structured to first provide the necessary back-ground and context, both in terms of financial trading concepts and relevant machine learning techniques. The background chapter introduces technical indicators, and finan-cial terms, while also reviewing modern tools for non-linear modeling and dimensionality reduction. The development and methodology chapter then details the construction of the predictive framework, beginning with the identification of broad market regimes dimen-sionality reduction technique combined clustering models, and the subsequent detection of finer sub-regimes. Extensive feature engineering is performed throughout, capturing price, momentum, volatility, and cross-asset relationships, ensuring the models have a rich informational foundation. Building on this, a regime-aware dense neural network is 2 trained globally across assets and regimes to learn general patterns, while regime-specific fine-tuned versions adapt these patterns to the individual regimes, providing a more pre-cise forecast of trading strategy performance. Finally, the results chapter evaluates the models both in terms of machine learning metrics, and practical investment outcomes, including annualized returns, and sensitivity to decision thresholds.
Additionally, this thesis considers the broader context in which the proposed frame-work operates. The regulatory environment relevant to financial markets and algorith-mic trading is discussed in Chapter 5, Section 5.1. The socio-economic conditions and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) objectives that shape market behavior and data availability are described in Chapter 5, Section 5.2.

2.1. Machine Learning Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP).
Uniform Manifold Ap-proximation and Projection (UMAP) is a modern technique for non-linear dimensional-ity reduction, widely used for both visualization and preprocessing in machine learning [13]. Similar to t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) [14], it projects high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while preserving structure, but it is faster, more scalable, and applicable beyond visualization.
The method assumes that data lie on a Riemannian manifold with a locally constant metric and local connectivity. Based on these assumptions, UMAP builds a weighted graph of neighborhood relationships and then seeks a low-dimensional embedding that preserves this fuzzy topological structure. In practice, this results in embeddings that reveal meaningful clusters and non-linear patterns, making UMAP a strong alternative to linear methods such as PCA.
Several hyperparameters guide the embedding process [15]. The most relevant are: • n_neighbors: controls the balance between local detail and global structure.
• min_dist: adjusts how tightly points can cluster in the low-dimensional space.
• n_components: sets the dimensionality of the output embedding.
• metric: defines the distance measure in the original space (e.g., Euclidean or co-sine).
Together, these parameters give UMAP flexibility to adapt to different datasets and tasks, making it a practical tool for both exploratory analysis and feature reduction in ma-4 Fig. 2.1. Gaussian Mixture Model with different covariance types (spherical, diagonal, tied and full). Reproduced from [15].
chine learning pipelines. In this thesis, the official umap-learn [13] Python [16] library is used for all experiments.
Distance Correlation.
Distance correlation is a statistical measure that captures both linear and nonlinear dependencies between variables. Unlike Pearson’s correlation, which only detects linear relationships, distance correlation equals zero if and only if the vari-ables are independent, making it a more robust tool for analyzing complex financial data.
[17]. In this thesis, distance correlation is used in applying dimensionality reduction and clustering in the regime detection framework.
The distance correlation between two random vectors X and Y is defined as dCor(X, Y) = dCov(X, Y) √dVar(X) dVar(Y) , (2.1) where dCov(X, Y) is the distance covariance and dVar(X) = dCov(X, X)[18].
Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs).
Gaussian Mixture Models [19] provide a proba-bilistic approach to clustering by assuming that data can be represented as a mixture of several Gaussian distributions. Each component captures a cluster with its own mean and covariance, allowing the method to model complex, non-spherical structures that simpler algorithms like k-means cannot. This flexibility makes GMMs particularly suitable when clusters overlap or when the underlying distribution of the data is not well represented by hard boundaries.
In this work, GMMs are employed using the sklearn.mixture library [20], which supports different covariance structures (spherical, diagonal, tied, and full) shown in Fig-ure 2.2. The implementation also provides tools for selecting the appropriate number of 5 components, ensuring that the model adapts to the complexity of the data.

Spectral Clustering.
Spectral Clustering is a powerful method for identifying clusters in datasets where traditional centroid-based approaches, such as k-means, struggle partic-ularly when clusters are non-convex, nested, or irregularly shaped. Instead of relying on distances to a cluster center, it analyzes the eigenstructure of a graph representation of the data to reveal natural groupings [22].
In practice, the algorithm begins by constructing an affinity matrix, which encodes pairwise similarities between data points. This can be done using a radial basis function (RBF) kernel, a nearest-neighbors graph, or a user-provided precomputed matrix. The normalized Laplacian of this graph is then computed, and its eigenvectors are used to embed the data in a lower-dimensional space, where clusters become easier to separate.
Finally, labels are assigned in this embedding space using strategies such as k-means or discretization.
For this thesis, we use the SpectralClustering scikit-learn implementation from [23], which allows flexibility in choosing the number of clusters, the affinity type, and the label assignment method. This approach is particularly good for detecting clusters that may not be convex and conventional methods would fail to capture.
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs).
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are probabilis-tic models designed to describe sequences of observations generated by an underlying stochastic process whose states are not directly observable [24]. Each observation at time 6 t depends on a hidden state Zt, and the sequence of hidden states is assumed to satisfy the Markov property, typically first-order meaning, that the current state Zt depends only on the previous state Zt−1.
Dense Neural Networks.
A dense neural network (also called a fully connected net-work) is a type of artificial neural network in which each neuron in one layer is connected to every neuron in the next layer. These networks are composed of layers that perform linear transformations followed by non-linear activation functions, allowing the model to learn complex, non-linear relationships in the data [25].
In practice, dense networks are typically organized as a stack of layers, where the output of one layer becomes the input to the next. Activation functions such as ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) introduce non-linearity, which is essential for capturing complex patterns.
Formally, for a multilayer perceptron with L layers, let x(0) ∈Rn0 be the input vector.
Each layer l = 1, . . . , L has weights W(l) ∈Rnl×nl−1, biases b(l) ∈Rnl, and activation function a(l). The output of layer l is given by x(l) = a(l)(︁W(l)x(l−1) + b(l))︁ The final output of the network is y = x(L).

Precision-Recall AUC (PR-AUC).
In binary classification, evaluating model perfor-mance is often more informative with the Precision-Recall (PR) curve than with ROC curves.
The PR curve plots precision (Positive Predictive Value, PPV) against recall (True Positive Rate, TPR) for different decision thresholds. Formally, for a given threshold: 7 Precision = TP TP + FP Recall = TP TP + FN where TP is the number of true positives, FP is false positives, and FN is false nega-tives.
The decision threshold is the probability value above which the model classifies an observation as positive. For instance, if the threshold is set to 0.5, any prediction with a probability higher than 0.5 is labeled positive, and anything below is labeled negative.
Adjusting the threshold allows control over the trade-off between precision and recall: increasing the threshold usually improves precision but reduces recall, while lowering it increases recall at the cost of precision. By visualizing this trade-off, one can identify thresholds that maintain high precision while achieving an acceptable recall, helping to resolve the classic precision-recall dilemma in a way that aligns with business goals or specific application needs.
The PR-AUC summarizes the overall performance by computing the area under the precision-recall curve. A higher PR-AUC indicates that the model is able to maintain high precision across a broad range of recall values [28].
Silhouette Score.
The Silhouette Coefficient is a widely used metric to evaluate the quality of clustering. For each data point, it compares the average distance to points within its own cluster (a) with the average distance to points in the nearest neighboring cluster (b) [29]. Formally, the Silhouette Coefficient for a sample is defined as: s = b −a max(a, b) The score ranges from −1 to 1: values close to 1 indicate that the sample is well matched to its cluster and far from neighboring clusters, values near 0 suggest overlapping clusters, and negative values imply potential misclassification, where the sample may be closer to a different cluster than its assigned one.
Davies-Bouldin Index.
The Davies-Bouldin (DB) index is a metric used to evaluate clustering quality. It quantifies the trade-off between cluster compactness and cluster separation by comparing within-cluster scatter to between-cluster distances. Lower DB values indicate better clustering: tight, well-separated clusters.[30].
Model and Scaler Persistence with joblib.
In machine learning projects, it is often necessary to save trained models and preprocessing objects (such as scalers or encoders) for later use, for example during deployment or production inference. Python’s joblib library provides a simple and efficient way to serialize these objects to disk and load them back without retraining [31].
8 Unlike Python’s built-in pickle, joblib is optimized for handling large numpy ar-rays, which are commonly present in machine learning models and preprocessing pipelines.
This ensures that saved scalers, one-hot encoders, or neural network models can be quickly reloaded while preserving all learned parameters, maintaining consistency between the training and deployment environments.
2.2. Finance Market Regimes.
Financial markets are not stationary, they tend to shift between pe-riods of distinct behavior. These periods, known as market regimes, reflect clusters of persistent market conditions that influence how assets move and how successful certain trading strategies can be [32]. Detecting changes in market regimes quickly is critical for investors and traders, as it allows them to adjust their strategies to current market conditions and manage risk more effectively. The same trading strategy can perform very differently depending on the regime. For instance, a strategy designed to profit from calm, rising markets may succeed during a bull market but struggle during a financial crisis or a volatile bear market.
Bull and Bear Markets.
Two of the most commonly referenced regimes are bull and bear markets. A bull market is a period characterized by rising prices and investor op-timism, where economic and financial indicators are generally favorable. Conversely, a bear market is a period of declining prices and heightened uncertainty, often associated with economic slowdown or crises. While these terms may seem straightforward, their exact boundaries are not fixed, and markets can fluctuate gradually or abruptly between them [33].
Defensive and Cyclical Assets.
In financial markets, assets can behave differently de-pending on the overall state of the economy. Defensive stocks belong to companies that provide essential goods or services that people buy regardless of economic conditions, such as consumer staples like food, household products, or healthcare [34]. These compa-nies tend to have stable earnings, pay consistent dividends, and their stock prices fluctuate less, offering investors a safer investment during uncertain or declining markets.
In contrast, cyclical or risk-on assets are more sensitive to economic cycles [35].
These include sectors like automobiles, airlines, hotels, or retail, which perform well when the economy is expanding but can lose significant value during recessions. Investors in these assets take on higher risk in exchange for the potential of higher returns during periods of economic growth.
By combining both defensive and cyclical assets, investors can balance stability with growth potential, adjusting their exposure depending on market conditions.
9 Federal Reserve: Tapering and Interest Rate Hikes.
In simple terms, the Federal Reserve (Fed) manages the US economy by controlling money and borrowing costs. Ta-pering means the Fed slowly buys fewer financial assets, which reduces the amount of money flowing in the economy. This is done when the economy is doing better and does not need as much support. Interest rate hikes mean the Fed makes borrowing more ex-pensive by raising the rates banks charge each other. This helps slow down spending and borrowing, which can keep inflation under control. Together, these tools aim to keep the economy stable: strong enough to grow but not so fast that prices rise too quickly.
2.3. Technical Indicators and Trading OHLCV Data.
In financial markets, each trading day for an asset (like a stock, ETF, or commodity) is summarized using OHLCV data: • Open (O): The price at which the asset starts trading for the day.
• High (H): The highest price reached during the day.
• Low (L): The lowest price reached during the day.
• Adjusted Close (C): The final price at the end of the trading day after accounting for any corporate actions [36].
• Volume (V): The total number of shares or contracts traded.
OHLCV provides a compact summary of both price movement and trading activity, making it the foundation for most market analysis and trading strategies.
Stock Tickers.
A ticker is a short, unique series of letters that represents a publicly traded financial asset, such as a stock, exchange-traded fund (ETF), or commodity, on a stock exchange. Tickers serve as a shorthand for investors, traders, and financial systems to quickly identify and refer to specific assets without using their full names.
For example: • AAPL represents Apple Inc., one of the largest technology companies in the world.
• SPY is an ETF that tracks the S&P 500 index, giving exposure to the performance of 500 large U.S. companies.
• USO corresponds to the United States Oil Fund, which reflects the price movements of crude oil.
• QQQ is an ETF that follows the NASDAQ-100 index, which includes major tech-nology and growth-oriented companies.
10 In practice, tickers allow anyone, from individual investors to automated trading sys-tems, to quickly reference and trade these assets efficiently. They are a standard tool in financial markets for communication, data analysis, and trading operations.
Returns.
Pt denotes the closing price of the asset on day t and we define the k-day decimal return as the proportional change in closing price over k days: Rk,t = Pt Pt−k −1, k ∈{1, 3, 5} Simple Moving Average (SMA).
The k-day SMA is the mean of the last k closing prices: SMAk,t = 1 k k−1 ∑︂ i=0 Pt−i Relative Strength Index (RSI).
RSI is a common technical indicator, a technical in-dicator is a calculation based on past price and/or volume of a financial asset, used to help identify trends, momentum, or potential turning points in the market. In this case RSI measures the relative magnitude of average gains versus average losses over a rolling window of length k. First, define the gain and loss on day t as ∆t = Pt −Pt−1, Gt = max(∆t, 0), Lt = max(−∆t, 0).
Then, the average gain and average loss over the past k days are AvgGaink,t = 1 k k−1 ∑︂ i=0 Gt−i, AvgLossk,t = 1 k k−1 ∑︂ i=0 Lt−i.
Finally, the RSI is computed as RSIk,t = 100 − 100 1 + AvgGaink,t AvgLossk,t .
Bollinger Bands.
Bollinger Bands are also technical indicators, they are constructed using a moving average and the standard deviation of prices over a rolling window of size k. Let σk,t = ⌜ ⎷ 1 k k−1 ∑︂ i=0 (Pt−i −SMAk,t)2 The upper and lower bands are then defined as: Upperk,t = SMAk,t + m · σk,t, Lowerk,t = SMAk,t −m · σk,t where m is a volatility multiplier.
11 Long and Short Positions.
In trading, taking a long position means buying an asset because you expect its price to rise. If the price goes up, you can sell it later at a higher price and make a profit. It is the most intuitive type of investment: buy low, sell high. A short position involves selling an asset you do not currently own, typically by borrowing it from a broker, with the expectation that its price will fall. Later, you buy it back at a lower price to return it to the lender, profiting from the difference. Essentially, shorting allows traders to benefit when prices drop.
Return on Investment (ROI) and Annualization.
Return on Investment (ROI) is a simple measure of how much a strategy or investment gains or loses relative to the amount of money initially allocated. In our work, we calculate the net return per trade and then compute the average over all trades to obtain a mean return, denoted as r ¯.
To make this measure comparable across different strategies and time frames, we an-nualize the ROI. Assuming there are 252 trading days in a year, and given that our strate-gies are evaluated over a fixed horizon H, the annualized ROI without reinvestment is computed as: ROIannualized = r ¯ × 252 H This formula essentially scales the average return per trade to a yearly level, providing an intuitive sense of performance over one year. Importantly, without reinvestment means that profits from one trade are not added to the capital for the next trade; each trade is treated independently, this simplifies the interpretation.
Example: Suppose a strategy produces an average return of 0.01 (or 1%) per trade over a 10-day horizon. The annualized ROI would be: ROIannualized = 0.01 × 252 10 = 0.252 or 25.2% per year This provides a simple, intuitive way to compare strategy performance on a yearly basis without involving compounding effects.
2.4. Alpaca API.
For historical market data, this thesis relies on the Alpaca API, a widely used platform for programmatic access to stock market information [37]. Alpaca provides high-quality, cleaned historical data with the advantage of handling corporate actions such as splits and dividends through adjusted price series. The data spans daily, minute, or even second-level bars, though in this work only daily bars were used.
One of the appealing features of Alpaca is that it is completely free to sign up and generate an API key, which is the only requirement to retrieve historical data. Once the 12 API key is obtained, data collection is straightforward: first, the tickers of interest are selected. A date range is specified, constrained by the earliest availability in the Alpaca database (from 2016 onwards) up to the most recent complete trading day. A request is then made to the API to retrieve daily OHLCV, and any other relevant fields, with automatic adjustment for corporate actions to ensure that calculated returns are accurate.
Using Alpaca in this manner, via alpaca-py , ensures reproducibility and consistency across all assets and time periods, while allowing programmatic access to large datasets essential for training and evaluating the trading strategy prediction models [38] [39].

DEVELOPMENT AND METHODOLOGY This chapter presents the complete development and methodology of the project, de-tailing the process used to capture, model, and predict market behavior through a combi-nation of feature engineering, regime detection, and strategy return classification. Build-ing on the theoretical foundations outlined in the previous chapter, the focus here is on the practical implementation: how raw financial and economic data are transformed into model-ready inputs, how latent market regimes are identified, and how these regimes in-form predictive models for short-term trading strategy returns.

To provide a visual overview, Figure 3.1 illustrates the full modeling pipeline system.
Raw market and economic data are first processed into engineered features capturing short- and medium-term trends, momentum, and macroeconomic sentiment detailed in Subsection 3.1.1. Each unique set of features are feed into the models. The pipeline starts with the regime detection module, which uses dimensionality reduction (UMAP) and clustering (GMM) to identify latent market states. Afterwards, a spectral clustering model that uses a new different set of features described in Subsection 3.2.1, divides bull 14 market into another two bull sub-regimes. On the other hand, classical trading strategies are implemented, such as moving average crossovers, RSI, and Bollinger Bands, where related variables and the strategies returns (target variable) are included. Those strategy variables, along with regime-derived features and an additional set of technical indicators serve as input to the global neural network model. It is trained to capture general patterns, and posterior fine-tuned to individual regimes so the network specializes to each detected market state. This system highlights the integration of financial domain knowledge with hierarchical machine learning models to predict short-term trading strategy returns in a regime-aware framework.
3.1. Market Regime Detection This model aims at identifying market regimes by capturing the state and sentiment of the market as well as the broader economic situation. The development steps consist on feature construction, preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, and clustering.
Fig. 3.2. Flowchart module of the Market Regime Detection The Aplaca API raw OHLCV data is sourced from four main subsets of financial assets: 1. United States Equity Indices: SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA.
2. Global (non-US) Equity Indices: EEM, EFA, FXI, EWZ.
3. Defensive Sectors: XLP, XLV, XLU.
4. Currencies: UUP, FXY, FXF, FXE, FXA, FXC.
15 3.1.1. Feature Construction The features are engineered in two layers. The first layer computes basic daily metrics such as 5-day returns and 14-day Relative Strength Index (RSI). The second layer aggre-gates these metrics into the variables that will serve as model inputs: • Mean 5-day return of US equity indices: This feature captures short-term mar-ket dynamics by averaging the 5-day returns across indices. It reflects the overall direction of the US market over the past trading week, helping the model detect immediate upward or downward trends.
• Momentum slope of US equity indices: For each index, a linear regression is fit over the last 10 observations of rolling 5-day returns. The average slope across the four indices provides a measure of medium-term momentum, showing whether recent trends are strengthening or weakening over approximately two weeks. This helps the model distinguish between temporary fluctuations and sustained market moves.
• Mean 14-day RSI of global (non-US) equity indices: By averaging the 14-day RSI, this feature indicates the relative strength or weakness of international equity markets. Higher values suggest that global markets are generally overbought, while lower values indicate potential oversold conditions, giving the model insight into worldwide market sentiment.
• Defensive vs. broad equity 14-day RSI spread: This feature compares the av-erage RSI of defensive sectors with the average RSI of US and global equities. A positive spread indicates that investors are favoring defensive or less cyclical stocks, which often happens during market uncertainty. Conversely, a negative spread sug-gests that riskier, more cyclical equities are stronger, signaling higher market con-fidence.
• Safe-haven vs. risk-on currency 5-day return spread: Currencies are critical indicators of global risk sentiment. Safe-haven currencies, such as the US Dollar (UUP), Japanese Yen (FXY), and Swiss Franc (FXF), typically appreciate when investors seek protection during uncertainty. In contrast, risk-sensitive currencies, such as the Euro (FXE), Australian Dollar (FXA), and Canadian Dollar (FXC), tend to strengthen during periods of economic expansion and higher risk appetite.
The feature is defined as the difference between the mean 5-day returns of the two groups.
All features are computed daily, and missing values due to rolling windows are removed.
Even though posterior dimensionality reduction is applied, a small number of features favors easier understanding and interpretation of regimes results, which vital for Machine Learning applications on this financial field.
16 3.1.2. Preprocessing Two preprocessing steps are applied to the feature matrix to improve model robustness and performance: 1. Outlier reduction: Winsorization at the 1st and 99th percentiles mitigates the in-fluence of extreme values: x(winsorized) t = ⎧ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎨ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎪ ⎩ q0.01(x), if xt < q0.01(x) q0.99(x), if xt > q0.99(x) xt, otherwise This step is crucial for capturing more subtle regime differences that would other-wise be overshadowed by extreme market moves. Limiting the impact of extreme market moves allows the model to better generalize and focus on more typical and less radical days, which are the majority of the cases.
2. Standardization: Features are scaled to zero mean and unit variance: x(scaled) t = xt −µx σx Standard scaling consistently outperformed MinMax in experiments, providing more stable clustering results. An alternative approach is to use sklearn Robust scaler, which is more resistant to outliers, but in our tests it produced slightly worse sepa-ration between clusters compared to the Winsorize + Standard scaling combination.
3.1.3. Dimensionality Reduction and Clustering 1. UMAP projection: The preprocessed feature matrix X was reduced to three di-mensions (NCOMP = 3) using the UMAP algorithm with parameters NNEIG = 15, min_dist = 0.01, and correlation as the distance metric: XUMAP = UMAP(X; NCOMP, NNEIG, min_dist, metric) The main reason for reducing the dimensions was to make the clusters possible to visualize. Four or more dimensions could not be plotted in a way that is easy to understand, while only two dimensions compressed the data too much and lost structure. Three dimensions was a great balance.
For the parameters, keeping the default number of neighbors (NNEIG = 15) gave the best and most stable results since it is considered the middle point between local versus global structure in the data. Lowering the minimum distance from 0.1 to 0.01 helped UMAP to create more compact and clearer clusters, which also made interpretation easier.
17 The distance metric was set to correlation, not only because in finance the relation-ships between assets matter more than the absolute price differences but also gave better results than Euclidean or Manhattan in this dataset.
2. Gaussian Mixture Model clustering: The reduced dataset XUMAP was clustered with a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) using K = 4 components and k-means++ initialization: {ℓ1, . . . , ℓT} = GMM(XUMAP, K) where ℓt is the cluster label at time t. Each day is assigned to a market regime based on the probability from the mixture model.
Choosing the number of clusters was an important step. Larger numbers (K ≥ 6) gave good internal metrics but were hard to interpret in practice. Very small numbers (K ≤3) lost important differences, with some clusters being too broad.
Four clusters gave a good mix of separation and interpretability.
Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are the standard for regime detection because they include time structure. However, they are more complex to estimate and can overfit.
GMMs are simpler since they only fit mixture components, but they do not use time information directly. To make up for this, two adjustments were used: • Time-informed features: Returns of several days instead of plain time-fixed OHLCV variables, and Indicators such as RSI and momentum were added so that some time structure is indirectly included.
• Post-clustering smoothing: A 5-day rolling majority vote was applied to the cluster labels. For each day t, the smoothed label ℓ ˜t is the most frequent cluster in the surrounding 5-day window: ℓ ˜t = arg max k count(︁{ℓt−2, . . . , ℓt+2} = k)︁ This reduced day-to-day noise and gave more stable regimes. A window of 5 days worked best: 3 days was too short and noisy, 7 days too long and slow to react.
The smoothing was not too harsh, with about 90% agreement between the original and smoothed labels, as shown in Table 3.1: Agreement Proportion Same Cluster 0.903 Different Cluster 0.097 TABLE 3.1. AGREEMENT BETWEEN SMOOTHED AND ORIGINAL CLUSTER ASSIGNMENTS.
Overall, the UMAP–GMM combination produced well-separated clusters that were also possible to visualize and explain, with a practical advantage compared to 18 HMMs, which are more formal and complex but less intuitive for communicat-ing results. Proving to be a feasible alternative to HMMs with their corresponding trade-offs.
3.1.4. Saving Models for Deployment To facilitate reproducibility and future deployment, the preprocessing and model objects are saved using joblib. This includes: • The standard scaler (trend_scaler.pkl) • The fitted UMAP model (trend_umap_model.pkl) • The trained GMM (trend_gmm_model.pkl) This ensures that the entire preprocessing and modeling pipeline can be reused for
