vi ABSTRACT OF THE DISSERTATION The Efficacy of a Regime-Switching Asset Pricing Model Conditioned on Market Volatility by David Baines Doctor of Business Administration in Finance Washington University in St. Louis, 2023 Brett Green, Andy Neuhierl, Guofu Zhou (Chair) In an attempt to explain stock prices in a simple and articulate manner, researchers in asset pricing have long employed a “one model fits all prices over time” approach. In this thesis, a regime-switching linear asset pricing model, conditioned on trailing market volatility, is intro-duced in an attempt to map specific linear model specifications to specific macroeconomic conditions which are quantifiable and observable at t. Called the Time-Robust Iterative Adaptive LASSO (TRIAL) model, this model computes the expected return more efficiently out-of-sample than a benchmark model which does not use volatility-defined regimes, yield-ing a risk-adjusted mean monthly return of 1.36%, compared to the “no regime” model return of 1.12%. Compared to a seminal model in asset pricing, the Fama-French 3-Factor Model (“FF3”), the TRIAL model evinces a higher monthly return than the FF3’s return of 1.23%, while also providing lower monthly volatility than the FF3, at 6.31% and 6.97%, respectively. The TRIAL model fits its distinct regimes well, having statistically significant, unique linear specifications for each regime. The TRIAL model is asymmetric to the popu-lar size and value factors across the regimes: it estimates big firms better than small firms and value firms better than growth firms. When four single-sort out-of-sample portfolios are created on size and value, the “big firm” portfolio yields a risk-adjusted mean monthly return of 2.38% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.27 over the 17-year testing period, well above any other benchmark model in the study.
vii Chapter 1 Motivation and Contribution 1.1 Motivation In an attempt to explain stock prices in a simple and articulate manner, researchers in asset pricing have long employed a “one model fits all prices over time” approach. With this approach, the researcher creates a statistical model, traditionally linear in nature, that attempts to capture the cross-sectional variation of returns. With this model, the researcher can then estimate the “exposure” of each model feature on that return to explain the return.
(In the literature, model features are called “characteristics” if they represent attributes of firms like market capitalization or book-to-market ratio, and “factors” if they represent returns of a (typically sorted) portfolio of characteristics. In this thesis, characteristics are the focus.) With this model, the researcher can then compute an “expected return” in t + 1 for any firm i, defined as the dot product of the the cross-sectional slope estimates of the characteristics in their model over the return space (denoted by βj) and the values of those characteristics for each firm i = 1, . . . , N in their study (denoted by Xi,t), plus a cross-sectional intercept term (denoted by α). In these models, the number of features can span j = 1, . . . , J. The generic mathematical representation of these linear models is Ri,t+1 = α + β1X1,i,t + · · · + βJXJ,i,t + ui,t+1, (1.1) 1 where Ri,t+1 is the excess return of firm i in time t + 1, β1,...,J are the slope estimates of characteristics X1,...,J,i,t, and ui,t+1 is the error term.
Notable works using this approach include Sharpe (1964), Fama and French (1993), Fama and French (2015), or Hou et al. (2014) for equities or Carhart (1997) for mutual funds.
These models are simple to estimate mathematically (they are only linear combinations of estimates and characteristic values, maybe with the addition of an intercept term), are simple to implement in practice (they require only off-the-shelf computing power), are economically intuitive (the value of the cross-sectional coefficient βj,t for characteristic j is the degree and direction of exposure the firm’s expected return E[Ri,t+1] has to a firm’s characteristic value Xi,j,t), and are relatively effective in explaining prices. Because of these attractive features, these models have been the primary models used in industry since their introduction, as discussed in Grinold and Kahn (2000).
A major drawback of this approach, however, is that pricing errors in linear time series models are heteroskedastic and “single-regime” linear models cannot efficiently estimate the slopes of the characteristic over time if the underlying space in which firm returns reside also varies with time. This effect is discussed in Potter (1999) in general and is shown for the Fama-French 3-Factor Model (”FF3”) specifically in Fig A.1. With this effect in mind, asset pricing researchers in the past two decades have begun to borrow non-linear time series estimation methods from the statistics and computer science literature in an effort to better capture the variation of returns over time. Using techniques such as auto-encoders (Gu et al., 2021), deep neural networks (Chen et al., 2021), or decision trees (Bryzgalova et al., 2021), researchers have found that these advanced methods can help estimate expected returns more consistently and efficiently in a time-varying setting, as well as also help solve for other well-documented estimation issues in empirical asset pricing such as the “curse of dimen-sionality”, the low signal-to-noise ratio, and the non-linear relationship between returns and 2 characteristics.1 In a general sense, the goal of these approaches is to capture the variation of returns consistently over time, as explained by a parsimonious set of characteristics in the model, while not overfitting the training data (avoiding “too much bias”) and ensuring robustness out of sample (avoiding “too much variance”) while doing so. To achieve this attractive result, however, these approaches incur three costs that limit their wide-spread use in industry: there is a high level of skill required to design and implement them, the compute architecture required to run them can be complex, and the economic explanations of the results can be muddled or non-existent.
1.2 Contribution With the goal of reducing heteroskedastic pricing errors through time while keeping the esti-mation process mathematically simple, computationally trivial, and economically intuitive, this thesis introduces a novel asset pricing model called the Time-Robust Iterative Adaptive LASSO (“TRIAL”) model. The TRIAL model is linear in its design, yet improves training fit and out-of-sample robustness relative to other single-regime linear models due to its ability to define and utilize distinct regimes, conditioned on elements which are observable at t. In this thesis, the conditioning function is defined in terms of market volatility, but this condi-tioning function could theoretically be any exogenous, observable proxy for macroeconomic health. The motivation is, intuitively, a model that explains stock prices should be a function of the macroeconomic state in which those firms reside. The implication is that it is this exogenous market force that is acting on firm returns, causing regime-linked pricing errors in the linear models and, if those market states can be captured and distinctly estimated, 1Although, there is some debate on the significance of non-linearity as discussed in Chen et al. (2021, p.3-4) regarding the regression of returns on “firm-specific characteristics in isolation” and as shown in Kelly et al. (2019) as their linear IPCA model fits time series returns effectively relative to non-linear approaches.
2https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data library.html 3 it should be possible to yield more consistent return forecasting through time. Empirically, it is shown here that the TRIAL model reduces the variance of these heteroskedastic errors only marginally over time, specifically relative to the FF3 model of Fama and French (1993), with standard deviations of the root-mean-squared forecast error (RMSFE) in the testing period of 5.25% and 5.64%, respectively. See Figure A.1 to see the RMSFE for both models.
While the pricing errors are similar, the mean monthly risk-adjusted return of the TRIAL model and the FF3 Model using the same portfolio construction methodology is 1.36% and 1.23%, respectively.
Market volatility can be used as a proxy for market health here thanks to work contributed by Schwert (1989), and firm-level characteristics such as firm leverage can be linked to market volatility via determinants such as interest rates, as shown in Black (1976) and Merton (1980). More formally, and shown in Proposition 1, the hypothesis tested here is there exists a set of firm-level characteristics, SG ∈J, where J is the full set of firm-level characteristics, that explains prices better than those not in SG in “good” economic states while there exists another, distinct set of characteristics, SB ∈J that explains prices better than those not in SB in “bad” macroeconomic states. In this thesis it is shown that the TRIAL model does in fact capture these market states and that, by doing so, the out of sample performance is enhanced. The TRIAL model produces a 1.36% mean monthly risk-adjusted return while a na¨ ıve fixed-effects panel model without regimes over the same period produces only a mean monthly risk-adjusted return of 0.90%, which is equivalent to the mean risk-adjusted return of all firms.
Proposition 1: For S ∈J, ∃SG, SB ∈J, where SG ̸= SB and |SG|, |SB| ̸= 0.
The idea of a dynamic asset pricing model specification is also explored by Bianchi et al.
(2019), although the key difference between that work and this one is, in their thesis, the 4 motivation is 1) to determine which characteristics contain the most persistent explanatory power over time (robust to any market state) and 2) to determine the degree to which model sparsity varies through business cycles.
In this thesis, the motivation is to determine if characteristics consistently and persistently map to specific market states such that, in a given market state at t, a reliable model specification can be used to effectively estimate expected returns in t + 1 out-of-sample.
Introduced by Hamilton (2010), regime-switching models allow the specification of a sta-tistical model to change in response to a contemporaneous conditioning variable. In this thesis, the conditioning behavior is achieved through use of a conditioning function instead of a variable. This conditioning function is defined as a discretized value of the (scaled) trailing 6-month market (S&P 500 TR) volatility, denoted as γ(M(t)). The advantage of this approach is the non-discretized form, M(t), is continuous, fully observable at t, and is deterministic, which makes it simple to calculate in practice at any time t. Furthermore, this thesis allows the entire specification of the asset pricing model to change instead of just the intercept as discussed in Hamilton (2010). This extension is possible because the estimations discussed here occur in the cross-section and not in the time series.
In this way, the expected return using the TRIAL model can be calculated as E[Ri,t+1] = Xi,t · S′|γ(M(t)), (1.2) where Xi,t is a 1 × J vector of characteristics for firm i at month t across characteristics j = 1, . . . , J, S is a 1 × J vector of slope estimates from the linear model specification using the Adaptive LASSO technique from Zou (2006) in the discrete regime defined by γ(·), and γ(M(t)) is the discrete state in terms of M(t), where γ(M(t)) ∈{1, 2, 3}.
In this thesis, γ(M(t)) = 1 signifies a “bad” state month (high volatility, where M(t) < 0.5), 5 γ(M(t)) = 2 signifies a “neutral” state month (neutral volatility, where 0.5 ≤M(t) ≤0.75), and γ(M(t)) = 3 signifies a “good” state month (low volatility, where M(t) > 0.75), where each month contains only one state class. For the sample 1955:01 to 2021:21, 12% of months were classified as “bad” state months, 55% were “neutral” state months, and 33% were classified as “good” state months. Details on M(·) can be found in Section 3.2.
A unique feature of the TRIAL model is its ability to parse through the multicollinearity found in the “factor zoo” as discussed in Cochrane (2011), Harvey et al. (2015), and Hou et al. (2018). To achieve this, the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) technique as discussed in Velleman and Welsch (1981) is used. Important to note, common characteristics found in other pricing models such as Size, Leverage, and Momentum factors are removed from the TRIAL estimation process and are never present in any regime specification due to their multicollinearity with other (and apparently more informative) characteristics. (See Table A.3 for the full list of characteristics that were never use in the regime estimation and model construction process.) Even without these much-lauded characteristics, however, the TRIAL model explains prices adequately out of sample.
Out of sample, from 2005:01 to 2021:12 (also called “the testing period”), the TRIAL model produces an average monthly risk-adjusted return of 1.36%. This is materially higher than the the stock universe return 0.90%, the S&P 500 Total Return Index (“S&P 500 TR”) return of 0.84%, and the Fama-French 3-Factor (“FF3”) mean monthly risk-adjusted return of 1.23%. To determine “if regimes matter,” a “no-regime” model was created which is identical in construction to the TRIAL model and portfolio, but only holds a single specification over the training period; this model produced a risk-adjusted mean monthly return of 1.12%.
Over the testing period, the TRIAL model evinced a risk-adjusted Sharpe ratio of 0.81 and each regime model held the highest Sharpe ratio for the regime state it was intended to explain. For example, the “good state” model had a Sharpe ratio of 2.63 in the “good state” 6 panel out of sample but hand a lower Sharpe ratio in the “neutral” (2.45) and “bad” (1.41) state panels; for more details, see Figure A.4. These values compare to Sharpe ratios of 0.19 from the total sample, 0.70 from the S&P 500 TR, and 0.64 from the FF3. Finally, the annualized risk-adjusted alpha for the TRIAL model was 13.75% out of sample, compared to -2.04% from the total sample, and 14.72% from the FF3. Overall, the TRIAL model performs strongly against its linear counterparts, is economically intuitive, is simple to estimate, and is robust out of sample.
The TRIAL model seems not to be robust to size and value. The TRIAL model fits larger firms better than smaller firms, and value firms better than growth firms. When creating four portfolios on size and value on the testing period, the “big firm” portfolio outperforms the three other portfolios with a mean monthly risk-adjusted return of 2.38%; the “value firm” portfolio is the second highest mean monthly return with a value of 1.72%. Monthly volatility for the “big firm” portfolio is about equal to the volatility of the “all-firm” TRIAL portfolio, with monthly return volatility of 6.48% and 6.31%, respectively. The combination of these higher monthly returns and the steady volatility combines for an annualized risk-adjusted Sharpe ratio of 1.27 for the “big firm” portfolio, 57% higher than the “all-firm” TRIAL portfolio of 0.81. Cumulative returns for all four size and value portfolios are displayed in Figure A.14.
The thesis is constructed as follows: Section 2 discusses the data used to train and test the TRIAL model, Section 3 discusses how TRIAL is trained and tested, Section 4 discusses the results and tests for robustness, and Section 5 concludes the thesis. References, figures, and tables follow.
7 Chapter 2 Data Firm returns and firm-level characteristic values were obtained from the Chen and Zim-mermann (2022) data set, 2 which are computed using data from CRSP-Compustat, IBES, OptionMetrics, 13F filings, and other sources (see Chen and Zimmermann (2022) for com-plete list). S&P 500 Total Return (TR) value weighted returns, for use in benchmarking and regression calculations, were also obtained from CRSP. Risk-free rates are from Ken French’s website.
The Freyberger et al. (2021) version of the Chen and Zimmermann (2022) data was used to ensure the use of complete matrices in the estimation process, which is discussed in more detail in Section 3.3. This is data completion process (via imputation) is important because, for the TRIAL model to be estimated as effectively as possible, as much information from the characteristics needs to be gleaned as possible to explain the available cross-sectional returns.
The Chen and Zimmermann (2022) data contains 207 characteristics from 153 thesiss that are widely cited as used for reliable time series and cross-sectional asset pricing in the literature (see Chen and Zimmermann (2022) for details, including the rationalization of why characteristics were included). After the Freyberger et al. (2021) “missing data” imputation process is applied to the 207 characteristics, 87 characteristics are left for use in the training and testing of the TRIAL model.
2Please visit https://www.openassetpricing.com for data details and definitions.
8 The training period is from 1955:01 to 2004:12 for 50 years of training data. The depth of the sample is to ensure many business cycles can be captured to properly estimate the distinct regime specifications. The testing sample is 2005:01 to 2021:12 for 17 years of out-of-sample evaluation. 1,543,713 stock-months are used in the training period and 804,583 stock-months are used in the testing period. The number of stocks used for entire data set, by month, are displayed in Figure A.2.
9 Chapter 3 Methodology 3.1 TRIAL Estimation Overview The purpose of the TRIAL model is two-fold: 1) to efficiently estimate characteristic slope estimates amid the “factor zoo” of characteristics to yield parsimonious cross-sectional pric-ing models (see Cochrane (2011), Harvey et al. (2015), Hou et al. (2018)), and 2) to associate characteristics with specific macroeconomic conditions using the hypothesis found in Propo-sition 1 to reduce heteroskedastic errors in the model. To achieve these two goals, there are series of steps in the estimation process that are summarized in this section and expanded upon in subsequent subsections.
The navigation of the factor zoo (synonymously “anomaly zoo” or “characteristic zoo”) is important in this context because, if that navigation is effective, we can start to separate the “signal from the noise” and find statistically significant connections between returns and characteristics, the main goal in empirical asset pricing research. To achieve this, we need to find orthogonality between characteristic signals as that will ensure returns are explained as “completely” as possible by the characteristics.
Once orthogonality is achieved with a set of characteristics on which the model can be trained, characteristics can then be mapped to regime sets using the assumption that different 10 characteristics explain returns in different economic conditions. (Bianchi et al. (2019) also explored this idea.) To capture these economic conditions in this thesis, the function M(t) is used. It’s important to note that a nuance of the TRIAL model is that it requires a defined, finite training period on which to estimate its regime specifications, and uses those fixed estimations throughout the testing period (potentially in perpetuity).
Ongoing research by the author aims to relax this restriction into an unsupervised, “online” context using a Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Ch. 3) and neural networks (van der Himst and Lanillos, 2020) so that the model can “learn” new estimations conditioned on the model’s “belief” of the state of the market at time t as the model progresses through time, but that is outside the scope of this version of the thesis.
Displayed as a series of steps, the following is an overview of how the TRIAL model spec-ifications are created and the overall model is constructed. The steps will be discussed in more detail in subsequent subsections.
1. Compute M(t) for t = 1, . . . , T across the training and testing periods.
2. Using Freyberger et al. (2021) characteristic and return values, find the Variance Infla-tion Factor (VIF) for each characteristic in the cross-sections at each time t, removing characteristics until all remaining characteristics have a VIF < 5 in each cross-section.
3. Use Adaptive LASSO in the cross-sections at each time t to regularize the cross-sectional models, using characteristics remaining after Step 2 as inputs.
Store the characteristics chosen in each t, then group on the regime.
4. Starting with the characteristics chosen in Step 3, build the regime-specific time series model using backward elimination to find regime-specific model parsimony by removing characteristics from each regime specification that do not add to the explanatory power of the model.
11 5. Using the coefficients in the regime-specific times series models, calculate the expected return in t + 1 for any firm i in t given M(t).
In 3.2, the construction of M(t) is discussed, 3.2 discusses the preparation of the data for Adaptive LASSO using the VIF, 3.4 discusses the cross-sectional Adaptive LASSO estima-tions, 3.5 discusses the building of the three regime specifications, and 3.6 discusses how TRIAL is applied across T to calculate the expected return and how the return portfolios for analysis and benchmarking are constructed.
3.2 Building M(t) M(t) is a continuous function, bounded from 0 to 1, which aims to describe the macroe-conomic state of the American economy at t. We can use market volatility as a proxy for market health here thanks to work such as Schwert (1989), and link characteristics to this market health proxy through concepts such as firm leverage and interest rates, as shown in Black (1976) and Merton (1980), respectively. It is on this function M(t) where regimes are defined, and on which the TRIAL model specifications are conditioned.
M(t) ∈(0.75, 1] indicates a “good” macroeconomic state and Mt ∈[0, 0.5) indicates a “bad” macroeconomic state.
Every value of M(t) ∈[0.5, 0.75] is labeled as a “neutral” macroeconomic state so statistical size and power is not lost by having a large “open” space between regimes where information on returns cannot be gleaned. All three classes will have their own time series specification to compute the expected return in t + 1; this is the regime-switching mechanic of TRIAL. To discretize M(t) into numerical classes by month, the notation γ(M(t)) is used, where γ(M(t)) = 2 is a “good” economic state month, γ(M(t)) = 1 is a “neutral” economic state month, and γ(M(t)) = 0 is a “bad” economic state 12 month. Every month in the study is classified as belonging to only one state. This definition of M(t) is recommended for use in practice because 1) it is tied to economic theory relating to uncertainty which allows for a simple interpretation of the characteristics found in each regime model, 2) it is deterministic, 3) it is fully observable, and 4) it is easily calculated.
The value of M(t) is defined as M(t) = 1 − σ6mo t −min σ6mo 1,...,t max σ6mo 1,...,t −min σ6mo 1,...,t , (3.1) where σ6mo is trailing six-month standard deviation of the S&P 500 Total Return index, max(min)σ6mo 1,...,t is the maximum (minimum) of σ6mo in 1, . . . , t, and σ6mo t is the σ6mo at t.
This method of standardization is called “scaling” and, in the edge case where new maxima (minima) of σ6mo present themselves in the test set (since the training period has defined bounds), M(t) just incorporates those values in 1, . . . , t. Since there is a large buffer on both bounds of M(t) such that the bound regimes will not lose their specification, the effect of regimes having to be re-specified as the model moves through time is not a concern.
The distribution of the different states across the training, testing, and total periods remains consistent which enable the TRIAL model to be trained and tested adequately. The “neutral” state is the most common state-month in both the training and testing periods: the definition of the boundary states as described by M(·), the “good” and “bad” states, are intended to reflect times of material market calmness or volatility, respectively. These state definitions were also chosen, specifically on high volatility side, to reflect common markers market instability or poor market health, such as NBER recessions. The discretized value of M(t), denoted by γ(M(t)), by month, across the are shown in Table A.1. From 1955:01 to 2021:12 (both training and testing periods), the value of M(t) can be found in Figure A.3, complete 13 with NBER recession overlays to anecdotally link M(·) to this common marker of market health.
3.3 Preparing the Data A significant issue when working with so many characteristics to explain returns is the con-cept of multicollinearity, an effect which “muddies the waters” of the statistical relationship between the characteristics and returns. To combat this, the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF), as summarized by Velleman and Welsch (1981), is used to reduce multicollinearity by re-moving collinear characteristics in the cross-section, thereby increasing the orthogonality -thus increasing the parsimonious “coverage” of variance in the available dimensions - of the characteristics passed to the cross-sectional Adaptive LASSO estimation process discussed in Section 3.4. As is common practice, the VIF process used here removes cross-sectional characteristics whose collinearity is greater than a specified threshold, VIF = 5, leaving only the characteristics whose orthogonality relative to other characteristics will ensure a statistically significant model fit in the training estimations. Given the large dimensional-ity of the characteristic zoo used to the train the TRIAL model (87 characteristics in each cross-section), the VIF approach will ensure the Adaptive LASSO coefficient estimates used in the building of the time series “all-regime” specifications in Section 3.5 for the “good”, “neutral”, and “bad” market states are econometrically sound.
The VIF values are calculated by regressing a vector of characteristic values j on the cross-sectional set of all characteristics not j, then using the R2 statistic from that regression in VIFj,t = 1 1 −R2 j,t , (3.2) 14 where VIFj,t is the VIF value for anomaly j at time t and R2 j,t is the R2 statistic when regressing anomaly j at time t on the set of characteristics that are not j in t.
To reduce this collinearity in each cross-section, the TRIAL model calculates all VIF values for all characteristics in cross-section, removes the characteristic with the largest VIF value, then recalculates the VIF values for the remaining characteristics.
This process repeats until all characteristics in the cross-section have a VIF value less than 5, leaving only the characteristics which would best provide efficiency in the estimation process during model training (discussed in Section 3.4). Starting with 87 characteristics in each cross-section, this VIF process returns a mean of 59 characteristics for use in the cross-sectional models, and the number of available characteristics for use in the cross-sectional models is consistent throughout time. Also, this number of available characteristics is sizable enough to provide many viable options to explain returns in different market states. Figure A.4 shows the number of characteristics that exit this VIF process throughout the training period.
In the “all-state” panel of the training data, most characteristics used in the study show only mild collinearity, with a few large exceptions. (See Figure A.5 for the variance of VIF values for each characteristic across the entire training period.) For example, the BMf and BMDec characteristics are almost the same value at any point t for any firm i, as BMDec uses trailing-year-end market equity in its ratio calculation to the firms’ trailing-year year-end book-to-market ratio, where BMf uses the most recent market equity value. When t is the last month of the year, the values are equivalent. The DivOmit and DivInit characteristics are also very similar in concept (one measures when a firm starts their dividend, the other when it stops) so their collinearity is also high, but easily explained. Other characteristics with high collinearity are not as easily explained, however, such as Spinoff (a binary variable signifying whether a firm that has “spun-off” from another firm in the last two years), IndIPO (a binary variable signifying whether a firm that has had its IPO in the last 6-36 months), 15 FirmAge (number of months since the start of CRSP coverage), and ExchSwitch (a binary variable signifying whether a firm switched from AMEX or NASDAQ to NYSE within the past year, or from NASDAQ to AMEX within the past year). Nonetheless, the iterative VIF process described above will remove these “noisy” predictors.
When taking into account the variance of VIF values of the characteristics in each state (“good”, “neutral”, and “bad”; see Section 3.2 for details and definitions), the “neutral” state shows the most overall variance in VIF values across the characteristics with a log variance of 34.58. The “good” state panel’s log variance is 29.05, the “bad” state panel is 28.79, and the total training period (all states) is 34.01. (Figures A.6, A.7, and A.8 show this graphically.) VIF values in all three state panels, as well as the total training period panel, are heavily right-skewed; Table A.2 displays the summary of the distribution of each panel. The analysis of these variances relate to the hypothesis that different states contain idiosyncratic relationships between returns and characteristics because materially unique variances in VIF value in each state imply a unique contemporaneous relationship between characteristics in each state.
This is most evident in the lower variances in the “good” and “bad” states. In this way, in the language of Proposition 1, it shows that there could exist a set of unique characteristics in each state that explain returns better than the other characteristics available. These results, specifically the smaller amount of statistical “noise” in the characteristics that a lower variance in VIF values implies in the “good” and “bad” state, are generally consistent with the findings in Bianchi et al. (2019) around the sparsity of characteristics over time and the anecdotal intuition that excess returns are linked to “good” (“bad”) characteristics in “good” (“bad”) macroeconomic states, the central motivation of this thesis.
16 3.4 Building cross-sectional Models with Adaptive LASSO With the input characteristics vetted through the VIF process to ensure efficiency in the cross-sectional estimations, the cross-sectional models can now be created to determine which characteristics in each t explain excess returns in t + 1. Given the linear nature of the estimation framework and the large number of characteristics used in the cross-sectional estimations, the Adaptive LASSO regularization technique from Zou (2006) is used to re-duce the cross-sectional dimensionality of the model. Adaptive LASSO is an extension of the original LASSO technique introduced in Tibshirani (1996). The Adaptive LASSO is attractive in this context because it works to ensure consistency in the estimations, yet is still computationally efficient. The same technique is used in Freyberger et al. (2021) when calculating their cross-sectional estimates which is the motivation for using it here as the estimation context is similar in both studies.
In each cross-section in the training period, the Adaptive LASSO process runs an initial LASSO estimation over the characteristics that have a VIF larger than 5 in t, as discussed in Section 3.3. The penalty term, λ, in each t, is just the minimum λ found via k-fold validation, with k = 10. The inverse of the absolute value of those coefficients are then fed as the penalty weight vector into another LASSO estimation, which yields the final cross-sectional coefficients for each t. This is the standard approach for Adaptive LASSO as discussed in Zou (2006). The Adaptive LASSO is estimated as β = arg min β ∥y − J X j=1 xjβj∥2 + λ J X j=1 wj|βj|, (3.3) where the penalty weight vector w is the inverse of the absolute value of the initial LASSO estimates, w = 1/|βLASSO|.
17 The frequency of how often the characteristics are returned by the Adaptive LASSO pro-cedure over the training period, in other words how many times each characteristic has a statistically significant impact on t+1 returns, is shown in Figure A.9. It is with these char-acteristics that each regime time series model is estimated as described in the next section.
Of the 87 characteristics that are passed into the Adaptive LASSO process throughout the training period, 77 are chosen by Adaptive LASSO at least once. The 10 that were never chosen by Adaptive LASSO are outlined in Table A.3. It is of note that there are charac-teristics that one would think we be a part of the models, specifically the Size, Leverage, and Illiquidity characteristics, given their prominence in the literature and their intuitive ties to macroeconomic states. All three were removed given their high VIF values and were never passed on the Adaptive LASSO procedure. Using this procedure, these characteristics are “thrown away” as they never had a statistically significant explanatory relationship to t + 1 returns in any cross-section when estimated with Adaptive LASSO, although they are included in the “single-regime” benchmark panel model specification outlined in the Section 3.5 to ensure the data preparation step outlined here is statistically helpful in the expla-nation of excess returns. The inference here is that, while these characteristics are left of out the TRIAL model, their influence on returns is being captured by other characteristics which simply evince a stronger orthogonality relative to the remaining characteristics in the cross-section. If this fact were not true, their stronger orthogonality would allow them to remain in the characteristic set as defined by the methodology of the VIF process.
While there is slight variation across regimes for a given characteristic, the TRIAL model’s state regimes include a characteristic relatively uniformly from regime to regime. Notably, the characteristics that appear most often in the cross-sectional estimations are slanted to-wards technical characteristics such as BetaFP, STreversal, IntMom, Mom6m, or MReversal.
This behavior is consistent with findings from many sources in the literature, most notably 18 the seminal work from Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) and the follow up analysis discussed in Jegadeesh and Titman (2001). These technical characteristics, most specifically variants of momentum, show a strong influence on the expected return across all economic market states tested.
3.5 Creating Regime Specifications The critical step in the setup of the TRIAL model is the building of regime-specific times series models.
These linear models are what are used to determine, then estimate, the characteristic coefficients that are used to calculate the expected return for t + 1 given a value of γ(M(t)). There is a unique regime model specification for each γ(M(t)). Each regime model is a fixed-effects panel model, Ri,t+1 = αi + β1X1,t + · · · + βJXJ,t + ui,t+1, (3.4) where Ri,t+1 is the expected return in t + 1 for firm i, β1,...,J are the panel estimates for characteristics 1, . . . , J, X1,...,J,t are the characteristic values, and ui,t is the error term. It’s of note that, due to the fixed-effects nature of the model, each firm has its own intercept and thus only the characteristic estimates and the characteristic values are required to compute the expected return.
To conduct the estimation process, the independent variables in the model estimations for each regime specification are the characteristics that were chosen at least once by the Adap-tive LASSO estimations in the cross-section. (The “good” and “neutral” training panels evinced 77 characteristics of the original 87, the “bad” training panel evinced 74.) When these panel models are estimated, they are also “tuned” via backwards elimination: the full 19 set of characteristics is passed to them for an initial estimation, then the characteristic with the highest p-value is iteratively removed until the adjusted-R2 cannot be improved. This technique is used to enforce model parsimony.
For completeness, two other models are also estimated: a single-regime linear panel model using every unique characteristic chosen by the Adaptive LASSO output in all regimes (77 characteristics), and a single-regime linear panel model using all available characteristics (87 characteristics). In the estimations and in this thesis, these are called the “no regime” and “no preparation” models, respectively. With these latter two additional specifications, it can be tested “if regimes matter” and “if orthogonality optimization and dimension reduction in the cross-section matters.” The results of these additional specifications are presented in Section 4. The specifications and their estimates of all five models can be found in Table 3.1.
Of note for these specifications are a few critical points. First, the sheer volume of coefficients is large. The “good” state model contains 60 covariates, the “neutral” 55, and the “bad” 48. Slightly validating the assumption that the regimes as defined by market volatility offer estimation parsimony is the fact that the two test models contain even more covariates than the regime specifications with 63 and 72 covariates for the “no regime” and “no preparation” models, respectively. Although the number of covariates is high for each specification, the statistical significance of a vast majority of them are sufficient at the 10% or 5% level, indi-cating a strong relationship between the characteristics in the regime-specific specifications in t and the excess returns in t + 1.
Second, is the very low and consistent R2 statistic in each model. The “good” state model seems to perform the best at fitting the excess returns in t + 1 but, at only 1.6%, the fit is “poor”, at least in terms of R2. args.summary:
This is a doctoral dissertation by David Baines (Washington University in St. Louis, Olin Business School, Doctor of Business Administration in Finance, May 2023) that introduces a novel asset pricing model called the Time-Robust Iterative Adaptive LASSO (TRIAL) model. The dissertation committee consisted of Guofu Zhou (Chair), Brett Green, and Andreas Neuhierl.

**Core Concept:** The TRIAL model is a regime-switching linear asset pricing model conditioned on trailing market volatility. Instead of the traditional "one model fits all prices over time" approach, it maps specific linear model specifications to distinct macroeconomic conditions that are quantifiable and observable at time t. The conditioning function M(t) is a continuous function bounded from 0 to 1, based on the trailing 6-month standard deviation of the S&P 500 Total Return index, scaled between its historical minimum and maximum. M(t) is discretized into three states: "bad" (high volatility, M(t) < 0.5), "neutral" (0.5 ≤ M(t) ≤ 0.75), and "good" (low volatility, M(t) > 0.75). In the sample (1955:01–2021:12), 12% of months were "bad," 55% "neutral," and 33% "good."

**Methodology:** The estimation process involves: (1) computing M(t) across training and testing periods; (2) using Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) analysis to remove collinear characteristics (threshold VIF < 5), reducing the initial 87 characteristics to a mean of 59 per cross-section; (3) applying Adaptive LASSO (Zou 2006) in cross-sections to regularize models and select characteristics; (4) building regime-specific fixed-effects panel models with backward elimination for parsimony; and (5) calculating expected returns in t+1 for any firm i given M(t). The training period is 1955:01 to 2004:12 (50 years), and the testing period is 2005:01 to 2021:12 (17 years). Data came from the Chen and Zimmermann (2022) dataset (CRSP-Compustat, IBES, OptionMetrics, 13F filings), with the Freyberger et al. (2021) imputation version used. 1,543,713 stock-months in training and 804,583 in testing.

**Key Findings:**
- The TRIAL model produced a risk-adjusted mean monthly return of 1.36%, compared to 1.12% for the "no regime" model, 0.90% for the stock universe, 0.84% for S&P 500 TR, and 1.23% for the Fama-French 3-Factor Model (FF3).
- The TRIAL model had lower monthly volatility than FF3 (6.31% vs. 6.97%).
- Risk-adjusted Sharpe ratio of 0.81 for TRIAL out-of-sample, versus 0.19 for the total sample, 0.70 for S&P 500 TR, and 0.64 for FF3.
- Annualized risk-adjusted alpha was 13.75% out-of-sample, versus -2.04% for the total sample and 14.72% for FF3.
- The TRIAL model reduced heteroskedastic pricing error variance marginally relative to FF3 (RMSFE standard deviations of 5.25% vs. 5.64%).
- Of the 87 characteristics passed to Adaptive LASSO, 77 were chosen at least once. Size, Leverage, and Illiquidity characteristics were never used due to multicollinearity (high VIF), yet the model still explained prices adequately.
- Technical/momentum characteristics (BetaFP, STreversal, IntMom, Mom6m, MReversal) appeared most frequently, consistent with Jegadeesh and Titman (1993, 2001).
- The TRIAL model is asymmetric to size and value factors: it estimates big firms better than small firms and value firms better than growth firms. The "big firm" portfolio yielded a risk-adjusted mean monthly return of 2.38% and Sharpe ratio of 1.27 over the testing period.
- The "good" state model contains 60 covariates, "neutral" 55, "bad" 48, versus 63 for the "no regime" and 72 for the "no preparation" models.
- R² statistics are low (best is 1.6% for the "good" state model), but a vast majority of coefficients are statistically significant at the 10% or 5% level.

**Propositions and Motivation:** The thesis tests Proposition 1: that there exists a set of firm-level characteristics that explains prices better in "good" economic states and a distinct set that explains prices better in "bad" states. The work is distinguished from Bianchi et al. (2019) by focusing on whether characteristics consistently map to specific market states (for reliable out-of-sample forecasting) rather than persistent explanatory power or sparsity through business cycles. The author notes ongoing research aims to extend the model to an unsupervised, "online" context using Markov Decision Processes and neural networks.

# MSCI Barra US Equity Model (USE4) Methodology & Handbook PDF

MSCI Barra US Equity Model (USE4) is a US multi-factor equity risk model for portfolio risk analysis, factor exposure measurement, volatility forecasting, performance attribution, and portfolio optimization.

# Barra Risk Factor Analysis: Evaluate Investment Risks

![]()
![](https://www.investopedia.com/thmb/QjjDWJ6G9nd7haO4gxonDboJ0fg=/200x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc():format(webp)/wk_headshot_aug_2018_02__william_kenton-5bfc261446e0fb005118afc9.jpg)

Investopedia / Michela Buttignol

### Key Takeaways

## What Is the Barra Risk Factor Analysis?

The Barra Risk Factor Analysis, developed by Barra Inc., is a comprehensive multi-factor model that measures a security's risk relative to the market using over 40 data metrics. It accounts for industry risk, investment themes, and company-specific risk—equipping investors and portfolio managers with crucial insights for making informed investment decisions. This analysis prioritizes the tradeoff between risk and return, an essential principle in finance, by assessing factors like earnings growth and volatility.

## Components and Applications of Barra Risk Factor Analysis

[Investors](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/investor.asp) and [portfolio managers](https://www.investopedia.com/articles/wealth-management/021816/portfolio-manager-job-description-average-salary.asp) focus on investment risk when evaluating markets. Measuring this risk is crucial for deciding which assets to invest in, as it determines the potential return by the end of a trading cycle. A key financial principle is the [tradeoff between risk and return](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/r/riskreturntradeoff.asp).

Portfolio managers measure [investment risk](https://www.investopedia.com/financial-edge/0812/5-investing-risk-factors-and-how-to-avoid-them.aspx) by evaluating how broad factors affect asset performance. Factor models show how [common and unique factors](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/f/fundamentals.asp) drive a security's returns. These models help assess how much each factor affects a portfolio's returns. Factor models can be broken down into single-factor and multiple-factor models. One multi-factor model that can be used to measure portfolio risk is the Barra Risk Factor Analysis model.

Bar Rosenberg, of Barra Inc., pioneered the Barra Risk Factor Analysis, which is detailed in several academic works. It incorporates a number of factors in its model that can be used to predict and control risk. The multi-factor risk model uses a number of key fundamental factors that represent the features of an investment. Some of these factors include yield, earnings growth, volatility, liquidity, [momentum](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/m/momentum.asp), size, [price-earnings ratio](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/p/price-earningsratio.asp), leverage, and growth; factors which are used to describe the risk or returns of a portfolio or asset by moving from quantitative, but unspecified, factors to readily identifiable fundamental characteristics.

The Barra Risk Factor Analysis model measures a security's relative risk with a single [value-at-risk](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/var.asp) (VaR) number. This number represents a percentile rank between 0 and 100, with 0 being the least volatile and 100 being the most [volatile](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/volatility.asp), relative to the U.S. market. For instance, a security with a value-at-risk number of 80 is calculated to have a greater level of price volatility than 80% of securities in the market and its specific sector. So, if Amazon is assigned a VaR of 80, it means that its stock is more price volatile than 80% of the stock market or the sector in which the company operates.

## The Bottom Line

The Barra Risk Factor Analysis is a robust multi-factor model developed by Barra Inc. to assess the risk of securities. This model utilizes over 40 data metrics, including earnings growth and share turnover, to evaluate industry, thematic, and company-specific risks. By measuring a security's relative risk with a percentile-based value-at-risk (VaR) number, it provides investors and portfolio managers with critical insights into asset volatility in comparison to the broader market and specific sectors. Understanding these factors can aid in making informed investment decisions.

Please refer to the disclaimer at the end of this document RV May 2011 1 of 8 Product Insight Multiple Industry Allocations in USE3 December 2011 Multiple Industry Allocations in the Barra US Equity Model (USE3) The Impact of Multiple Industries on Risk Forecasts and Return Attribution December 2011 Shuang Li Introduction The Barra US Equity Model (USE3) utilizes a proprietary industry scheme which includes multiple industry membership. A stock can have up to five non-zero industry exposures which sum to 100%. The methodology is detailed in the Barra USE3 Model Handbook (1998). A similar approach is taken in the Barra Japan and Barra Mexico equity models. Multiple industry allocations provide more accurate risk prediction as well as more insight into sources of return. Additionally, Barra’s multiple industry models capture changes in a company’s risk profile as soon as new business activity is reported. In this paper, we examine the impact of accurately attributing multiple industry membership on risk forecasts. First we analyze the characteristics of equities with multiple industry allocations. We then demonstrate the impact of multiple industry exposures on risk forecasts. We focus on the inaccurate risk estimation that single industry allocation introduces to individual equity risk forecasts. Lastly we perform a case study on a stock with a varied history of industry membership - Ford Motor Company – analyzing its industry exposures, industry factor returns and their contribution to the return of Ford stock. Multiple Industry Exposures for US Equities The Barra USE3 Model Estimation Universe comprises a large, liquid segment of the US equity market, (see Barra USE3 Model Handbook (1998)). Table 1 shows the market capitalization distribution of USE3 Estimation Universe stocks with different number of industry memberships at the end of 2000, the end of 2005 and the end of June 2011. The tables show that a significant portion of the US equity market has exposure to multiple industries in the Barra USE3 model. As of December 29th, 2000, over 48% of stocks by market cap in the US equity market were exposed to more than one industry. 11 stocks had exposure to the maximum five industries. While that figure dropped slightly by June 30th, 2011 stocks that were exposed to more than one industry were larger market capitalization companies. args.summary:
This MSCI Product Insight (December 2011) examines the impact of multiple industry allocations in the Barra US Equity Model (USE3). The USE3 model assigns stocks to up to five non-zero industry exposures that sum to 100%, providing more accurate risk prediction and greater insight into sources of return compared to single-industry models. A similar approach is used in the Barra Japan and Mexico equity models.

Key findings from the paper:

**Market Distribution of Multiple Industry Exposures:**
- As of December 29, 2000, over 48% of US equity market cap was exposed to more than one industry, with 11 stocks having maximum five-industry exposure.
- By June 30, 2011, stocks with multiple industry exposures were predominantly larger market-capitalization companies, with the average capitalization of five-industry stocks exceeding $60bn.
- The number of stocks with 3-4 industry exposures approximately halved between 2000 and 2011, reflecting a consolidation trend.
- Stocks with four and five industry exposures were the most heavily traded (measured by mean 20-day volume), reflecting greater liquidity in large, diverse businesses.

**Impact on Risk Forecasts (analysis of nine stocks with five industry exposures as of June 30, 2011):**
- Calculating risk using multiple industries generally results in LOWER total risk forecasts, reflecting the diversification of these companies.
- Significant total risk differences were observed for Loews Corp (3.67% difference), Caterpillar (3.87%), and General Electric (3.57%).
- Industry risk differences were even larger, with Caterpillar showing a 4.71% difference, Loews 3.95%, and GE 3.44%.
- A single industry approach can mask small exposures to particularly volatile industries.

**Ford Motor Company Case Study:**
- Ford's industry exposures evolved from 1976-2011: solely Motor Vehicles & Parts (1976-1988), added Financial Services from 1988, and briefly Industrial Services from 2005-2006.
- Financial Services and Industrial Services were the better-performing industries over the period, while Motor Vehicles & Parts factor returns declined from the late 1990s to 2011, with a significant drop in late 2008.
- Ford's relatively small Financial Services exposure contributed positively to its return, while the large Motor Vehicles & Parts exposure contributed negatively after 2000.
- A single-industry model would incorrectly allocate the Financial Services contribution as stock-specific return.
- Ford's total cumulative return was positive over 1976-2011, driven primarily by Risk Index and stock-specific effects; industry effects were strongly positive through 1998 but became negative after 2008.

**Conclusion:** Multiple industry allocation provides greater insight into return drivers and better understanding of a firm's business activities. Industry exposure and risk play an important role in risk and return decomposition, and this sophistication differentiates Barra models from alternative single-industry approaches.

Models based upon an incomplete or misspecified factor set will necessary suffer from forecasting bias, and not surprisingly the design of a model’s factor structure plays a key role in the interpretation of both factor returns and factor risk decompositions. Historically, Barra’s equity models (including Barra US Equity Model (USE3) featured a set of distinct style and industry factors, customized for the specific market at hand. Daily style and industry factor returns are estimated by regressing a cross section of asset returns onto a set of asset-level style and industry exposures. The time-series of these daily estimated factor returns are ultimately used to build the factor covariance matrix which powers all Barra risk analytics.     industries industries styles styles i f X f X r (1) In USE3, style factor exposures are constructed such that the aggregate cap-weighted market (estimation universe) is style neutral. This implies that the return of the market is encapsulated fully by the industry factor set. Assuming that specific returns are normally distributed about 0, the weighted sum of the industry factor returns will equate to the return of the market. industry industry Market f X r  (2) The industry returns estimated in USE3 can be interpreted as the return of a 100% net long style neutral industry portfolio. As such, these industry factor portfolios are fully invested in the market and subject to general market volatility, in addition to industry specific dynamics. From a risk attribution perspective, since the biggest driver of equity volatility tends to be general market volatility, the industry factor set exhibits substantially higher volatility than the corresponding dollar-neutral style set, and tends to exhibit an elevated degree of correlation during periods of market turmoil. The newly launched Barra US Equity Model (USE4) model’s factor structure diverges from the preceding USE3 model in one primary way. USE4 introduces a market factor and a uses a constrained regression for factor return estimation. Each asset in the estimation universe has unit exposure to the market factor and a constraint is imposed on the regression such that the cap-weighted sum of all of the industry factor returns equals zero. Adding in a dummy intercept factor (to which all assets have exposure of 1) does not alter the regression fit in any way, and by forcing the cap-weighted industry factor returns sum to zero, we are able to effectively remove the collinearity in the factor structure (sum of all industry factor exposures= market factor exposure). This results in industry factor returns which can be interpreted as additional return net of the market return. For example, an industry return of -1% in USE4 would imply that that industry underperformed the market by 100 basis points, rather than denoting an absolute return. The industry factor portfolios in USE4 are dollar-neutral portfolios which capture the return of a pure industry relative to the market and net of style effects. At this point, it is worth noting that by adding the market factor return obtained from the constrained regression mentioned above to each of the estimated industry factor returns, we would result in industry factors returns that are analogous in spirit to the returns estimated via the unconstrained regression methodology used in the USE3 model. The introduction of the intercept does not change the fit of the model, and while disentangling market and industry specific returns can add additional insight, the real value of the USE4 factor structure lies in the ability to have greater responsiveness in the estimates of net long industry correlations. Recall that historically Barra has used a longer half-life for factor correlation estimates than for factor volatility estimates. The rationale here is that while it is desirable for the model to respond to market volatility in a timely fashion, it is essential that an adequate number of effective observations be used to estimate factor correlations to ensure that the factor covariance matrix remains well-conditioned. args.summary:
This MSCI Model Insights feature article (December 2011, by Stacy Cuffe) examines the introduction of a market factor in the Barra US Equity Model (USE4) and why it matters for risk forecasting, compared to the predecessor USE3 model.

Key points:
- In USE3, style factor exposures were constructed so the aggregate cap-weighted market was style neutral, with market returns fully encapsulated by the industry factor set. Industry factor returns could be interpreted as returns of 100% net long style-neutral industry portfolios, subject to general market volatility in addition to industry-specific dynamics.
- USE4 diverges from USE3 primarily by introducing a market factor and using a constrained regression for factor return estimation. Each asset has unit exposure to the market factor, and a constraint is imposed so the cap-weighted sum of industry factor returns equals zero. This removes collinearity (sum of industry exposures = market factor exposure).
- As a result, USE4 industry factor returns can be interpreted as additional returns net of the market return (e.g., an industry return of -1% means the industry underperformed the market by 100 basis points). Industry factor portfolios in USE4 are dollar-neutral portfolios capturing pure industry returns relative to the market and net of style effects.
- Adding the market factor return to each estimated industry factor return in USE4 would yield industry factor returns analogous to those estimated in USE3, confirming that adding the intercept doesn't change model fit.
- The real value of the USE4 structure lies in greater responsiveness in estimates of net long industry correlations. Barra historically used a longer half-life for factor correlation estimates than for volatility estimates to keep the factor covariance matrix well-conditioned (essential for portfolio optimization), but this made correlations slow to respond to market changes.
- During the fall of 2008, when realized industry correlations skyrocketed, the model estimated without a market factor was slow to perceive the change, and correlation levels stayed elevated or kept trending upward even after relative market tranquility returned.
- The correlation between two net long industries is a direct function of the volatility of the market factor, which is estimated with a shorter half-life and responds to volatility changes much more quickly. The market factor volatility is also subject to scaling based on Barra's Volatility Regime Adjustment factor.
- In the fall of 2008, industry correlation estimates based on market factor volatility reflected the upward trend almost immediately and have since begun to subside, while those based on traditional correlation of net long industry returns trended upward slowly and didn't peak until mid-2011.
- The gradual evolution of correlations in the old model led to a period of risk underestimation in 2009, followed by overestimation lingering for the subsequent two years. The market factor in USE4 mitigates this effect and provides timelier risk forecasts.
args.key_excerpts: "Models based upon an incomplete or misspecified factor set will necessary suffer from forecasting bias, and not surprisingly the design of a model's factor structure plays a key role in the interpretation of both factor returns and factor risk decompositions."

Barra's Multiple-Factor Models for risk (e.g. USE3, USE4, CNE5) are much like those models used in empirical asset pricing studies such as CAPM, Fama-French three-factor model and others.

I'm not very sure about the deep-seated differences between the Barra models and asset pricing models from the theoretical asset pricing lens, though I know what they are doing mathematically.

As we all know, when we test market efficiency in the framework of Fama and MacBeth (1973), we simply add predetermined explanatory variables to the month-by-month cross-section regressions of returns on market beta (**i.e., only market beta is controlled in the regression**). If all differences in expected return are explained by beta, the average slopes on the additional variables should not be reliably different from zero. Otherwise, we say we find a "market anomaly".

My question is, when we add other variables to the month-by-month regressions, do we need to **control those variables used in Barra Models as well as market beta**? Does it suffices to only include market beta as control variable for the search of market anomalies? Is there any academic journal article that uses Barra models' variables as control variables?

This might be better laid out as a comment, but I would like to quote _Active Portfolio Management by Grinold & Kahn (2000)_ (Expected Returns and the APT, Chapter 7) in support of @nbbo2's (and the others) comment on Barra being a model of covariance and not of returns:

> The Barra risk model was constructed to help portfolio managers control risk, not to explained expected returns. However, it does attempt to capture those aspects of the market that cause some groups of stocks to behave differently from others.

In that, the primary purpose of the Barra risk models serve to (1) decompose the risk and explain the variation in returns and (2) predict the risks of these factors themselves.

EDIT - to Mark's Question

My opinion as to why the Barra risk models that require returns decomposition to decompose risk are taken as risk models and not returns models (as compared to common asset pricing models such as the CAPM, APT, FFX etc.), is that risk models take the realized/ex-post returns as the "correct" returns, and their main goal is to explain the systematic variation in the cross-section of returns across assets i.e. risk decomposition through the use of structural factors.

This is different from asset pricing models that do not assume the realized/ex-post returns are "correct" and much rather determine what is the "correct" equilibrium rate of return. This is also why asset pricing models are known as equilibrium pricing models. The assets with returns or prices that deviate from these equilibrium rates of return are subject to a form of price convergence called risk arbitrage (Investments by Bodie, Kane and Marcus). These rates of return may not always exist due to limits to arbitrage in the real world...

To summarize, I think the goal of the model is what classifies the Barra risk models to be called risk rather than return models.

Hopefully I understood your question correctly.

args.summary:
This is a Quantitative Finance Stack Exchange question asking whether BARRA's Multiple-Factor Risk models (USE3, USE4, CNE5) are rational asset pricing models. The questioner notes that BARRA models are mathematically similar to empirical asset pricing models like CAPM and Fama-French, and asks whether variables used in BARRA models need to be controlled for (alongside market beta) when searching for market anomalies in Fama-MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions, and whether any academic journal articles use BARRA model variables as control variables.

The question was asked by user "Gödel" on September 29, 2019, and edited by Richard Hardy on March 12, 2025. It was viewed about 1,000 times and has two answers.

Key answers and insights:
1. **Comment by nbbo2**: BARRA's model is a model of covariance (not of returns), used to predict portfolio volatility, whereas Fama-French is a model of returns used to assess whether portfolio performance exceeds model predictions.

2. **Answer by caio teles (Oct 7, 2024)**: BARRA's risk factor analysis is not an asset pricing model but a tool to manage risk. Asset pricing models aim to explain average returns of assets/portfolios, and factors must carry premium to explain distortion of mean returns.

3. **Answer by KaiSqDist (Mar 29, 2025)**: Quoting Grinold & Kahn's "Active Portfolio Management" (2000), Chapter 7: "The Barra risk model was constructed to help portfolio managers control risk, not to explain expected returns. However, it does attempt to capture those aspects of the market that cause some groups of stocks to behave differently from others." The primary purposes are to (1) decompose risk and explain variation in returns, and (2) predict the risks of these factors themselves. The key distinction is that risk models treat realized/ex-post returns as "correct" and focus on systematic variation decomposition, while asset pricing (equilibrium) models determine what the "correct" equilibrium rate of return should be, with deviations subject to risk arbitrage.

Discussion in comments highlights that BARRA models involve monthly returns on the left-hand side and 68 exposures (13 risk characteristics + 55 industry weights) times factor return coefficients on the right-hand side, and that the model is considered a risk model because it uses realized returns as correct and focuses on factor return estimation rather than prediction. References to Rudd and Clasing's text on BARRA model details and a JSTOR article (jstor.org/stable/2330027) by the original BARRA model developer were also mentioned.
args.key_excerpts: "Barra's model is a model of covariance (not of returns). You would use it to predict the volatility of a portfolio. Fama French is a model of returns, it is used to assess if the performance of your portfolio exceeds the prediction of their model." — nbbo2

This is a CFA® Level III lesson (Part II) on the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS®), presented by instructor Jim from AnalystPrep (posted January 11, 2026, ~880 views). The lesson covers composite construction, return calculations, discretion rules, reporting requirements, linking past performance, and verification.

KEY TOPICS COVERED:

1. **Composite Return Calculation Methods (3 methods):**
   - **Beginning Assets Weighting Method**: Simple weighted average using beginning-of-period asset values as weights (like WACC calculation)
   - **Beginning Assets + Weighted Cash Flows (Modified Dietz)**: Accounts for external cash flows during the period
   - **Aggregate Return Method**: Treats the entire composite as if it were one individual security/portfolio
   - All three methods produce nearly identical results (e.g., ~15% in the example), and the institute requires disclosure of whichever method is used but doesn't prefer one over another.
   - Worked example: Portfolios A, B, C with beginning assets of $50, $40, and $60 (total $150), ending at $18,590. Modified Dietz cash flow weighting factors (71%, 48%, 35%) and returns of 9.11% (A), ~6.7% (B), and ~26.9% (C) were demonstrated.

2. **Discretion & Composite Construction Rules:**
   - All actual, fee-paying, discretionary segregated accounts MUST be included in at least one composite
   - Non-fee-paying discretionary accounts MAY be included but require additional disclosure
   - Non-discretionary segregated accounts and pooled funds must NOT be included
   - No model portfolios or simulations allowed in composites
   - Client restrictions don't automatically make a portfolio non-discretionary—only if they materially impact strategy execution
   - The definition of "material" is up to each manager's discretion
   - Patterns of significant external cash flows may render a portfolio non-discretionary
   - A clearly written definition of discretion must be applied consistently

3. **Composite Construction Details:**
   - Hierarchical definition: Investment mandate → Asset classes → Style → Benchmarks → Risk/return characteristics
   - New portfolios included at the beginning of the first full month after being placed under manager control (e.g., control on March 15th means inclusion starts April 1st)
   - Terminated portfolios: excluded after the end of the last full month (e.g., termination effective June 30th means included only through May 31st)
   - Portfolio switching between composites requires documented change in mandate/objective/strategy
   - Temporary removal allowed for significant cash flows; minimum asset levels must be applied consistently

4. **Reporting Requirements:**
   - At least 5 years of performance history (built up year-by-year if firm is newer), extending to 10 years
   - Required elements: composite & benchmark returns, number of portfolios (if 6 or more), composite assets, total firm assets
   - 3-year annualized ex-post standard deviation of composite AND benchmark (required)
   - Internal dispersion measures (high-low range, equally weighted or asset-weighted standard deviation) to convey risk/variability to clients

5. **Linking Past Performance:**
   - When firms merge/acquire, past performance may be linked if: all decision makers are substantially employed by the new/acquiring firm (not just 2 of 13), the firm possesses supporting records, and there's no break in the track record

6. **Verification (Recommended, NOT Required):**
   - Performed by qualified, independent third-party verifier
   - Firm-wide scope only—cannot verify a single composite, pooled fund, or portfolio
   - Process: planning (understand firm operations/policies), sampling (considering number of composites, total assets, years), and testing (recordkeeping, recalculation of returns, composite construction, GIPS report accuracy, marketing materials consistency)
   - Verifiers must confirm portfolio holdings/income/cash flows are evidenced by independent documentation (e.g., brokerage statements)
   - Benefits: credibility, improved internal processes, higher quality performance presentations
   - Firms failing to meet all requirements may not claim compliance

The instructor recommends working through all 23 practice problems at the end of the reading (~46 minutes) and emphasizes knowing the math even though LOS statements say "explain" rather than "calculate."
