This is the Fourth Edition (December 17, 1996) of the RiskMetrics Technical Document, a joint publication by J.P. Morgan and Reuters. RiskMetrics is a set of tools for measuring market risk within the "Value-at-Risk" (VaR) framework, comprising: (1) market risk measurement methodologies, (2) volatility and correlation data sets, and (3) software systems implementing these methods. It covers portfolios of fixed income instruments, equities, foreign exchange, commodities, and derivatives across over 30 countries.

**Purpose and Background:**
The methodology is made publicly available to promote transparency of market risks, establish a benchmark for market risk measurement, and provide clients with sound risk management advice. J.P. Morgan launched RiskMetrics in October 1994. In June 1996, J.P. Morgan signed an agreement with Reuters to cooperate on a new, more powerful version. J.P. Morgan retains responsibility for methodology development, while Reuters handles data sourcing, production, and distribution.

**Value-at-Risk Definition:**
VaR measures the maximum potential change in value of a portfolio with a given probability over a pre-set horizon. A worked example: a USD 100 million DEM/USD position with a 0.565% daily standard deviation yields a VaR of 1.65σ = 0.932%, or $932,000 over a 24-hour period at 95% confidence. A second example combining interest rate risk (10-year German bond, 0.605% std dev) and FX risk with correlation of −0.27 produces a diversified VaR of $1.168 million using the formula VaR = √(σ²_interest_rate + σ²_FX + 2ρ·σ_IR·σ_FX).

**Key Methodology Components:**
- Risk measurement framework (Part I) covering the practical application of risk estimation
- Statistics of financial market returns (Part II) including the RiskMetrics model of financial returns as a modified random walk, EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) forecasting methodology, and optimal decay factor determination
- Risk modeling of financial instruments (Part III) with a 3-step process: (1) identifying exposures and cash flows, (2) mapping cash flows onto RiskMetrics vertices (1m, 3m, 6m, 12m, 2yr, 3yr, 4yr, 5yr, 7yr, 9yr, 10yr, 15yr, 20yr, 30yr), and (3) computing VaR
- RiskMetrics data sets (Part IV) covering data sources, time series, and file formats
- Backtesting and performance assessment (Part V)
- Appendices covering conditional normality tests, delta-gamma accuracy, BIS regulatory requirements, and Internet access

**Handling Nonlinear Positions:**
RiskMetrics offers two methods for options/nonlinear risk: (1) an analytical approximation using Taylor series expansion (delta approximation and delta-gamma approximation, incorporating the option's gamma for curvature), and (2) structured Monte Carlo simulation. The analytical approach approximates value changes, while Monte Carlo fully revalues portfolios under scenarios. Both use the same RiskMetrics volatility and correlation estimates.

**What's New in the Fourth Edition:**
- Expanded framework for options risk analysis without time-consuming simulations
- Better information on tails of distributions (accounting for non-normal distributions)
- Data synchronization algorithm for products trading in different time zones
- New markets added: additional FX, fixed income, and equity data for Southeast Asia and Latin America
- Price volatility definition changed to a total return concept
- Revised mapping algorithms and equity portfolio risk estimation techniques
- Excel add-in published for importing volatilities and correlations directly into spreadsheets

# The Role of RiskMetrics in Analyzing Value at Risk (VaR)

![Investopedia logo ]()
![Investopedia logo ](https://www.investopedia.com/thmb/EB2rZE10GSPEE_DCb4nBdtQP7pA=/200x200/filters:no_upscale():max_bytes(150000):strip_icc():format(webp)/Group1805-3b9f749674f0434184ef75020339bd35.jpg)

### Key Takeaways

Get personalized, AI-powered answers built on 27+ years of trusted expertise.

RiskMetrics is a methodology that an investor can use to calculate the value at risk (VaR) of a portfolio of investments.

Launched in 1994 by J.P. Morgan, RiskMetrics was upgraded by the company in partnership with Reuters in 1996. The companies teamed up to make the data used in RiskMetrics widely available to individual investors. RiskMetrics is now owned by MSCI.

The aim of RiskMetrics is to improve the transparency of market risks, create a benchmark for measuring them, and provide investors with better information on managing market risks.

## Understanding RiskMetrics Methodology for VaR

VaR is, at its core, focuses on the potential downside risk of an investment.

The RiskMetrics methodology for calculating [VaR](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/var.asp) assumes that a portfolio or any asset's returns follow a normal distribution over time. Following [J.P. Morgan](https://www.investopedia.com/articles/markets/020916/analyzing-porters-five-forces-jpmorgan-chase-jpm.asp)'s and [Reuters](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/r/reuters.asp)' release of its [volatility](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/volatility.asp) and correlation data sets, the [variance](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/v/variance.asp)-covariance method used to calculate the VaR became an industry standard, as RiskMetrics intended.

For example, the profit and loss distribution of an investment portfolio is assumed to be normally distributed. Using the RiskMetrics methodology to calculate the VaR, the [portfolio manager](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/p/portfoliomanager.asp) must first select a confidence level and a lookback period.

Suppose the lookback period selected is one trading year, or 252 days. The confidence level selected is 95%, and the corresponding [z-score](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/z/zscore.asp) value must be multiplied by the [standard deviation](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/standarddeviation.asp) of the portfolio.

### Important

VaR is essentially a measurement of the potential downside risk of an investment.

The actual daily standard deviation of the portfolio over one trading year is 3.67%. The z-score for 95% is 1.645.

The VaR for the portfolio, under the 95% confidence level, is -6.04% (-1.645 \* 3.67%). Therefore, there is a 5% probability that the loss of the portfolio, over the given [time horizon](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/t/timehorizon.asp), will exceed 6.04%.

## Applying RiskMetrics to Calculate Value at Risk

Another method to calculate the VaR of a portfolio is to use the correlations and standard deviations of stock returns provided by RiskMetrics. This method also assumes that stock returns follow a [normal distribution](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/n/normaldistribution.asp).

The first step to calculating VaR is taking the square of the allocated funds for the first asset, multiplied by the square of its standard deviation, and adding that value to the square of the allocated funds for the second asset multiplied by the square of the second asset's standard deviation.

That value is then added to two multiplied by the allocated funds for the first asset multiplied by the allocated funds for the second asset multiplied by the first and second asset's volatility and the [correlation](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/correlation.asp) between the two assets.

For example, suppose a portfolio has two assets with $5 million allocated to stock ABC and $8 million allocated to stock DEF. Respectively, the price volatility of stock ABC and stock DEF is 2.98% and 1.67% for a one-day period.

The correlation between the two stocks is 0.67. The value at risk is $258,310.93 (sqrt(($5 million)^2 \* (0.0298)^2 + ($8 million)^2 \* (0.0167)^2 + (2 \* $5 million \* $8 million \* 0.0298 \* 0.0167 \* 0.067)).

FRBNY ECONOMIC POLICY REVIEW / APRIL 1996 39 R Evaluation of Value-at-Risk Models Using Historical Data Darryll Hendricks esearchers in the ﬁeld of ﬁnancial economics have long recognized the importance of mea-suring the risk of a portfolio of ﬁnancial assets or securities. Indeed, concerns go back at least four decades, when Markowitz’s pioneering work on portfolio selection (1959) explored the appropriate deﬁ-nition and measurement of risk. In recent years, the growth of trading activity and instances of ﬁnancial market instability have prompted new studies underscoring the need for market participants to develop reliable risk mea-surement techniques.1 One technique advanced in the literature involves the use of “value-at-risk” models. These models measure the market, or price, risk of a portfolio of ﬁnancial assets—that is, the risk that the market value of the portfolio will decline as a result of changes in interest rates, foreign exchange rates, equity prices, or commodity prices. Value-at-risk models aggregate the several components of price risk into a single quantitative measure of the potential for losses over a speciﬁed time horizon. These models are clearly appealing because they convey the market risk of the entire portfolio in one number. Moreover, value-at-risk measures focus directly, and in dollar terms, on a major reason for assessing risk in the ﬁrst place—a loss of portfolio value. Recognition of these models by the ﬁnancial and regulatory communities is evidence of their growing use.
For example, in its recent risk-based capital proposal (1996a), the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision endorsed the use of such models, contingent on important qualitative and quantitative standards. In addition, the Bank for International Settlements Fisher report (1994) urged ﬁnancial intermediaries to disclose measures of value-at-risk publicly. The Derivatives Policy Group, afﬁli-ated with six large U.S. securities ﬁrms, has also advocated the use of value-at-risk models as an important way to measure market risk. The introduction of the RiskMetrics database compiled by J.P. Morgan for use with third-party value-at-risk software also highlights the growing use of these models by ﬁnancial as well as nonﬁnancial ﬁrms.
Clearly, the use of value-at-risk models is increas-The views expressed in this article are those of the authors and do not necessarily reﬂect the position of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York or the Federal Reserve System.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York provides no warranty, express or implied, as to the accuracy, timeliness, com-pleteness, merchantability, or ﬁtness for any particular purpose of any information contained in documents produced and provided by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York in any form or manner whatsoever.
40 FRBNY ECONOMIC POLICY REVIEW / APRIL 1996 ing, but how well do they perform in practice? This article explores this question by applying value-at-risk models to 1,000 randomly chosen foreign exchange portfolios over the period 1983-94. We then use nine criteria to evaluate model performance. We consider, for example, how closely risk measures produced by the models correspond to actual portfolio outcomes.
We begin by explaining the three most common categories of value-at-risk models—equally weighted mov-ing average approaches, exponentially weighted moving average approaches, and historical simulation approaches.
Although within these three categories many different approaches exist, for the purposes of this article we select ﬁve approaches from the ﬁrst category, three from the second, and four from the third.
By employing a simulation technique using these twelve value-at-risk approaches, we arrived at measures of price risk for the portfolios at both 95 percent and 99 per-cent conﬁdence levels over one-day holding periods. The con-ﬁdence levels specify the probability that losses of a portfolio will be smaller than estimated by the risk mea-sure. Although this article considers value-at-risk models only in the context of market risk, the methodology is fairly general and could in theory address any source of risk that leads to a decline in market values. An important lim-itation of the analysis, however, is that it does not consider portfolios containing options or other positions with non-linear price behavior.2 We choose several performance criteria to reﬂect the practices of risk managers who rely on value-at-risk measures for many purposes. Although important differ-ences emerge across value-at-risk approaches with respect to each criterion, the results indicate that none of the twelve approaches we examine is superior on every count.
In addition, as the results make clear, the choice of conﬁ-dence level—95 percent or 99 percent—can have a sub-stantial effect on the performance of value-at-risk approaches.
INTRODUCTION TO VALUE-AT-RISK MODELS A value-at-risk model measures market risk by determin-ing how much the value of a portfolio could decline over a given period of time with a given probability as a result of changes in market prices or rates. For example, if the given period of time is one day and the given probability is 1 percent, the value-at-risk measure would be an estimate of the decline in the portfolio value that could occur with a 1 percent probability over the next trading day. In other words, if the value-at-risk measure is accurate, losses greater than the value-at-risk measure should occur less than 1 percent of the time.
The two most important components of value-at-risk models are the length of time over which market risk is to be measured and the conﬁdence level at which market risk is measured. The choice of these components by risk manag-ers greatly affects the nature of the value-at-risk model.
The time period used in the deﬁnition of value-at-risk, often referred to as the “holding period,” is discretion-ary. Value-at-risk models assume that the portfolio’s com-position does not change over the holding period. This assumption argues for the use of short holding periods because the composition of active trading portfolios is apt to change frequently. Thus, this article focuses on the widely used one-day holding period.3 Value-at-risk measures are most often expressed as percentiles corresponding to the desired conﬁdence level.
For example, an estimate of risk at the 99 percent conﬁ-dence level is the amount of loss that a portfolio is expected to exceed only 1 percent of the time. It is also known as a 99th percentile value-at-risk measure because the amount is the 99th percentile of the distribution of potential losses on the portfolio.4 In practice, value-at-risk estimates are calculated from the 90th to 99.9th percen-tiles, but the most commonly used range is the 95th to 99th percentile range. Accordingly, the text charts and the Clearly, the use of value-at-risk models is increasing, but how well do they perform in practice?
FRBNY ECONOMIC POLICY REVIEW / APRIL 1996 41 tables in the appendix report simulation results for each of these percentiles.
THREE CATEGORIES OF VALUE-AT-RISK APPROACHES Although risk managers apply many approaches when cal-culating portfolio value-at-risk models, almost all use past data to estimate potential changes in the value of the port-folio in the future. Such approaches assume that the future will be like the past, but they often deﬁne the past quite differently and make different assumptions about how markets will behave in the future.
The ﬁrst two categories we examine, “variance-covariance” value-at-risk approaches,5 assume normality and serial independence and an absence of nonlinear posi-tions such as options.6 The dual assumption of normality and serial independence creates ease of use for two reasons.
First, normality simpliﬁes value-at-risk calculations because all percentiles are assumed to be known multiples of the standard deviation. Thus, the value-at-risk calcula-tion requires only an estimate of the standard deviation of the portfolio’s change in value over the holding period.
Second, serial independence means that the size of a price move on one day will not affect estimates of price moves on any other day. Consequently, longer horizon standard devi-ations can be obtained by multiplying daily horizon stan-dard deviations by the square root of the number of days in the longer horizon. When the assumptions of normality and serial independence are made together, a risk manager can use a single calculation of the portfolio’s daily horizon standard deviation to develop value-at-risk measures for any given holding period and any given percentile.
The advantages of these assumptions, however, must be weighed against a large body of evidence suggest-ing that the tails of the distributions of daily percentage changes in ﬁnancial market prices, particularly foreign exchange rates, will be fatter than predicted by the normal distribution.7 This evidence calls into question the appeal-ing features of the normality assumption, especially for value-at-risk measurement, which focuses on the tails of the distribution. Questions raised by the commonly used normality assumption are highlighted throughout the article.
In the sections below, we describe the individual features of the two variance-covariance approaches to value-at-risk measurement.
EQUALLY WEIGHTED MOVING AVERAGE APPROACHES The equally weighted moving average approach, the more straightforward of the two, calculates a given portfolio’s variance (and thus, standard deviation) using a ﬁxed amount of historical data.8 The major difference among equally weighted moving average approaches is the time frame of the ﬁxed amount of data.9 Some approaches employ just the most recent ﬁfty days of historical data on the assumption that only very recent data are relevant to estimating potential movements in portfolio value. Other approaches assume that large amounts of data are necessary to estimate potential movements accurately and thus rely on a much longer time span—for example, ﬁve years.
The calculation of portfolio standard deviations using an equally weighted moving average approach is (1) , where denotes the estimated standard deviation of the portfolio at the beginning of day t. The parameter k speci-ﬁes the number of days included in the moving average (the “observation period”), xs, the change in portfolio value on day s, and , the mean change in portfolio value. Fol-lowing the recommendation of Figlewski (1994), is always assumed to be zero.10 Consider ﬁve sets of value-at-risk measures with periods of 50, 125, 250, 500, and 1,250 days, or about two months, six months, one year, two years, and ﬁve years of historical data. Using three of these ﬁve periods of time, Chart 1 plots the time series of value-at-risk measures at biweekly intervals for a single ﬁxed portfolio of spot for-eign exchange positions from 1983 to 1994.11 As shown, the ﬁfty-day risk measures are prone to rapid swings. Con-versely, the 1,250-day risk measures are more stable over long periods of time, and the behavior of the 250-day risk measures lies somewhere in the middle.

HISTORICAL SIMULATION APPROACHES The third category of value-at-risk approaches is similar to the equally weighted moving average category in that it relies on a speciﬁc quantity of past historical observations (the observation period). Rather than using these observa-tions to calculate the portfolio’s standard deviation, how-ever, historical simulation approaches use the actual percentiles of the observation period as value-at-risk mea-sures. For example, for an observation period of 500 days, the 99th percentile historical simulation value-at-risk mea-sure is the sixth largest loss observed in the sample of 500 outcomes (because the 1 percent of the sample that should exceed the risk measure equates to ﬁve losses).
In other words, for these approaches, the 95th and 99th percentile value-at-risk measures will not be constant multiples of each other. Moreover, value-at-risk measures for holding periods other than one day will not be ﬁxed multiples of the one-day value-at-risk measures. Historical simulation approaches do not make the assumptions of normality or serial independence. However, relaxing these assumptions also implies that historical simulation approaches do not easily accommodate translations between multiple percentiles and holding periods.

In particular, very abrupt shifts occur in the 99th percentile measures for the 125-day historical simulation approach.

SIMULATIONS OF VALUE-AT-RISK MODELS This section provides an introduction to the simulation results derived by applying twelve value-at-risk approaches to 1,000 randomly selected foreign exchange portfolios and assessing their behavior along nine performance criteria (see box). This simulation design has several advantages.
First, by simulating the performance of each value-at-risk approach for a long period of time (approximately twelve years of daily data) and across a large number of portfolios, we arrive at a clear picture of how value-at-risk models would actually have performed for linear foreign exchange portfolios over this time span. Second, the results give insight into the extent to which portfolio composition or choice of sample period can affect results.
It is important to emphasize, however, that nei-ther the reported variability across portfolios nor variabil-ity over time can be used to calculate suitable standard errors. The appropriate standard errors for these simulation results raise difﬁcult questions. The results aggregate information across multiple samples, that is, across the 1,000 portfolios. Because the results for one portfolio are not independent of the results for other portfolios, we can-not easily determine the total amount of information pro-The simulation results provide a relatively complete picture of the performance of selected value-at-risk approaches in estimating the market risk of a large number of portfolios.
FRBNY ECONOMIC POLICY REVIEW / APRIL 1996 45 vided by the simulations. Furthermore, many of the performance criteria we consider do not have straightfor-ward standard error formulas even for single samples.15 These stipulations imply that it is not possible to use the simulation results to accept or reject speciﬁc statistical hypotheses about these twelve value-at-risk approaches. Moreover, the results should not in any way be taken as indicative of the results that would be obtained for portfolios including other ﬁnancial market assets, spanning other time periods, or looking forward. Finally, this article does not contribute substantially to the ongoing debate about the appropriate approach to or interpretation of “backtesting” in conjunction with value-at-risk model-ing.16 Despite these limitations, the simulation results do provide a relatively complete picture of the performance of selected value-at-risk approaches in estimating the market risk of a large number of linear foreign exchange portfolios over the period 1983-94.
For each of the nine performance criteria, Charts 4-12 provide a visual sense of the simulation results for 95th and 99th percentile risk measures. In each chart, the verti-cal axis depicts a relevant range of the performance crite-rion under consideration (value-at-risk approaches are arrayed horizontally across the chart). Filled circles depict the average results across the 1,000 portfolios, and the boxes drawn for each value-at-risk approach depict the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 95th percentiles of the distri-bution of the results across the 1,000 portfolios.17 In some charts, a horizontal line is drawn to highlight how the results compare with an important point of reference.
Simulation results are also presented in tabular form in the appendix.
DATA AND SIMULATION METHODOLOGY This article analyzes twelve value-at-risk approaches. These include ﬁve equally weighted moving average approaches (50 days, 125 days, 250 days, 500 days, 1,250 days); three expo-nentially weighted moving average approaches (λ=0.94, λ=0.97, λ=0.99); and four historical simulation approaches (125 days, 250 days, 500 days, 1,250 days).
The data consist of daily exchange rates (bid prices collected at 4:00 p.m. New York time by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York) against the U.S. dollar for the following eight currencies: British pound, Canadian dollar, Dutch guil-der, French franc, German mark, Italian lira, Japanese yen, and Swiss franc. The historical sample covers the period January 1, 1978, to January 18, 1995 (4,255 days).
Through a simulation methodology, we attempt to determine how each value-at-risk approach would have per-formed over a realistic range of portfolios containing the eight currencies over the sample period. The simulation methodol-ogy consists of ﬁve steps: 1.
Select a random portfolio of positions in the eight curren-cies. This step is accomplished by drawing the position in each currency from a uniform distribution centered on zero. In other words, the portfolio space is a uniformly distributed eight dimensional cube centered on zero.1 2.
Calculate the value-at-risk estimates for the random port-folio chosen in step one using the twelve value-at-risk approaches for each day in the sample—day 1,251 to day 4,255. In each case, we draw the historical data from the 1,250 days of historical data preceding the date for which the calculation is made. For example, the ﬁfty-day equally weighted moving average estimate for a given date would be based on the ﬁfty days of historical data preceding the given date.
3.
Calculate the change in the portfolio’s value for each day in the sample—again, day 1,251 to day 4,255. Within the article, these values are referred to as the ex post port-folio results or outcomes.
4.
Assess the performance of each value-at-risk approach for the random portfolio selected in step one by comparing the value-at-risk estimates generated by step two with the actual outcomes calculated in step three.
5.
Repeat steps one through four 1,000 times and tabulate the results.

MEAN RELATIVE BIAS The ﬁrst performance criterion we examine is whether the different value-at-risk approaches produce risk measures of similar average size. To ensure that the comparison is not inﬂuenced by the scale of each simulated portfolio, we use a four-step procedure to generate scale-free measures of the relative sizes for each simulated portfolio.
First, we calculate value-at-risk measures for each of the twelve approaches for the portfolio on each sample date. Second, we average the twelve risk measures for each date to obtain the average risk measure for that date for the portfolio. Third, we calculate the percentage difference between each approach’s risk measure and the average risk measure for each date. We refer to these ﬁgures as daily rel-ative bias ﬁgures because they are relative only to the average risk measure across the twelve approaches rather than to any external standard. Fourth, we average the daily relative biases for a given value-at-risk approach across all sample dates to obtain the approach’s mean relative bias for the portfolio.
Intuitively, this procedure results in a measure of size for each value-at-risk approach that is relative to the average of all twelve approaches. The mean relative bias for a portfolio is independent of the scale of the simulated portfolio because each of the daily relative bias calculations on which it is based is also scale-independent. This inde-pendence is achieved because all of the value-at-risk approaches we examine here are proportional to the scale of the portfolio’s positions. For example, a doubling of the scale of the portfolio would result in a doubling of the value-at-risk measures for each of the twelve approaches.
Mean relative bias is measured in percentage terms, so that a value of 0.10 implies that a given value-at-risk approach is 10 percent larger, on average, than the average of all twelve approaches. The simulation results suggest that differences in the average size of 95th percen-Actual 99th percentiles for the foreign exchange portfolios considered in this article tend to be larger than the normal distribution would predict.

ANNUALIZED PERCENTAGE VOLATILITY The third performance criterion we review is the tendency of the risk measures to ﬂuctuate over time for the same portfolio. For each portfolio and each value-at-risk approach, we calculate the annualized percentage volatility by ﬁrst taking the standard deviation of the day-to-day percentage changes in the risk measures over the sample period. Second, we put the result on an annualized basis by multiplying this standard deviation by the square root of 250, the number of trading days in a typical calendar year.
We complete the second step simply to make the results comparable with volatilities as they are often expressed in the marketplace. For example, individual foreign exchange rates tend to have annualized percentage volatilities in the range of 5 to 20 percent, although higher ﬁgures some-times occur. This result implies that the value-at-risk approaches with annualized percentage volatilities in excess of 20 percent (Charts 6a and 6b) will ﬂuctuate more over time (for the same portfolio) than will most exchange rates themselves.
Our major observation for this performance cri-terion is that the volatility of risk measures increases as reliance on recent data increases. As shown in Charts 6a and 6b, this increase is true for both the 95th and 99th percentile risk measures and for all three categories of value-at-risk approaches. This result is not surprising, and indeed it is clearly apparent in Charts 1-3, which depict time series of different value-at-risk approaches over the sample period. FRACTION OF OUTCOMES COVERED Our fourth performance criterion addresses the fundamental goal of the value-at-risk measures—whether they cover the portfolio outcomes they are intended to capture. We calculate the fraction of outcomes covered as the percentage of results where the loss in portfolio value is less than the risk measure.
For the 95th percentile risk measures, the simula-tion results indicate that nearly all twelve value-at-risk approaches meet this performance criterion (Chart 7a).
For many portfolios, coverage exceeds 95 percent, and only the 125-day historical simulation approach captures less than 94.5 percent of the outcomes on average across all 1,000 portfolios. In a very small fraction of the random portfolios, the risk measures cover less than 94 percent of the outcomes.
Interestingly, the 95th percentile results suggest that the equally weighted moving average approaches actu-ally tend to produce excess coverage (greater than 95 per-cent) for all observation periods except ﬁfty days. By contrast, the historical simulation approaches tend to pro-vide either too little coverage or, in the case of the 1,250-day historical simulation approach, a little more than the desired amount. The exponentially weighted moving average approach with a decay factor of 0.97 produces exact 95 percent coverage, but for this approach the results are more variable across portfolios than for the 1,250-day historical simulation approach.
Compared with the 95th percentile results, the 99th percentile risk measures exhibit a more widespread tendency to fall short of the desired level of risk coverage.
Only the 1,250-day historical simulation approach attains 99 percent coverage across all 1,000 portfolios, as shown in Chart 7b. Of course, the consequences of such a shortfall in perfor-mance depend on the particular circumstances in which the value-at-risk model is being used. A coverage level of 98.2 percent when a risk manager desires 99 percent implies that the value-at-risk model misclassiﬁes approxi-mately two outcomes every year (assuming that there are 250 trading days per calendar year).
Overall, the results in Charts 7a and 7b support the conclusion that all twelve value-at-risk approaches either achieve the desired level of coverage or come very close to it on the basis of the percentage of outcomes mis-classiﬁed. Clearly, the best performer is the 1,250-day his-torical simulation approach, which attains almost exact coverage for both the 95th and 99th percentiles, while the worst performer is the 125-day historical simulation approach, partly because of its short-term construction.19 One explanation for the superior performance of the 1,250-day historical simulation is that the unconditional distri-bution of changes in portfolio value is relatively stable and that accurate estimates of extreme percentiles require the use of long periods. These results underscore the problems associated with the assumption of normality for 99th per-centiles and are consistent with ﬁndings in other recent studies of value-at-risk models.20 MULTIPLE NEEDED TO ATTAIN DESIRED COVERAGE The ﬁfth performance criterion we examine focuses on the size of the adjustments in the risk measures that would be needed to achieve perfect coverage. We therefore calculate on an ex post basis the multiple that would have been required for each value-at-risk measure to attain the desired level of coverage (either 95 percent or 99 percent).
This performance criterion complements the fraction of outcomes covered because it focuses on the size of the potential errors in risk measurement rather than on the percentage of results captured.
For 95th percentile risk measures, the simulation results indicate that multiples very close to one are sufﬁ-cient (Chart 8a). Even the 125-day historical simulation approach, which on average across portfolios is furthest from the desired outcome, requires a multiple of only 1.04.
On the whole, none of the approaches considered here appears to understate 95th percentile risk measures on a systematic basis by more than 4 percent, and several appear to overstate them by small amounts.
For the 99th percentile risk measures, most value-at-risk approaches require multiples between 1.10 and 1.15 to attain 99 percent coverage (Chart 8b). The 1,250-day historical simulation approach, however, is markedly superior to all other approaches. On average across all port-folios, no multiple other than one is needed for this approach to achieve 99 percent coverage. Moreover, com-pared with the other approaches, the historical simulations in general exhibit less variability across portfolios with respect to this criterion.
The fact that most multiples are larger than one is not surprising. More signiﬁcant is the fact that the size of the multiples needed to achieve 99 percent coverage exceeds the levels indicated by the normal distribution. For example, when normality is assumed, the 99th percentile would be about 1.08 times as large as the 98.4th percentile, a level of coverage comparable to that attained by many of the approaches (Chart 7b). The multiples for these approaches, shown in Chart 8b, are larger than 1.08, providing further evidence that the normal distribution does not accurately approximate actual distributions at points near the 99th percentile. More generally, the results also suggest that sub-stantial increases in value-at-risk measures may be needed to capture outcomes in the tail of the distribution. Hence, shortcomings in value-at-risk measures that seem small in probability terms may be much more signiﬁcant when con-sidered in terms of the changes required to remedy them.

These results lead to an important question: what distributional assumptions other than normality can be used when constructing value-at-risk measures using a variance-covariance approach? The t-distribution is often cited as a good candidate, because extreme outcomes occur more often under t-distributions than under the normal distribution.21 A brief analysis shows that the use of a t-distribution for the 99th percentile has some merit.
To calculate a value-at-risk measure for a single percentile assuming the t-distribution, the value-at-risk measure calculated with the assumption of normality is multiplied by a ﬁxed multiple. As the results in Chart 8b suggest, ﬁxed multiples between 1.10 and 1.15 are appro-priate for the variance-covariance approaches. It follows that t-distributions with between four and six degrees of freedom are appropriate for the 99th percentile risk mea-sures.22 The use of these particular t-distributions, how-ever, would lead to substantial overestimation of 95th percentile risk measures because the actual distributions near the 95th percentile are much closer to normality.
Since the use of t-distributions for risk measurement involves a scaling up of the risk measures that are calcu-lated assuming normality, the distributions are likely to be useful, although they may be more helpful for some per-centiles than for others.

For shorter periods, the maxi-mum multiple would likely be lower.

CORRELATION BETWEEN RISK MEASURE AND ABSOLUTE VALUE OF OUTCOME The eighth performance criterion assesses how well the risk measures adjust over time to underlying changes in risk. In other words, how closely do changes in the value-at-risk measures correspond to actual changes in the risk of the portfolio? We answer this question by determining the cor-relation between the value-at-risk measures for each approach and the absolute values of the outcomes. This cor-relation statistic has two advantages. First, it is not affected by the scale of the portfolio. Second, the correlations are rel-atively easy to interpret, although even a perfect value-at-risk measure cannot guarantee a correlation of one between the risk measure and the absolute value of the outcome.
For this criterion, the results for the 95th percen-tile risk measures and 99th percentile risk measures are almost identical (Charts 11a and 11b). Most striking is the superior performance of the exponentially weighted mov-ing average measures. This ﬁnding implies that these approaches tend to track changes in risk over time more accurately than the other approaches.
It is important not to view value-at-risk measures as a strict upper bound on the portfolio losses that can occur.

This article (FRBNY Economic Policy Review, April 1996) by Darryll Hendricks evaluates the performance of value-at-risk (VaR) models by applying twelve approaches to 1,000 randomly chosen foreign exchange portfolios over the period 1983-94, using nine performance criteria.

**Background and Context:** Value-at-risk models measure the market/price risk of a portfolio by aggregating price risk components into a single quantitative measure of potential losses over a specified time horizon. Their use has grown, endorsed by the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision (1996a), the BIS Fisher report (1994), the Derivatives Policy Group, and J.P. Morgan's RiskMetrics database. The study focuses on one-day holding periods at both 95% and 99% confidence levels, but does not consider options or nonlinear positions.

**Three Categories of VaR Approaches:**
1. **Equally weighted moving average approaches** (5 variants: 50, 125, 250, 500, and 1,250 days of historical data) - calculate variance using a fixed amount of historical data; assume normality and serial independence. The 50-day measures are prone to rapid swings, while 1,250-day measures are more stable.
2. **Exponentially weighted moving average approaches** (3 variants: decay factors λ=0.94, 0.97, 0.99) - emphasize recent observations; equivalent to IGARCH(1,1) conditional volatility models. Lower decay factors produce more variable risk measures but capture short-term volatility movements.
3. **Historical simulation approaches** (4 variants: 125, 250, 500, 1,250 days) - use actual percentiles of the observation period as VaR measures; do not assume normality or serial independence. The 125-day approach produces abrupt shifts in risk measures.

**Data and Methodology:** Daily exchange rates (bid prices, 4:00 p.m. NY time, collected by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York) against the U.S. dollar for eight currencies (British pound, Canadian dollar, Dutch guilder, French franc, German mark, Italian lira, Japanese yen, Swiss franc), covering January 1, 1978 to January 18, 1995 (4,255 days). The simulation used five steps: select random portfolios (positions drawn from uniform distribution centered on zero, ±$100 million), calculate VaR estimates for each day (days 1,251-4,255) using preceding 1,250 days of data, calculate actual portfolio value changes, assess performance, and repeat 1,000 times.

**Nine Performance Criteria and Key Results:**
1. **Mean relative bias:** For 95th percentile, differences in average size across approaches are small. For 99th percentile, historical simulation approaches produce systematically larger risk measures (the 1,250-day historical simulation is ~13% larger than average). Actual 99th percentiles tend to be larger than the normal distribution predicts.
2. **Root mean squared relative bias:** Dispersion in risk measures across approaches on a given day falls in the 10-15% range (higher for 99th percentile); differences of 30-50% between approaches on a given day are not uncommon. The λ=0.99 exponentially weighted approach exhibits very low bias.
3. **Annualized percentage volatility:** Volatility of risk measures increases as reliance on recent data increases. Historical simulation approaches are more variable than equally weighted approaches for fixed observation periods.
4. **Fraction of outcomes covered:** All twelve approaches achieve desired coverage or come very close. The 1,250-day historical simulation is the best performer, attaining almost exact coverage for both percentiles. For 99th percentile, most approaches cover only 98.2-98.8% of outcomes (implying ~2 misclassified outcomes per year).
5. **Multiple needed to attain desired coverage:** For 95th percentile, multiples very close to 1 suffice (worst case 1.04). For 99th percentile, most approaches require multiples of 1.10-1.15; the 1,250-day historical simulation requires no multiple other than one. This provides evidence that the normal distribution does not accurately approximate actual distributions near the 99th percentile.
6. **Average multiple of tail event to risk measure:** Average tail events are 30-40% larger than risk measures for both percentiles, exceeding normal distribution predictions.
7. **Maximum multiple of tail event to risk measure:** Maximum tail events are 3-4 times the 95th percentile risk measure and ~2.5 times the 99th percentile risk measure. The 1,250-day historical simulation is not clearly superior for this criterion.
8. **Correlation between risk measure and absolute value of outcome:** Exponentially weighted moving average measures perform best at tracking changes in risk over time. Shorter observation periods lead to higher correlations. The 1,250-day historical simulation risk measures are essentially uncorrelated with actual outcomes, revealing little about changes in portfolio risk over time.
9. **Mean relative bias for risk measures scaled to desired coverage:** (Content truncated in original).

**Key Conclusions:**
- None of the twelve approaches is superior on every criterion.
- The choice of confidence level (95% vs. 99%) substantially affects performance.
- The normality assumption is more reasonable for the 95th percentile than the 99th percentile; actual distributions have fatter tails.
- T-distributions with 4-6 degrees of freedom are appropriate for 99th percentile risk measures (with fixed multiples of 1.10-1.15), but would overestimate 95th percentile measures.
- VaR measures should not be viewed as strict upper bounds on portfolio losses.
- The 1,250-day historical simulation approach excels at coverage and accuracy of extreme percentiles but performs poorly at tracking changes in risk over time.
- The exponentially weighted approaches excel at tracking changes in risk but produce more variable measures.

**Limitations:** Results cannot be used to accept or reject statistical hypotheses; results are specific to linear foreign exchange portfolios over 1983-94 and should not be generalized to other assets or periods. The article does not address the "backtesting" debate.

This is a Semantic Scholar page for the academic paper "Comparing Sharpe ratios: So where are the p-values?" by John Douglas Opdyke, published on 30 November 2007 in the Journal of Asset Management (volume 8, pages 308-336, DOI: 10.1057/PALGRAVE.JAM.2250084, Corpus ID 154172914).

The paper addresses a gap in financial statistics: since Jobson and Korkie (1981), derivations of the asymptotic distribution of the Sharpe ratio that are practically usable for generating confidence intervals or conducting one- and two-sample hypothesis tests have relied on the restrictive assumption of normally distributed returns, which is now widely refuted. Opdyke presents an easily implemented formula for the asymptotic distribution of the Sharpe ratio that is valid under very general conditions — stationary and ergodic returns.

The paper has 158 citations and 69 references. Key citing works include:
- "Connecting Sharpe ratio and Student t-statistic, and beyond" (Benhamou, 2018)
- "Distribution and statistics of the Sharpe Ratio" (Benhamou)
- "Estimated Sharpe ratio of asset returns with fat tails: theory and empirical evidence" (Kao, Lee, Lee, 2025)
- "Alternative Methods to Derive Statistical Distribution of Sharpe Performance Measure" (Kao & Lee, 2013)
- "Robust Performance Hypothesis Testing with the Sharpe Ratio" (Ledoit & Wolf, 2008) — 890 citations, a very influential follow-up
- "Interval estimation for the Sharpe Ratio when returns are not i.i.d. with special emphasis on the GARCH(1,1) process with symmetric innovations" (Capitani, 2012)
- "Testing Sharpe Ratio: Luck or Skill?" (Benhamou, Saltiel, Guez, Paris, 2019)
- "THE SHARPE RATIO EFFICIENT FRONTIER" (Bailey & Prado, 2012)

Important referenced works include "The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios" (Lo, 2002, 773 citations), "Performance Hypothesis Testing with the Sharpe and Treynor Measures" (Jobson & Korkie, 1981, highly influential), and studies on fat-tailed, leptokurtic, and asymmetric return distributions (Jondeau & Rockinger 2003; Komunjer 2004; Harris & Küçüközmen 2001; Patterson & Heravi 2003).

## Abstract

This paper generalizes the results in Lo ([2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR56 "Lo AW (2002) The statistics of Sharpe ratios. Financ Anal J 58:36–47")) by allowing the distributions of asset returns exhibiting fat tails with the tail index 0 <_κ_< 4. We show that the asymptotic behavior of the estimated Sharpe ratio is biased and converges at a slower rate as 2<_κ_< 4. Therefore, the risk-return payoff information provided by the estimated Sharpe ratio can be misleading. It is also shown that the asymptotic unbiasedness and normality of the estimated Sharpe ratio can only be established as asset returns have a finite (4 + _ε_)th moment with _ε_ ≥ 0, i.e., _κ_> 4. Of particular interest are the cases as the tail index 2 <_κ_< 4, where the ex ante Sharpe ratio is well defined, and an inference method is developed. Empirical examples are used to illustrate the derived results, and an empirical study on major ETFs and mutual funds suggests caution in using the Sharpe ratio for comparing investment performance.

## 1 Introduction

Sharpe ratio, in terms of the excess return achieved per risk taken, has been the most widely used measure of a portfolio manager’s ability to perform consistently in practice, including mutual fund performance measure (Sharpe [1966](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR79 "Sharpe WF (1966) Mutual fund performance. J Bus 39(1, Part 2: Supplement on Security Prices):119–138"); Farnsworth et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR35 "Farnsworth H, Ferson W, Jackson D, Todd S (2002) Performance evaluation with stochastic discount factors. J Bus 75:473–583")), as well as hedge fund performance measure (Li, Xu and Zheng [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR53 "Li H, Xu Y, Zhang X (2016) Hedge fund performance evaluation under the stochastic discount factor framework. J Financ Quant Anal 51:231–257")). In addition to performance measure, Sharpe ratio also has profound implications in asset pricing: it provides a lower bound on the volatility of the stochastic discount factor (e.g., see Shiller [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR81 "Shiller RJ (1982) Consumption, asset markets, and macroeconomic fluctuations. Carnegie Mellon Conf Ser Public Policy 17:203–238"); Hansen and Jagannathan [1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR42 "Hansen LP, Jagannathan R (1991) Restrictions on intertemporal marginal rates of substitution implied by asset returns. J Polit Econ 99:225–262"); Cochrane and Hansen [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR17 "Cochrane JH, Hansen LP (1992) Asset pricing explorations for macroeconomics. NBER Macroecon Annu 7:115–165"); Hansen and Jagannathan [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR43 "Hansen LP, Jagannathan R (1997) Assessing specification errors in stochastic discount factor models. J Finance 52:557–590")), and plays a role in the statistical tests that compare alternative asset pricing models (Gibbons, Ross and Shanken, [1989](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR36 "Gibson M, Ross S, Shanken J (1989) A test of the efficiency of a given portfolio. Econometrica 57:1121–1152"); Barillas and Shanken [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR3 "Barillas F, Shanken J (2017) Which alpha? Rev Financ Stud 30:1316–1338"), [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR4 "Barillas F, Shanken J (2018) Comparing asset pricing models. J Finance 73:715–754"); Barillas et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR5 "Barillas F, Kan R, Robotti C, Shanken J (2019) Model comparison with Sharpe ratios. J Financ Quant Anal 55:1840–1874"); Chib et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR13 "Chib S, Zeng X, Zhao L (2020) On comparing asset pricing models. J Finance 75:551–577")).

In practice, Sharpe ratio is estimated as the ratio of the sample mean to the standard deviation of the excess returns over a period of time. Subject to sampling errors, the accuracy of the estimated Sharpe ratio is always the focus of attention. In literature, debates over whether a negative Sharpe ratio occurred in bear markets is a reliably performance measure had been brought up (Scholz [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR76 "Scholz H (2007) Refinements to the Sharpe ratio: comparing alternatives for bear markets. J Asset Manag 7:347–357")). Bailey and Lopez de Prado ([2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR2 "Bailey DH, de Lopez Prado M (2012) The Sharpe ratio efficient frontier. J Risk 15:13")) showed that Sharpe ratios tend to be overstated in the case of hedge funds with fat-tailed distributed asset returns. Being a lower bound to the volatility of the stochastic discount factor (SDF), Hansen and Jagannathan ([1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR42 "Hansen LP, Jagannathan R (1991) Restrictions on intertemporal marginal rates of substitution implied by asset returns. J Polit Econ 99:225–262")) also noticed the alternative perspective on the equity premium puzzle (Mehra and Prescott,[1985](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR60 "Mehra R, Prescott EC (1985) The equity premium: a puzzle. J Monet Econ 15:145–161")) that the annualized Sharpe ratio of the postwar U.S. value-weighted stock index implies a very high volatility of the SDF, which is inconsistent with the volatility predicted by an averaged level of relative risk aversion coefficient.

Notwithstanding with the above questionable issues, the desired properties of asymptotic unbiasedness and normality of the estimated Sharpe ratio had been established under various assumptions in literature for the past 40 years (Jobson and Korkie [1981](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR47 "Jobson JD, Korkie BM (1981) Performance hypothesis testing with Sharpe and Treynor measures. J Finance 36:889–908"); Hodges et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR45 "Hodges CW, Taylor RL, Yoder JA (1997) Stocks, bonds, the Sharpe ratio, and the investment horizon. Financ Anal J 53:74–80"); Lo [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR56 "Lo AW (2002) The statistics of Sharpe ratios. Financ Anal J 58:36–47"); Merten [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR63 "Merten E (2002) Comments on the correct variance of estimated Sharpe ratios in Lo (2002, FAJ) when returns are i.i.d. Res Note, 
                  http://www.elmarmertens.org
                  
                "); Christie [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR14 "Christie S (2005) Is the Sharpe ratio useful in asslocation? MAFC Research Paper 31, Applied Finance Center, Macquarie University"); Opdyke [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR70 "Opdyke JD (2007) Comparing Sharpe ratios: so where are the p-values? J Asset Manag 8:208–336"); Schmid and Schmid [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR75 "Schmid F, Schmidt R (2010) Statistical inference for Sharpe ratio. In: Berkelaar A, Coche J, Nyholm K (eds) Interest Rate Models, Asset Allocation and Quantitative Techniques for Central Banks and Sovereign Wealth Funds. Palgrave, London")). Nevertheless, the above literature all require the assumption that asset returns have finite fourth moments, which is more restrictive than the assumption of finite second moments. As empirical studies often show that asset returns exhibit fat tails that do not allow finite kurtosis, i.e., finite fourth moment (Mandelbrot [1963](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR59 "Mandelbrot B (1963) The variation of certain speculative prices. J Bus 36:394–419"); Fama [1965](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR32 "Fama EF (1965) The behavior of stock market prices. J Bus 38:34–105"); Cont et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR20 "Cont R, Bouchaud JP, Potters M (1997) Scaling in financial data: stable laws and beyond. In: Dubrulle B, Graner F, Sornette D (eds) Scale invariance and beyond. Springer, Berlin"); Cont [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR18 "Cont R (2001) Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues. Quant Finance 1:223–236"); Dacorogna et al. [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR21 "Dacorogna M, Gencay R, Müller U, Olsen R, Pictet O (2001) An Introduction to High Frequency Finance. Academic Press, London"); Rachev [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR72 "Rachev ST (2003) Handbook of Heavy Tailed Distributions in Finance. Elsevier, Amsterdam")), one would now question whether properties of asymptotic unbiasedness and normality of the estimated Sharpe ratio can still be established.

Fat-tailed distributed asset returns crucially affect risk calculation, portfolio selection, and asset pricing, and thus they may be profound to financial institution risk managers. When asset returns exhibit fat tails, the sample standard deviation often under estimate the volatility associated with damaging extreme events occurred during adverse market movements. In financial market, damaging extreme events occurred during adverse market movements often increase the connection between otherwise disparate assets, with negative feedback loops developed to result in sharp declines in asset prices (Danielsson et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR22 "Danielsson J, Shin HS, Zigrand JP (2013) Endogenous and systemic risk. In: Haubrich JG, Lo AW (eds) Quantifying Systemic Risk. Univ Chicago Press, Chicago")). The negative feedback loops are evidenced by the empirically observed volatility clustering phenomenon (Mandelbrot [1963](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR59 "Mandelbrot B (1963) The variation of certain speculative prices. J Bus 36:394–419"); Ding et al. [1983](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR27 "Ding Z, Granger C, Engle R (1983) A long memory property of stock market returns and a new model. J Empir Finance 1:83–106"); Bollerslev [1986](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR7 "Bollerslev T (1986) Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. J Econometrics 31:307–327"); Bollerslev et al. [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR9 "Bollerslev T, Chou R, Kroner K (1992) Arch modeling in finance. J Econometrics 52:5–59"); Ding and Granger [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR26 "Ding Z, Granger C (1996) Modeling volatility persistence of speculative returns: a new approach. J Econometrics 73:185–215"); Guillaume et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR39 "Guillaume D, Dacorogna M, Dave R, Müller U, Olsen R, Pictet O (1997) From the birds eye view to the microscope: a survey of new stylized facts of the intraday foreign exchange markets. Finance Stoch 1:95–131"); Cont [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR18 "Cont R (2001) Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues. Quant Finance 1:223–236")). In addition to the volatility clustering phenomenon, one often observes insignificant autocorrelations of log-returns, but hyperbolic-decay autocorrelations of the absolute log-returns (Davis and Mikosch, [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR25 "Davis RA, Mikosch T (1998) The sample autocorrelations of heavy-tailed processes with applications to ARCH. Ann Stat 26:2049–2080"); Mikosch and Starica [2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR64 "Mikosch T, Starica C (2000) Limit theory for the sample autocorrelations and extremes of a GARCH(1,1) process. Ann Stat 28:1427–1451"); Cont [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR19 "Cont R (2005) Long range dependency in financial markets. Fractals Eng 159–179"); Basrak et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR6 "Basrak B, Davis RA, Mikosch T (2002) Regular variation of GARCH processes. Stoch Proc Appl 99:95–116"); Mikosch and Starica [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR65 "Mikosch T, Starica C (2004) Non-stationarities in financial time series, the long-range dependence and the IGARCH effects. Rev Econ Stat 86:378–390")). The GARCH (Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) model could exhibit vastly different behavior of log-returns ranging from fat-tails, insignificant autocorrelations, and volatility clustering; however, when fitting GARCH models to typical log-return data, it is often found an estimated finite second order moment, but an infinite fourth order moment, e.g., Engle and Bollerslev ([1986](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR7 "Bollerslev T (1986) Generalized autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity. J Econometrics 31:307–327")), Andersen and Bollerslev (1997), and Engle and Patton (2001). No mathematical description of the tail behavior for processes generated by the GARCH model was developed till the work of Basrak et al. ([2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR6 "Basrak B, Davis RA, Mikosch T (2002) Regular variation of GARCH processes. Stoch Proc Appl 99:95–116")b). Later, Lange (2011) extended the results of Basrak et al. ([2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR6 "Basrak B, Davis RA, Mikosch T (2002) Regular variation of GARCH processes. Stoch Proc Appl 99:95–116")b) to the ARMA-GARCH model. In particular, it was established that the estimates of the AR parameters in an AR-GARCH model remain consistent as long as the innovations have finite second-order moment, but infinite fourth-order moment. Therefore, this study adopts an AR-GARCH model that combines the dependency structure in the mean of an auto-regressive (AR) model and in the variance of a GARCH model, respectively, to model the asset returns (Liu et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR55 "Liu J, Li WK, Li CW (1997) On a threshold autoregression with conditional heteroscedastic variances. J Stat Plan Inference 62:279–300"); Ling,[1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR54 "Ling S (1999) On the probabilistic properties of a double threshold ARMA conditional heteroskedastic model. J Appl Probab 36:688–705"); Lanne and Saikkonen, [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR84 "Lanne M, Saikkonen P (2005) Nonlinear GARCH models for highly persistent volatility. Econom J 8:251–276"); Cline [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR16 "Cline DBH (2007) Stability of nonlinear stochastic recursions with application to nonlinear AR-GARCH models. Adv Appl Probab 39:462–491"); Meitz and Saikkonen [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR61 "Meitz M, Saikkonen P (2008) Stability of nonlinear AR-GARCH models. J Time Ser Anal 29:453–475"); Lange[2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR49 "Lange T (2011) Tail behavior and OLS estimation in AR-GARCH model. Stat SinEconom J 21:1191–1200 "); Shao [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR77 "Shao X (2010) A self-normalized approach to confidence interval construction in time series. J R Stat Soc Ser B 72:343–366"), [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR78 "Shao X (2015) Self-normalization for time series: a review of recent developments. J Am Stat Assoc 110:1797–1817")). The asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio is derived under four scenarios that depend on the tail index _κ_ of the asset returns: (_i_) 0 <_κ_< 1, (_ii_) 1 <_κ_< 2, (_iii_) 2 <_κ_< 4, and (_iv_) _κ_> 4. In (_i_), we show that the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio converges at the rate \(\:\sqrt{T}\) to a distribution that is highly concentrated at the two modes + _c_ and -_c_, for some constant _c_ as 0 <_κ_< 1. In (_ii_), as 1 <_κ_< 2, the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio converges at the rate \(T^\phi, \phi = 1/\kappa-1/2 < 1/2\)_,_ to a distribution skewed with a long right (left) tail as the mean return is positive (negative). In (_iii_), the asymptotic distribution of the difference between the estimated and population Sharpe ratios converges at the rate \(n^\phi, \phi = 1 - 2/\kappa < 1/2\), to a stable distribution with the tail index _κ_/2 plus a positive (negative) bias term as the mean return is positive (negative). Lastly, in (_iv_), the asymptotic distribution of the difference between the estimated and population Sharpe ratios converges at the rate \(\:\sqrt{T}\) to a normal distribution with mean zero, and the estimated Sharpe ratio is asymptotically unbiased.

In summary, when asset returns are fat-tailed distributed, either the population Sharpe ratio does not exist as the tail index 0<_κ_< 2, or the estimated Sharpe ratio has a positive (negative) bias if the population mean return is positive (negative) converges at the rate slower than the squared root of the sample size as the tail index 2 <_κ_< 4. The estimated Sharpe ratio is asymptotically unbiased and normally distributed only as the tail index _κ_> 4. The fat-tailed distributed asset returns may well explain why negative Sharpe ratios are unreliable in bear markets, or why the estimated Sharpe ratios are overstated for hedge funds with positive return. At the same time, our results might well explain the equity premium puzzle observed by Hansen and Jagannathan ([1991](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR42 "Hansen LP, Jagannathan R (1991) Restrictions on intertemporal marginal rates of substitution implied by asset returns. J Polit Econ 99:225–262")) that the annualized Sharpe ratio of the postwar U.S. value-weighted stock index is overstated. Empirical examples are given to illustrate the above results.

In addition, we provide an inference method based on the subsampling method (Politis and Romano [1994](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR71 "Politis DN, Romano JP (1994) Large sample confidence regions based on subsamples under minimal assumptions. Ann Stat 22:2031–2050")) and conduct empirical studies using CRSP funds data. Our empirical results show that when applying the largest-cap ETFs and mutual funds, the estimated κ values are all below 4, indicating that the daily returns of the major ETFs and mutual funds exhibit fat tails, and imply that the Sharpe ratio is not asymptotically normal and may be biased. Therefore, one should exercise caution when using the Sharpe ratio for comparing investment performance, especially in daily or high-frequency studies.

The paper is organized as follows. Section[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#Sec2) reviews the existing literature on the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio. Section[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#Sec3) develops a AR(1)-GARCH (1,1) model and derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio when the asset returns obey an AR(1)-GARCH (1,1) model with the tail index 0 <_κ_< 1, 1 <_κ_< 2, 2 <_κ_< 4, and _κ_> 4, respectively. Empirical studies are given to illustrate the derived distributional results in Sect.[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#Sec4). Section[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#Sec6) provides an inference method and its empirical applications. Section[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#Sec7) concludes the paper.

## 2 Related literature

We briefly review the existing literature on the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio. For the Sharpe measure to be relevant, assets’ excess returns over an _T_-period horizon need to be stationary with a finite population variance (e.g., see Hodges et al. [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR45 "Hodges CW, Taylor RL, Yoder JA (1997) Stocks, bonds, the Sharpe ratio, and the investment horizon. Financ Anal J 53:74–80")). In literature, the most adopted stationarity assumption is _i.i.d._. Under the assumption of _i.i.d._ normally distributed excess returns, the estimated Sharpe ratio is non-central t distributed and biased (Miller and Gehr [1978](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR66 "Miller RE, Gehr AK (1978) Sample size bias and sharpe’s performance measure: a note. J Financ Quant Anal 12:943–946"); Lee and Chen [1979](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR51 "Lee CF, Chen SN (1979) Sampling properties of composite performance measures and their implications. Fac Working Pap Univ Ill Urbana-Champaign 541"); Chen and Lee [1981](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR12 "Chen SN, Lee CF (1981) The sampling relationship between sharpe’s performance measure and its risk proxy: sample size, investment horizon, and market condition. Manage Sci 27:607–618")). For an _T_-period horizon, without the normality assumption, it is shown that the estimated Sharpe ratio of _i.i.d._ excess returns with finite population variance is asymptotically unbiased and asymptotically normally distributed (Jobson and Korkie [1981](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR47 "Jobson JD, Korkie BM (1981) Performance hypothesis testing with Sharpe and Treynor measures. J Finance 36:889–908"); Lo [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR56 "Lo AW (2002) The statistics of Sharpe ratios. Financ Anal J 58:36–47")). Later, the asymptotically normal distribution is improved by Merten ([2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR63 "Merten E (2002) Comments on the correct variance of estimated Sharpe ratios in Lo (2002, FAJ) when returns are i.i.d. Res Note, 
                  http://www.elmarmertens.org
                  
                ")) that incorporates the skewness and kurtosis of the excess returns’ non-normal distribution.

Another often adopted stationarity is the strictly-stationary-ergodic assumption that considers the stylized fact of predictable and serial correlated excess returns (Shiller [1981](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR80 "Shiller RJ (1981) Do stock prices move too much to be justified by subsequent changes in dividends? Am Econ Rev 71:421–436"), [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR81 "Shiller RJ (1982) Consumption, asset markets, and macroeconomic fluctuations. Carnegie Mellon Conf Ser Public Policy 17:203–238"); Lo and MacKinlay [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR57 "Lo AW, MacKinlay AC (1988) Stock prices do not follow random walks: evidence from a simple specification test. Rev Financ Stud 1:515–528"); Fama and French [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR33 "Fama EF, French KR (1988) Permanent and temporary components of stock prices. J Polit Econ 96:246–273"), [1989](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR34 "Fama EF, French KR (1989) Business conditions and expected returns on stocks and bonds. J Financ Econ 25:23–49"); Nelson and Kim [1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR68 "Nelson DB, Kim MJ (1993) Predictable stock returns: the role of small sample bias. J Finance 48:641–661"); Cont [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR18 "Cont R (2001) Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues. Quant Finance 1:223–236")). Under the strictly-stationary-ergodic assumption, the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio was derived by Lo ([2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR56 "Lo AW (2002) The statistics of Sharpe ratios. Financ Anal J 58:36–47")), Christie ([2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR14 "Christie S (2005) Is the Sharpe ratio useful in asslocation? MAFC Research Paper 31, Applied Finance Center, Macquarie University")) and Opdyke ([2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR70 "Opdyke JD (2007) Comparing Sharpe ratios: so where are the p-values? J Asset Manag 8:208–336")) using the generalized method of moment (GMM) approach (Hansen [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR41 "Hansen LP (1982) Large sample properties of generalized method of moments estimators. Econometrica 50:1029–1054")). In Schmid and Schmid ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR75 "Schmid F, Schmidt R (2010) Statistical inference for Sharpe ratio. In: Berkelaar A, Coche J, Nyholm K (eds) Interest Rate Models, Asset Allocation and Quantitative Techniques for Central Banks and Sovereign Wealth Funds. Palgrave, London")), the same asymptotic distribution was derived based on the GMM approach as the excess returns follows a strictly-stationary α-mixing GARCH (1,1) process[Footnote 1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#Fn1).

However, a key assumption of the GMM method, usually applied in the context of semiparametric models, is the existence of the finite 4th moment of asset returns (Hansen [1982](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR41 "Hansen LP (1982) Large sample properties of generalized method of moments estimators. Econometrica 50:1029–1054")), which is very restrictive as asset returns often exhibit fat tails that do not allow finite 2nd moment or finite population variance, not to mention finite 4th moment. (Mandelbrot [1963](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR59 "Mandelbrot B (1963) The variation of certain speculative prices. J Bus 36:394–419"); Bollerslev et al. [1992](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR9 "Bollerslev T, Chou R, Kroner K (1992) Arch modeling in finance. J Econometrics 52:5–59"); Davis and Mikosch [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR25 "Davis RA, Mikosch T (1998) The sample autocorrelations of heavy-tailed processes with applications to ARCH. Ann Stat 26:2049–2080"); Mikosch and Starica [2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR64 "Mikosch T, Starica C (2000) Limit theory for the sample autocorrelations and extremes of a GARCH(1,1) process. Ann Stat 28:1427–1451"); Cont [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR18 "Cont R (2001) Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues. Quant Finance 1:223–236"); Lange, 2011). Therefore, the above works using GMM approach exclude all the cases with fat-tailed distributed asset returns. It is the aim of this study to derive the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio under more general conditions including fat-tailed distributed asset returns, which will be given in the following sections.

## 3 Asymptotic distribution of estimated Sharpe ratio under AR (1)-GARCH (1, 1) model

Suppose a series of excess returns {_R_ _t_, 1≤_t_≤_T_} is observed during a period of time (0,_T_], where the time-_t_ excess return _R_ _t_ is assumed to be symmetrically distributed around the location parameter _µ_ _R_ so that _E_(_R_ _t_)=_µ_ _R_ if _E_(_R_ _t_) exists. Consider the estimated Sharpe ratio,

$$\:\:\widehat{SR}=\stackrel{-}{R}/{S}_{R}$$

where \(\:\stackrel{-}{R}\:\)and _s_ _R_ are the sample mean and sample standard deviation of the excess returns {_R_ _t_, 1≤_t_≤_T_}. Let _r_ _t_ =_R_ _t_-_µ_ _R_ be the centered excess return, 1 ≤ _t_ ≤ _T_. The AR(1)-GARCH (1,1) model is formulated as:

$$r_t=\rho r_{t-1}+X_t$$

 (1) 

where 1≤_t_≤_T_, _ρ_ is the AR-parameter, _X_ _t_ is the innovation term.

$$X_t=\sqrt{h_t}\;\varepsilon_t$$

 (2) 

where _h_ _t_ = _α_ 0 + _h_ _t_−1 _A_ _t_ is the conditional variance with.

$$A_t=\beta_1\;\varepsilon_{t-1}^2+\beta_2$$

 (3) 

_α_ 0> 0, _β_ 1> 0, 0 <_β_ 2< 1 are the GARCH parameters. The assumptions by Mikosch and Starica ([2000](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR64 "Mikosch T, Starica C (2000) Limit theory for the sample autocorrelations and extremes of a GARCH(1,1) process. Ann Stat 28:1427–1451")), Basrak et al. ([2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR6 "Basrak B, Davis RA, Mikosch T (2002) Regular variation of GARCH processes. Stoch Proc Appl 99:95–116")), Meitz and Saikkonen ([2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR61 "Meitz M, Saikkonen P (2008) Stability of nonlinear AR-GARCH models. J Time Ser Anal 29:453–475")), and Lange (2011) are adopted and summarized as follows:

*   **Assumption 1.** The re-scaled innovations _ε_ 1, …, _ε_ _T_ are i.i.d. with E(_ε_ 1) = 0 and ∃_δ_ 0> 0 so that E|_ε_ 1|_δ_<∞ for all δ<_δ_ 0, and \(\mathrm E\left|\varepsilon_1\right|^{\delta_0}=\infty\). In addition, _ε_ _t_ has positive and lower semi-continuous density in an interval symmetric around zero on R.

*   **Assumption 2**. The AR-parameter satisfying |ρ|<1 _._

*   **Assumption 3.**The GARCH parameters β 1 and β 2 satisfy E[ln(At)] < 0, where At is defined in (3).

Assumption 1 implies the re-scaled innovation _ε_ _t_ is independent of {_r_ _s_, _s_<_t_}. Assumption 3 agrees with the necessary and sufficient condition for the sequence of conditional variances {_h_ _t_: 1≤_t_≤_T_} to be strictly-stationary-ergodic by Nelson ([1990](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR67 "Nelson DB (1990) Stationarity and persistence in the GARCH model. Econom Theory 6:318–334")). Under Assumptions 1–3, {_r_ _t_: 1≤_t_≤_T_} is strictly-stationary-ergodic and _β_-mixing is due to Meitz and Saikkonen ([2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR61 "Meitz M, Saikkonen P (2008) Stability of nonlinear AR-GARCH models. J Time Ser Anal 29:453–475")). In addition, Meitz and Saikkonen ([2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11156-025-01474-6#ref-CR61 "Meitz M, Saikkonen P (2008) Stability of nonlinear AR-GARCH models. The regular variation of the centered excess returns {_r_ _t_:1≤_t_≤_T_} was derived by Lange (2011) under a very restrict condition that the innovation _X_ _t_ has finite second-order moment but infinite (4 + _ε_)th moment, where _ε_≥0 depends on the dependence structure of the time series of asset returns, which is equivalent to condition that the tail index 2 <_κ_< 4. However, financial data often exhibits heavy tails with tail index 0 <_κ_< 2 that do not allow finite 2nd moment (Embrechts et al. $$E\left(A_t^\frac\kappa2\right)=1$$

In the following, rewrite the estimated Sharpe ratio \(\:\widehat{SR}=\stackrel{-}{R}/{S}_{R}\:\)as

$$\:\widehat{SR}=\frac{{\mu_{R}}+\overline{r}}{{s}_{r}}={St}_{T}/\sqrt{T}+{\mu}_{R}/{s}_{r}$$

where.
