This is an open-access original research article published in the Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting (Volume 67, pages 869–889, 2026), published December 29, 2025, by Lie-Jane Kao (Affiliation 1), Cheng-Few Lee (Affiliation 2), and Han-Hsing Lee (Affiliation 3). A correction to the article was published on February 5, 2026.

The paper generalizes Lo's (2002) results on the statistics of Sharpe ratios by allowing asset returns to exhibit fat tails with tail index 0 < κ < 4. The authors derive the asymptotic distribution of the estimated Sharpe ratio under an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) model across four scenarios depending on the tail index κ of asset returns:

- (i) 0 < κ < 1: The asymptotic distribution converges at rate √T to a distribution highly concentrated at two modes +c and -c.
- (ii) 1 < κ < 2: The asymptotic distribution converges at rate T^φ (φ = 1/κ − 1/2 < 1/2) to a skewed distribution with a long right (left) tail depending on whether mean return is positive (negative).
- (iii) 2 < κ < 4: The estimation error converges at rate n^φ (φ = 1 − 2/κ < 1/2) to a stable distribution with tail index κ/2 plus a positive (negative) bias term.
- (iv) κ > 4: The estimation error converges at rate √T to a normal distribution with mean zero, and the estimated Sharpe ratio is asymptotically unbiased.

Key findings: When asset returns are fat-tailed (0 < κ < 2), the population Sharpe ratio does not exist. When 2 < κ < 4, the estimated Sharpe ratio has a positive (negative) bias when mean return is positive (negative) and converges slower than √T. Asymptotic unbiasedness and normality only hold when κ > 4 (finite (4+ε)th moment).

The authors argue fat-tailed distributions may explain why negative Sharpe ratios are unreliable in bear markets, why hedge fund Sharpe ratios are overstated, and the equity premium puzzle observed by Hansen and Jagannathan (1991).

Methodology: The paper uses an AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) model with three assumptions regarding rescaled innovations (i.i.d., zero mean), AR parameter (|ρ|<1), and GARCH parameters (E[ln(A_t)] < 0). The asymptotic distributions are established via self-normalized sums and stable random variables.

Empirical analysis: Daily excess returns of eight portfolios constructed by K. French (January 2, 2000 to March 29, 2019; T = 4,840 days) were analyzed, including size, short-term reversal, momentum, and operating profitability-based portfolios. An inference method based on subsampling (Politis and Romano 1994) is provided, and empirical studies using CRSP fund data show that for major ETFs and mutual funds, the estimated κ values are all below 4, indicating fat tails in daily returns. This implies the Sharpe ratio is not asymptotically normal and may be biased, so caution is advised when using the Sharpe ratio for comparing investment performance, especially in daily or high-frequency studies.
args.key_excerpts: "We show that the asymptotic behavior of the estimated Sharpe ratio is biased and converges at a slower rate as 2<κ<4. Therefore, the risk-return payoff information provided by the estimated Sharpe ratio can be misleading."

## Abstract

An intersection–union test for supporting the hypothesis that a given investment strategy is optimal among a set of alternatives is presented. It compares the Sharpe ratio of the benchmark with that of each other strategy. The intersection–union test takes serial dependence into account and does not presume that asset returns are multivariate normally distributed. An empirical study based on the G–7 countries demonstrates that it is hard to find significant results due to the lack of data, which confirms a general observation in empirical finance.

Keywords:

[ergodicity](/search?q=ergodicity); [Gordin’s condition](/search?q=Gordin%E2%80%99s+condition); [heteroscedasticity](/search?q=heteroscedasticity); [intersection–union test](/search?q=intersection%E2%80%93union+test); [Jobson–Korkie test](/search?q=Jobson%E2%80%93Korkie+test); [performance measurement](/search?q=performance+measurement); [Sharpe ratio](/search?q=Sharpe+ratio)

## 1. Motivation

This work builds upon [Frahm et al.](#B13-risks-06-00040) ([2012](#B13-risks-06-00040)), in which the authors argue why joint and multiple testing procedures should be applied in order to judge whether or not some investment strategy is optimal among a set of several alternatives. [Frahm et al.](#B13-risks-06-00040) ([2012](#B13-risks-06-00040)) can be understood as a complement to [DeMiguel et al.](#B8-risks-06-00040) ([2009](#B8-risks-06-00040)), who doubt that portfolio optimization on the basis of time-series information is worthwhile at all. Indeed, modern portfolio theory suffers from a serious drawback, namely that portfolio weights are very sensitive to estimation risk. It is well known that portfolio optimization fails on estimating expected asset returns.

[DeMiguel et al.](#B8-risks-06-00040) ([2009](#B8-risks-06-00040)) show that well-established investment strategies are not significantly better than the naive strategy, i.e., the equally weighted portfolio. Of course, this does not mean that naive diversification is optimal, but we usually do not have enough observations in order to prove the opposite. They highlight a general problem of empirical finance, namely that hypothesis testing is difficult due to the lack of data. This is all the more true if there is more than one (single) null hypothesis. The results reported by [DeMiguel et al.](#B8-risks-06-00040) ([2009](#B8-risks-06-00040)) are convincing, but their statistical methodology does not take the undesirable effects of joint and multiple testing into account. The same holds true for similar studies (see, e.g., [Fletcher 2011](#B11-risks-06-00040); [Low et al. 2016](#B21-risks-06-00040)). By contrast, the test presented in this work is designed to address those problems.

The literature provides a wide range of different investment strategies (see, e.g., [Burgess 2000](#B6-risks-06-00040); [Conrad and Kaul 1998](#B7-risks-06-00040); [DeMiguel et al. 2009](#B8-risks-06-00040); [Menkhoff et al. 2012](#B23-risks-06-00040); [Sawik 2012](#B31-risks-06-00040); [Shen et al. 2007](#B35-risks-06-00040); [Szakmary et al. 2010](#B36-risks-06-00040); [Vrugt et al. 2004](#B38-risks-06-00040); [Zagrodny 2003](#B39-risks-06-00040)) and we are typically concerned with the question of whether a given investment strategy is optimal among a set of alternatives.[1](#fn001-risks-06-00040) In order to validate our hypothesis, we usually compare the performance of our benchmark, e.g., its certainty equivalent or Sharpe ratio, with the performance of each other strategy that is taken into consideration. Let be the number of investment strategies and be our benchmark. We may suppose that without loss of generality. Furthermore, let be a (column) vector of performance measures. Now, first of all, consider the hypotheses

That is, states that our benchmark is optimal. After performing a (joint) hypothesis test, we could reject the null hypothesis in favor of the alternative hypothesis . In this case, we could say that there exists some strategy that is better than our benchmark, but not which one.[2](#fn002-risks-06-00040) By contrast, if we are not able to reject , we must not conclude that our benchmark is optimal. A well-known method for testing the intersection of a number of single null hypotheses is studied by [Roy](#B30-risks-06-00040) ([1953](#B30-risks-06-00040)), which is called a union–intersection test ([Sen and Silvapulle 2002](#B33-risks-06-00040)). However, union-intersection tests are not the object of this work.

By contrast, I consider here the following hypotheses:Now, the joint null hypothesis asserts that our benchmark is not optimal. If we are able to reject , our benchmark turns out to be (significantly) optimal among all alternatives. By contrast, in the case in which we cannot reject the null hypothesis, we must not conclude that our benchmark is outperformed by any other strategy. Applying a test for might be the primary goal both in theoretical and in practical applications of portfolio theory.

The former test can be rewritten, equivalently, aswhereas the latter test readsThis explains the chosen symbols for the null and the alternative hypothesis. However, in the following, I focus on the latter test and write only “” and “” for notational convenience.

The test proposed in this work is very simple: The null hypothesis is rejected if and only if we can reject each single hypothesis in favor of . Let be the event that is rejected. The probability that all single null hypotheses are rejected amounts to

If is true for some we must have that , where denotes the significance level of the (single) hypothesis test for . Under , at least one single null hypothesis must be true and thus we have that

At first glance, this testing procedure might seem to suffer from a lack of power because it does not take the dependence structure of the single test statistics into account. Nonetheless, it is a likelihood-ratio test that is commonly referred to as an intersection–union test ([Berger 1997](#B2-risks-06-00040)). Thus, it inherits the general asymptotic optimality properties of likelihood-ratio tests that are known from likelihood theory (see, e.g., [van der Vaart 1998, chp. 15 and 16](#B37-risks-06-00040)). Another striking feature might be the fact that the overall test has the same significance level as each single test. This is because is rejected only if all single tests lead to a rejection and so we need no Bonferroni correction in order to preserve the significance level of each single test. For more details on that topic, see [Berger](#B2-risks-06-00040) ([1997](#B2-risks-06-00040)) as well as [Sen and Silvapulle](#B33-risks-06-00040) ([2002](#B33-risks-06-00040)).

In this work, I present an intersection–union test in order to decide whether a given investment strategy is optimal among a set of alternative strategies. This is done with respect to the Sharpe ratio. Joint and multiple tests for the Sharpe ratio are applied also in [Frahm et al.](#B13-risks-06-00040) ([2012](#B13-risks-06-00040)) by using a stationary block–bootstrap procedure. By contrast, I provide here analytical results. I refrain from assuming that asset returns are serially independent and multivariate normally distributed. Each single test represents a (nonparametric) generalization of the Jobson–Korkie test ([Jobson and Korkie 1981](#B17-risks-06-00040); [Memmel 2003](#B22-risks-06-00040)). Finally, I apply the intersection–union test to historical data.

The same problem is addressed by [Ledoit and Wolf](#B19-risks-06-00040) ([2008](#B19-risks-06-00040)) as well as [Schmid and Schmidt](#B32-risks-06-00040) ([2009](#B32-risks-06-00040)) in a bivariate setting. However, the intersection–union test presented here is motivated by a multivariate point of view, i.e., , and its primary goal is to avoid any kind of selection bias that can occur when testing a joint hypothesis. Thus, it cannot be said that the intersection–union test is “better” or “worse” than the tests proposed by [Ledoit and Wolf](#B19-risks-06-00040) ([2008](#B19-risks-06-00040)). It is hardly possible to provide any general answer to this question at all ([Ledoit and Wolf 2008, sct. 4 and 5](#B19-risks-06-00040)). Instead, I try to fill a gap between [Frahm et al.](#B13-risks-06-00040) ([2012](#B13-risks-06-00040)) as well as [Ledoit and Wolf](#B19-risks-06-00040) ([2008](#B19-risks-06-00040)):

## 2. The Intersection–Union Test

### 2.1. Gordin’s Condition

In the following, “” denotes almost sure convergence, whereas “” stands for convergence in distribution. Let be the price of some asset or, more generally, the value of some strategy at time . Throughout this work, the terms “asset” and “strategy” as well as “price” and “value” are used synonymously. The asset return after Period t is defined as .[3](#fn003-risks-06-00040) I assume that the return process is (strongly) stationary with expected return and variance . The process shall also be ergodic. This means that for each integrable function f of R, where the random variable R has the same distribution as each component of . This guarantees that every finite moment of R can be consistently estimated by the corresponding moment estimator. The return process is ergodic if it is mixing ([Bradley 2005](#B4-risks-06-00040)). More precisely, for all , the random vector is asymptotically independent of as ([Hayashi 2000, p. 101](#B16-risks-06-00040)).

The ergodicity of implies that , where is the sample mean of . Put another way, the return process satisfies the Strong Law of Large Numbers. In order to preserve the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), i.e., , we need an additional requirement. This is known as Gordin’s condition ([Hayashi 2000, p. 402](#B16-risks-06-00040)). Let be the history of at time . It is assumed that converges in mean square to as and, according to [Hayashi](#B16-risks-06-00040) ([2000, p. 403](#B16-risks-06-00040)), we must have thatwith for . It can be shown that , where is the autocovariance function of ([Hayashi 2000, Proposition 6.10](#B16-risks-06-00040)). The number is referred to as the large-sample variance of , whereas represents its stationary variance. In the following, I assume that and that Gordin’s condition is satisfied not only for but also for .

The aforementioned requirements can easily be extended to any d-dimensional return process ([Hayashi 2000, p. 405](#B16-risks-06-00040)) and applied to a broad class of standard time-series models. There exists a number of alternative criteria for the CLT, which can be found, e.g., in [Brockwell and Davis](#B5-risks-06-00040) ([1991, p. 213](#B5-risks-06-00040)) as well as [Hamilton](#B14-risks-06-00040) ([1994, p. 195](#B14-risks-06-00040)). However, to the best of my knowledge, Gordin’s condition represents the most unrestrictive set of assumptions about the serial dependence structure of a stochastic process ([Eagleson 1975](#B9-risks-06-00040)). In particular, it can be considered a natural generalization of the CLT for martingale difference sequences ([Hayashi](#B16-risks-06-00040) [2000, p. 106](#B16-risks-06-00040)).

It is worth emphasizing that the number of dimensions, d, is supposed to be fixed. At least, we have to assume that . If tends to a finite number, the CLT might become invalid and other interesting issues, which are well-known from random matrix theory, can arise ([Frahm and Jaekel 2015](#B12-risks-06-00040)). By contrast, if the number of observations relative to the number of strategies is sufficiently large, we may expect that the CLT is satisfied under the aforementioned conditions.

I suppose, without loss of generality, that the risk-free interest rate is constantly zero. That is, I implicitly refer to asset returns in excess of the risk-free interest rate that can be observed at the beginning of each period. The Sharpe ratio ([Sharpe 1966](#B34-risks-06-00040)) is frequently used as a performance measure both in theory and in practice. In the following section, I present the intersection–union test, which can be applied in order to judge whether a given investment strategy possesses the largest Sharpe ratio among a set of alternatives. This can be done under the quite general assumptions about the return process mentioned above.

### 2.3. Empirical Study

In order to demonstrate the intersection–union test, I consider monthly excess returns on the MSCI stock indices for the G–7 countries, i.e., Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK and USA, from January 1970 to January 2018. ## 3. Conclusions

In portfolio optimization, we are often concerned with the question of whether a given investment strategy is optimal among a set of alternatives. In this work, I presented an intersection–union test for the null hypothesis that the benchmark is suboptimal in terms of the Sharpe ratio. The proposed test can easily be implemented. Furthermore, it accounts for serial dependence and it does not presume that asset returns are multivariate normally distributed. Thus, it is compatible with the stylized facts of empirical finance. However, an empirical study demonstrates that, in most practical applications, it is hard to reject the null hypothesis due to the lack of data.

This is a scientific article titled "An Intersection–Union Test for the Sharpe Ratio" by Gabriel Frahm, published in the journal Risks (MDPI) in 2018, Volume 6, Issue 2, Article 40 (DOI: 10.3390/risks6020040). The author is affiliated with the Chair of Applied Stochastics and Risk Management, Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Helmut Schmidt University, Hamburg, Germany. The article was received 26 February 2018, revised 12 April 2018, accepted 13 April 2018, and published 19 April 2018. It is part of the special issue "Risk vs Performance Measures: Robustness, Elicitability and Time-Dependency."

MAIN TOPIC AND PURPOSE: The paper presents an intersection–union test to determine whether a given investment strategy is optimal (has the largest Sharpe ratio) among a set of alternative strategies. The test addresses problems of joint and multiple testing that prior studies (e.g., DeMiguel et al. 2009) did not account for.

KEY METHODOLOGY:
- The null hypothesis is that the benchmark is suboptimal in terms of Sharpe ratio; rejecting it supports the claim that the benchmark is significantly optimal among all alternatives.
- The test rejects the null only if every single hypothesis can be rejected (i.e., if the largest p-value of all single tests falls below the significance level α). No Bonferroni correction is needed since all single tests must be rejected.
- It is a likelihood-ratio test (intersection–union test, per Berger 1997) inheriting asymptotic optimality properties.
- Each single test is a nonparametric generalization of the Jobson–Korkie test (1981), corrected by Memmel (2003) for a typographical error.
- The test accounts for serial dependence via Gordin's condition (rather than assuming serial independence or multivariate normality), making it compatible with stylized facts of empirical finance (heteroscedasticity, serial dependence).
- Closed-form expressions for standard errors are derived (rather than using bootstrapping as in prior work by Frahm et al. 2012).
- A box-kernel-type HAC (heteroscedasticity-autocorrelation consistent) estimator is used for large-sample variances.
- Key assumption: the benchmark must be chosen before examining Sharpe ratios to avoid selection bias; can be applied out-of-sample if benchmark chosen based on historical data.
- The test is distinguished from bivariate tests by Ledoit and Wolf (2008) and Schmid and Schmidt (2009), which lack a multivariate perspective.

EMPIRICAL STUDY: Monthly excess returns on MSCI stock indices for the G–7 countries (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK, USA) from January 1970 to January 2018 (sample size 577 observations), using 3-month US Treasury bill rate as the risk-free rate. The equally weighted portfolio (EWP) of all G-7 countries was chosen as benchmark, justified by international diversification arguments (Jorion 1985).

KEY EMPIRICAL FINDINGS:
- First-order autocorrelations of asset returns do not significantly differ from zero, but there is strong evidence of conditional heteroscedasticity in monthly asset returns.
- Large-sample variance estimates for asset returns did not differ much from stationary ones (except Japan, where large-sample variance was more than twice the stationary variance), but large-sample variances of squared returns were always more than twice their stationary counterparts—confirming it is inappropriate to ignore serial dependence.
- UK had the largest Sharpe ratio in the sample period, so the EWP could not be shown to be significantly optimal. Interestingly, the EWP had the largest Sharpe ratio before the 2007–2008 financial crisis.
- Only Italy satisfied the stringent condition (t-statistic above the critical threshold) for rejecting the null hypothesis.
- Standard errors of Sharpe ratios are large relative to estimates despite the large number of observations—a common problem in financial econometrics/performance measurement.
- The Jobson–Korkie assumption (serial independence + multivariate normality) underestimates standard errors for some indices but overestimates them for others.

CONCLUSIONS: The intersection–union test can be easily implemented, accounts for serial dependence, and does not presume multivariate normality. However, the empirical study demonstrates it is hard to reject the null hypothesis in most practical applications due to lack of data—confirming a general observation in empirical finance that comparing investment strategies by historical observation is very difficult, especially under joint or multiple hypothesis testing (as in Frahm et al. 2012).

<webpage_content>
# The Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio: Bias-Adjustment, Confidence Intervals, Hypothesis Testing and Minimum Track Record Length

10 minute read

The Sharpe ratio[1](#fn:1) is one of the most commonly used measure of financial portfolio performance, but because it is deeply rooted in mean-variance theory, its usage with return distributions deviating from normality (e.g. hedge funds, cryptocurrencies) is frequently questioned[2](#fn:2).

One solution to this issue is to switch to a probabilistic framework, under which the Sharpe ratio computed from a finite sample of observed returns is considered as [a statistical estimator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estimator) affected by error of an unobservable true Sharpe ratio, with the greater the non-normality of returns the greater the estimation error.

In this blog post inspired by the paper *Comparing Sharpe ratios: So where are the p-values?* from Opdyke[3](#fn:3), I will summarize the main results of this probabilistic framework and I will use them to analyze the performances of a Bitcoin trading strategy recently published by the creator of the Bitcoin Stock-to-Flow model [PlanB](https://twitter.com/100trillionUSD).

> * A Google sheet corresponding to this post is available [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IeMHUZLv_EezYscrEtaW0KQKsyS6PSvY6mkIrR6ewE4/edit?usp=sharing)

### Mathematical preliminaries

Let be:

* $r\_1,…,r\_T$ the observed returns of an asset/fund/portfolio/trading strategy/etc. over $T$ periods of time
* $\hat{\mu}$ the arithmetic average of these returns $\hat{\mu} = \frac{\sum\_{t=1}^{T} r\_t}{T}$
* $\hat{\sigma}$ the standard deviation[4](#fn:4) of these returns $\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum\_{t=1}^T (r\_t - \overline{\mu})^2 }{T}}$
* $r\_f$, the value of the risk free rate

Then, the Sharpe ratio $\widehat{SR}$ of the observed asset/fund/portfolio/trading strategy/etc. is defined as

\[\widehat{SR} = \frac{\hat{\mu} - r\_f}{\hat{\sigma}}\]

The usage of hats above emphases that $\hat{\mu}$, $\hat{\sigma}$ and $\widehat{SR}$ are quantities computed from the observed sample of returns $r\_1,…,r\_T$ while the true arithmetic average return $\mu$, the true standard deviation $\sigma$ and the true Sharpe ratio $ SR = \frac{\mu - r\_f}{\sigma} $ are quantities associated with an unobservable return generating process.

It follows that $\hat{\mu}$, $\hat{\sigma}$ and $\widehat{SR}$ are statistical estimators of their true counterparts, subject to estimation error.

Extending the work of Mertens[5](#fn:9) and Christie[6](#fn:8), Opdyke[3](#fn:3) derives the asymptotic statistical distribution for $\widehat{SR}$ under the general assumption of stationarity and ergodicity of returns

\[\widehat{SR} \overset{a}{\sim} N \left( SR, \frac{1 - \kappa SR + (\gamma - 1) \frac{SR^2}{4}}{T} \right)\]

, where $\kappa$ and $\gamma$ are respectively the true skewness and the true kurtosis of the unobservable return generating process.

This asymptotic statistical distribution provides a theoretical basis for making inference about the Sharpe ratio *under the […] realistic conditions of time-varying conditional volatilities, serial correlation, and otherwise non-iid returns*[3](#fn:3), and Opdyke uses it to establish several properties of the Sharpe ratio estimator $\widehat{SR}$.

#### Confidence intervals for $\widehat{SR}$

The asymptotic statistical distribution for $\widehat{SR}$ enables to build three [confidence intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval) at a confidence level $100(1 - \alpha)$% for $\widehat{SR}$.

Using the notation $\widehat{SE(\widehat{SR})} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \hat{\kappa} \widehat{SR} + (\hat{\gamma} - 1) \frac{\widehat{SR}^2}{4}}{T}}$ for the estimator of the standard error of $\widehat{SR}$, these are[7](#fn:11):

* The two-sided confidence interval

\[\left[ \widehat{SR} - z\_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}} \widehat{SE(\widehat{SR})}, \widehat{SR} + z\_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}} \widehat{SE(\widehat{SR})} \right]\]

* The lower one-sided confidence interval

\[\left] -\infty, \widehat{SR} + z\_{1-\alpha} \widehat{SE(\widehat{SR})} \right]\]

* The upper one-sided confidence interval

\[\left[\widehat{SR} - z\_{1-\alpha} \widehat{SE(\widehat{SR})} , +\infty \right[\]

, where the quantity $\hat{\kappa}$ (resp. $\hat{\gamma}$) is an estimator of $\kappa$ (resp. $\gamma$) computed from the observed sample of returns $r\_1,…,r\_T$ and $z\_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}$ (resp. $z\_{1-\alpha}$) is the $1−\frac{\alpha}{2}$ (resp. $1-\alpha$) [critical value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_value) of the standard normal distribution.

Using [one of the interpretations of confidence intervals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confidence_interval#Interpretation), each of these confidence intervals represents values that are not [statistically significantly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_significance) different from $\widehat{SR}$ at a confidence level $100(1 - \alpha)%$.

It is interesting to note that while $\widehat{SR}$ depends only on

* The arithmetic average of the observed returns $\hat{\mu}$
* The standard deviation of the observed returns $\hat{\sigma}$

, the standard error of $\widehat{SR}$ depends on

* The arithmetic average of the observed returns $\hat{\mu}$
* The standard deviation of the observed returns $\hat{\sigma}$
* The skewness of the observed returns $\hat{\kappa}$
* The kurtosis of the observed returns $\hat{\gamma}$
* The number of observed returns[8](#fn:13) $T$

Figure 1, taken from Bailey and de Prado[9](#fn:10), illustrates how exactly the standard error of $\widehat{SR}$ is impacted by the true skewness and the true kurtosis in the case of a return generating process made of a mixture of two Gaussians with $SR$ equal to 1.

 [![Standard error of the Sharpe ratio estimator as a function of skewness and kurtosis](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-bailey-de-prado-example.png)](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-bailey-de-prado-example.png) 

Figure 1. Standard error of the Sharpe ratio estimator $\widehat{SR}$ with a true Sharpe ratio $SR = 1$, as a function of true skewness and true kurtosis. Source: Bailey and de Prado.

 

As they put it[9](#fn:10):

> although skewness and kurtosis does not affect the point estimate of $SR$, it greatly impacts its confidence bands, and consequently its statistical significance.

More on *kurtosis does not affect the point estimate of $SR$* right away, though.

#### Small sample bias of $\widehat{SR}$

Opdyke[3](#fn:3) provides the following bias adjustment formula for $\widehat{SR}$, valid for any return distribution

\[E \left[ \widehat{SR} \right] = SR \left( 1 + \frac{1}{4} \frac{\gamma - 1}{T} \right)\]

Thus, while it is true that kurtosis does not affect the point estimate of $SR$, kurtosis do affect the unbiased point estimate of $SR$!

#### Hypothesis testing for $\widehat{SR}$

The asymptotic statistical distribution for $\widehat{SR}$ also enables to create [statistical tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistical_hypothesis_testing).

In the context of performance evaluation, a test of interest is to determine whether a given value of $\widehat{SR}$ is statistically significantly greater than a reference Sharpe ratio $c$, with typically:

* A reference Sharpe ratio of $c = 0$ reflecting excess returns relative to the risk free rate[10](#fn:14)
* A reference Sharpe ratio of $c = 1$ (annualized) reflecting excess returns relative to volatility

For this test:

* The exact statistical test to use is the [one-sided right-tailed hypothesis test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-_and_two-tailed_tests) with significance level $\alpha$[11](#fn:12)

\[H\_0: SR \leq c \textrm{} \textrm{ v.s. } H\_1: SR > c\]

* The [*t*-statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-statistic)[3](#fn:3) is equal to

\[t = \frac{\widehat{SR} - c}{ \sqrt{\frac{1 - \hat{\kappa} \widehat{SR} + (\hat{\gamma} - 1) \frac{\widehat{SR}^2}{4}}{T}} }\]

* The critical value is $z\_{1-\alpha}$, the $1-\alpha$ critical value of the standard normal distribution
* The [*p*-value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-value) is equal to

\[p = 1 - \Phi(t)\]

, where $\Phi$ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.

* Opdyke[3](#fn:3) provides guidance on the [type I and type II errors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_I_and_type_II_errors), reproduced in Figure 2 for convenience.

 [![Simulation study results on the level and the power of the right-tailed test for the Sharpe ratio estimator](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-opdyke-table.png)](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-opdyke-table.png) 

Figure 2. Simulation study results on the level and the power of the right-tailed test for the Sharpe ratio estimator $\widehat{SR}$. Source: Opdyke.

 

#### The Probabilistic Sharpe ratio $\widehat{PSR}$

To avoid referring to the statistical machinery of hypothesis testing, Bailey and de Prado[9](#fn:10) introduced the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* $\widehat{PSR}(c)$, defined as the probability that the Sharpe ratio estimator $\widehat{SR}$ is greater than a reference Sharpe ratio $c$, which

> takes [negative skewness and fat tails] into account and delivers a corrected, atemporal measure of performance expressed in terms of probability of skill

The *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* is by definition equal to 1 minus the *p*-value of the hypothesis test from the previous section, so that[12](#fn:15)

\[\widehat{PSR}(c) = \Phi\left( \frac{\widehat{SR} - c}{ \sqrt{\frac{1 - \hat{\kappa} \widehat{SR} + (\hat{\gamma} - 1) \frac{\widehat{SR}^2}{4}}{T}} } \right )\]

To be noted that the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* provides the same level of information as the *p*-value of this hypothesis test, so that using one or the other is a matter of personal preference.

#### The Minimum Track Record Length $\widehat{MinTRL}$

Because the value of the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* increases with the number of observed returns, which corresponds to the length of the track record in case of a fund or a trading strategy, Bailey and de Prado[9](#fn:10) also introduced the *Minimum Track Record Length* $\widehat{MinTRL}(c)$, defined as the minimum number of observed returns required to ensure at a confidence level $100(1 - \alpha)$% that $\widehat{SR}$ is greater than a reference Sharpe ratio $c$.

The *Minimum Track Record Length* is equal to[13](#fn:16)

\[\widehat{MinTRL}(c) = \left( 1 - \hat{\kappa} \widehat{SR} + (\hat{\gamma} - 1) \frac{\widehat{SR}^2}{4} \right) \left( \frac{ z\_{1-\alpha} }{\widehat{SR} - c} \right)^2\]

### Implementation in **Portfolio Optimizer**

In **Portfolio Optimizer**, the following endpoints are implemented:

* [`/portfolios/analysis/mean-variance/sharpe-ratio/confidence-interval`](https://docs.portfoliooptimizer.io/), to compute the various confidence intervals for the Sharpe ratio of a portfolio
* [`/portfolios/analysis/mean-variance/sharpe-ratio/probabilistic`](https://docs.portfoliooptimizer.io/), to compute the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* of a portfolio

### Examples of usage

#### Skillful hedge fund styles

I will first reproduce the results of Bailey and de Prado[9](#fn:10) and perform an analysis of the [HFRI Indices](https://www.hfr.com/hfri-index-characteristics).

For this, I use the monthly indices levels over the period from the 31st December 1999 to the 30th May 2011[14](#fn:17) downloaded [from the HFR website](https://www.hfr.com/family-indices/hfri) and compute the values $\widehat{SR}$, $\widehat{PSR}(0)$ and $\widehat{PSR}(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt12})$[15](#fn:18).

The results are reported in Figure 3.

 [![Performance analysis on HFR Indices](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-hfr-indices.png)](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-hfr-indices.png) 

Figure 3. Probabilistic Sharpe ratio analysis on HFR Indices.

 

Compared to Bailey and de Prado[9](#fn:10), data for three indices are missing[16](#fn:19) plus the computed values for the other indices are slightly different[17](#fn:20), but their two conclusions remain unaltered:

* Most of the HRF Indices exhibit a *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* greater than 0 at a 95% confidence level
* Only 9 (+1, more on this below) HRF Indices exhibit a *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* greater than 0.5 (annualized) at a 95% confidence level

One remark though.

The computations for the index *HFRI Fund Weighted Composite Index - GBP* completely differ between Bailey and de Prado and my reproduction, with for example a Sharpe ratio of $\approx 0.181$ v.s. $\approx 0.327$.

So, I strongly suspect that the underlying *HFRIFWIG* index data are not the same and that using Bailey and de Prado data, the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* of this index would not have been greater than 0.5 (annualized) at a 95% confidence level!

#### Analysis of a Bitcoin trading strategy

[PlanB](https://twitter.com/100trillionUSD), the anonymous creator of the Bitcoin Stock-to-Flow model, recently released a trading strategy for Bitcoin.

This strategy, relying on [the RSI technical indicator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_strength_index), is described in details PlanB’s article *Quant Investing 101*[18](#fn:21) and produces the portfolio equity curve displayed in Figure 4, based on the reproduction of PlanB’s strategy by [Andrea Meleri](https://twitter.com/100trillionUSD/status/1557440918734704644).

 [![PlanB Bitcoin RSI strategy - Portfolio equity curve](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-planb-bitcoin-strategy-portfolio-values.png)](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-planb-bitcoin-strategy-portfolio-values.png) 

Figure 4. PlanB Bitcoin RSI strategy - Portfolio equity curve.

 

This strategy produces an annualized Sharpe ratio of $\approx 1$, but what about the statistical significance of this Sharpe ratio, especially since this strategy trades infrequently?

Thanks to the probabilistic framework presented in this blog post, it is possible to answer this question using for example the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio*.

Indeed, as highlighted by Bailey and de Prado[9](#fn:10):

> It is not unusual to find strategies with irregular trading frequencies, such as weekly strategies that may not trade for a month. This poses a problem when computing an annualized Sharpe ratio, and there is no consensus as how skill should be measured in the context of irregular bets. Because PSR measures skill in probabilistic terms, it is invariant to calendar conventions.

I choose to compute the values $\widehat{PSR}(0)$, $\widehat{PSR}(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt 12})$, $\widehat{PSR}(\frac{0.75}{\sqrt 12})$ and $MinTRL(\frac{0.75}{\sqrt 12})$ at a confidence level of 95%, which are reported in Figure 5.

 [![PlanB Bitcoin strategy - Probabilistic Sharpe ratio analysis](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-planb-bitcoin-strategy-analysis.png)](/assets/images/blog/sharpe-ratio-planb-bitcoin-strategy-analysis.png) 

Figure 5. PlanB Bitcoin strategy - Probabilistic Sharpe ratio analysis.

 

The values of $\widehat{PSR}(0)$ and $\widehat{PSR}(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt 12})$ support the hypothesis that this strategy exhibit some interesting performances, but the value of $\widehat{MinTRL}(\frac{0.75}{\sqrt 12})$ implies that around four years of additional returns[19](#fn:22) are required in order to support the hypothesis that the real annualized Sharpe ratio of this strategy is greater than 0.75, which is still very far from 1!

In conclusion, this strategy definitely seems to be a good strategy, but due to its nature, there is not enough data yet to support the hypothesis that it is very good.

### Conclusion

This is the end of this post, the first one in a series about the probabilistic framework for the Sharpe ratio.

In the second post of this series, I will present an additional result from Opdyke[3](#fn:3) which enables to test whether two estimated Sharpe ratios are statistically different.

Meanwhile, and especially if you are a trading strategy developer, do not hesitate to do like [QuantConnect](https://www.quantconnect.com/forum/discussion/6483/probabilistic-sharpe-ratio/p1) and implement the *Probabilistic Sharpe ratio* as a performance evaluation metric, whether in-house or though a Web API call to **Portfolio Optimizer**!

args.summary:
This blog post presents the probabilistic framework for the Sharpe ratio, based primarily on Opdyke's paper "Comparing Sharpe ratios: So where are the p-values?" (2007) and Bailey and de Prado's work. The post explains the mathematical foundations, including the asymptotic statistical distribution of the Sharpe ratio estimator under stationarity and ergodicity, which incorporates skewness (κ) and kurtosis (γ) into the estimation error. Key concepts covered include:

1. **Confidence intervals**: Three types (two-sided, lower one-sided, upper one-sided) built from the asymptotic distribution, where the standard error depends on mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, and number of observations T.

2. **Small sample bias**: The bias adjustment formula E[SR̂] = SR(1 + (1/4)(γ−1)/T) shows that kurtosis, while not affecting the point estimate, does affect the unbiased point estimate.

3. **Hypothesis testing**: A one-sided right-tailed test (H0: SR ≤ c vs. H1: SR > c) with t-statistic and p-value based on the standard normal distribution.

4. **Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR)**: Defined as the probability that the Sharpe ratio exceeds a reference ratio c, equal to 1 minus the p-value of the hypothesis test. It accounts for non-normality (negative skewness, fat tails) and is invariant to calendar conventions, making it suitable for strategies with irregular trading frequencies.

5. **Minimum Track Record Length (MinTRL)**: The minimum number of observations required to ensure at a confidence level that the Sharpe ratio exceeds a reference value.

The post includes two empirical applications:
- **HFR Indices analysis**: Reproduces Bailey and de Prado's results, confirming that most HFRI indices exhibit a PSR greater than 0 at 95% confidence, and only 9 indices exhibit a PSR greater than 0.5 (annualized).
- **PlanB Bitcoin RSI trading strategy analysis**: The strategy produces an annualized Sharpe ratio of ≈1, but PSR values suggest more data is needed. The MinTRL(0.75/√12) value of ≈184 implies about 4 years of additional returns (≈48 monthly data points) are required to support the hypothesis that the true annualized Sharpe ratio exceeds 0.75.

The post also mentions implementation in Portfolio Optimizer via two API endpoints: `/portfolios/analysis/mean-variance/sharpe-ratio/confidence-interval` and `/portfolios/analysis/mean-variance/sharpe-ratio/probabilistic`. A second post in the series is planned to cover testing whether two estimated Sharpe ratios are statistically different.
args.key_excerpts: "It is not unusual to find strategies with irregular trading frequencies, such as weekly strategies that may not trade for a month. This poses a problem when computing an annualized Sharpe ratio, and there is no consensus as how skill should be measured in the context of irregular bets. Because PSR measures skill in probabilistic terms, it is invariant to calendar conventions."

## Highlights

*   •We provide the distribution of the difference between maximum Sharpe ratios. 
*   •This is derived under general assumptions, both with and without short sales. 
*   •It forms the basis for incremental variable tests under very general assumptions. 
*   •We characterize the long-only solution and provide conditions for global optimality. 

## Abstract

Most existing results on the distribution of the maximum Sharpe ratio depend on the assumption of multivariate normal return distributions. We use recent results from the literature to provide an analytical representation of the distribution of the difference between two maximum Sharpe ratios for much less restrictive distributional assumptions, both with and without short sales. Knowing the distribution of the difference enables us to test ex ante whether or not the inclusion of additional variables leads to a significant improvement in the maximum Sharpe ratio. In addition, we characterize the optimal long-only solution and provide conditions for global optimality.

## Keywords

## Introduction

Particularly in times of low interest rates and decreasing risk premia, investors look for potential improvements to their portfolios by including new asset classes. Also within asset classes, the performance might be improved by considering variables such as book-to-market or momentum as potential return drivers. For some of these variables, their impact on average returns is generally accepted, since there exists both a sound theoretical foundation and solid empirical evidence. For others, it is less clear whether their inclusion significantly enhances the portfolio opportunity set. Fama and French (2015) discuss the related literature and criticize the standard line of argument used there, which employs Fama and MacBeth (1973) cross-sectional regressions to sort stocks into portfolios and illustrates the (seeming) importance of a new candidate variable on the basis of univariate return spreads. Fama and French (2015) demonstrate that judging a variable’s importance by the univariate spread it produces in average returns overestimates its positive impact compared to the true impact observed when adding this variable in a portfolio context.

When starting from an existing portfolio, only the incremental improvement from new additions is relevant. If a candidate component improves the portfolio opportunity set, it should be included, and disregarded otherwise. In classical portfolio theory,1 if a riskless asset is available, this may be recast into an equivalent statement formulated in terms of the Sharpe ratio: A candidate component should be included if and only if it significantly increases the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio. Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken (1989) note that their approach to testing portfolio efficiency, which is formulated in a regression framework, can also be interpreted as a test for the significance in the Sharpe ratio improvement caused by the improvement in the opportunity set.

The Sharpe ratio has some well-known shortcomings: It is based on the standard deviation, which is not a coherent risk measure in the sense of Artzner, Delbaen, Eber, and Heath (1999). Moreover, real-world return distributions are not necessarily multivariate normal, but frequently exhibit skewness and excess kurtosis. To account for these deviations from multivariate normality, extensions to the Sharpe ratio have been proposed (see, e.g., Biglova, Ortobelli, Rachev, & Stoyanov, 2004). Despite these shortcomings and the existence of alternatives that are theoretically more appealing, the Sharpe ratio is still the most widely used reward-to-risk ratio in practice, and it may even be the main relevant criterion for many practitioners. A portfolio manager considering a new variable may hence be interested in testing whether or not its inclusion would lead to a significant increase in the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio. Fama and French (2015) discuss the use of Gibbons et al. (1989) (GRS) tests for this purpose and illustrate a major disadvantage of these tests from a practical perspective: Since the tests assume that unlimited short sales are allowed, they may indicate a significant increase in the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio in cases where the portfolios leading to this increase require unrealistic leverage. Fama and French (2015) illustrate numerically that despite highly significant GRS statistics, Sharpe ratio improvements for a long-only investor from adding a third variable to an initial set of two are typically very small. A further disadvantage of the GRS statistic is its assumption of multivariate normal asset returns.

The reason why Fama and French (2015) resort to numerical illustrations for the case of the long-only investor is the lack of a suitable test for the difference between the maximum Sharpe ratios that are attainable with and without an incremental variable when short sales are not allowed. In this paper, we derive such a test for an ex ante comparison of optimal portfolios from different investment opportunity sets, which generalizes their GRS-based test not only for the long-only case, but also for deviations from multivariate normality. Furthermore, whereas the GRS-based test is formulated such that one of the investment opportunity sets is a proper subset of the other, our test allows for comparing any two investment opportunity sets. To derive our test, we will use recent results by Maller, Roberts, and Tourky (2016) on the distribution of the maximum Sharpe ratio under quite general distributional assumptions. The resulting formulae form the basis for comparing maximum Sharpe ratios for two investment opportunity sets. This includes, but is not limited to, testing whether increasing a given investment opportunity set significantly increases the maximum attainable Sharpe ratio.

One potential technical issue that arises with maximization of the Sharpe ratio in the long-only case is in the nature of the optimization problem. The long-only constraints make the problem quasi-concave, which in principle may give rise to multiple (local) optima. However, as noted in Stoyanov, Rachev, and Fabozzi (2007), since the function _g_(_x_) (see e.g., Eq. (1) in Section 3) is a ratio of a linear and a _differentiable_ convex function, the ratio is pseudo-concave in its argument. It is known (Stoyanov et al., 2007) that local extrema of pseudo-concave function are also global. For quasi-concave functions defined in a non-empty convex set, the optimal solution is an extreme point of the convex set. As an additional contribution of this paper, we provide conditions that allow us to check whether any such extreme point is indeed the global optimum we are looking for.

The difference in maximum attainable Sharpe ratios is closely related to mean-variance spanning tests, where the object of interest is usually the entire efficient frontier constructed from the available risky assets. In one sense, the problem studied in this paper appears to be simpler, since it involves only the tangency portfolio (as opposed to the entire efficient frontier). However, most existing mean-variance spanning tests suffer from the assumption of unlimited short sales, and many of these tests assume (conditional) multivariate normality of returns. The relation of this paper to the literature on mean-variance spanning tests will be discussed in more detail in Section 2.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 3 reviews recent results on the distribution of the maximum Sharpe ratio when asset returns are not assumed to be multivariate normal. Section 4 provides a general result for the distribution of the difference between two maximum Sharpe ratios, both with and without short sales. Section 5 briefly discusses potential applications. Section 6 illustrates our results using a numerical example, and Section 7 concludes.

This is a research article published in the European Journal of Operational Research (Volume 265, Issue 2, pages 571-579, dated 1 March 2018, DOI: 10.1016/j.ejor.2017.08.018) by Michael Hanke and Spiridon Penev. The paper addresses a gap in portfolio theory by deriving the analytical distribution of the difference between two maximum Sharpe ratios under much less restrictive distributional assumptions than existing methods, both with and without short sales.

Key points of the paper:
- Most existing results on the distribution of the maximum Sharpe ratio assume multivariate normal return distributions. This paper relaxes that assumption using recent results from Maller, Roberts, and Tourky (2016) on the distribution of the maximum Sharpe ratio under general distributional assumptions.
- Knowing the distribution of the difference between two maximum Sharpe ratios enables ex ante testing of whether adding incremental variables (e.g., new asset classes, book-to-market, momentum) significantly improves the maximum Sharpe ratio.
- The paper generalizes the Gibbons, Ross, and Shanken (1989) (GRS) test, which has two major practical disadvantages: it assumes unlimited short sales (may indicate significant improvements that require unrealistic leverage for long-only investors) and assumes multivariate normal returns.
- Unlike the GRS-based test (which requires one investment opportunity set to be a proper subset of another), the proposed test allows comparison of any two investment opportunity sets.
- The paper characterizes the optimal long-only solution and provides conditions for global optimality, addressing the quasi-concave nature of the Sharpe ratio maximization problem under long-only constraints (the function is pseudo-concave, so local extrema are also global).
- The difference in maximum Sharpe ratios is closely related to mean-variance spanning tests.
- A numerical example uses daily data from Kenneth French's data library, with a 15-year estimation window (August 1, 2000 to July 31, 2015, n=3773), starting with the 5-industries portfolios and the Fama-French 3 factors dataset for the risk-free rate.
- The paper was supported by the Australian Research Council's Discovery Project Funding Scheme (project DP 160103489).
- The article has been cited by 5 other works (including papers on Sharpe ratio fair value via option valuation, parameter-free robust optimization for the maximum-Sharpe portfolio problem, and an intersection-union test for the Sharpe ratio).

## Highlights

*   •We assess the performance of fixed-income mutual funds using regime-switching models. 
*   •Fund returns are described by two distinct volatility related bull and bear regimes. 
*   •Canadian fixed-income fund managers do not have selection abilities. 
*   •Canadian fixed-income fund managers have worse performance during recessions. 
*   •There is mixed evidence on timing abilities of fixed-income fund managers. 

## Abstract

We use Markovian regime-switching models to assess the performance of Canadian fixed-income mutual funds from 1980 to 2011. Fund returns are well described by two distinct volatility related bull and bear regimes. While the selection performance of Canadian fixed-income funds is negative, it is regime dependent and deteriorates during recessions. We also find mixed results on the timing ability of fund managers with poor performance for Canadian inflation protected fixed-income funds, Canadian long-term fixed-income funds, and Canadian money market funds groups. Finally, we show that a multivariate regime-switching model is superior to univariate models given the dynamic market conditions and the fund portfolios’ cross-correlations.

## Introduction

The past fifty years have witnessed an unprecedented development in mutual fund theories and portfolio evaluation which has coincided with more accessible and complete databases. Concurrent with a significant growth in the mutual funds industry, advancement in asset pricing theory and econometric tools met the explosive demand in mutual fund performance evaluation.1 However, the sudden crash in mutual funds after the 2008 financial meltdown challenged classical pricing models and prompted the development of better techniques to estimate the dynamic risks involved in volatile portfolios.

This paper tries to identify skilled Canadian fixed-income fund managers given the variation of an unobservable market risk factor that affects mutual fund returns. Traditional approaches generally evaluate performance based on passive observable benchmarks and assume constant portfolio exposures to market conditions. However, bond portfolios have dynamic market exposures to different market conditions due to active management strategies and to variation in the underlying assets. Therefore, an evaluation procedure that measures fund performance while accounting for time-varying management and market circumstances will yield robust inferences compared to the traditional approach. We examine various specifications of univariate and multivariate Markovian regime-switching models for performance evaluation.

Bond fund performance evaluation theories have developed since the 1990s, with most empirical literature based on linear unconditional asset pricing models. Similar to the evidence for equity fund performance, bond fund performance results generally show that managers rarely outperform corresponding benchmarks and their portfolio returns are skewed to the left. Cornell and Green (1991) report that the performance of low grade bonds is similar to that of high quality bonds after controlling for risk factors. Elton, Gruber, and Blake (1993) find that U.S. bond fund managers underperform their benchmarks, and Elton, Gruber, and Blake (1995) use economic factors to corroborate their earlier result. Silva, Cortez, and Armada (2003) confirm these U.S. findings using European bond fund data. Moneta (2015) reports that active bond fund managers earn abnormal profit equal to their expenses. Their after cost abnormal returns are nil. Ayadi and Kryzanowski (2011) conclude that the selection performance of Canadian bond funds after (before) management-related costs is negative (positive) using a conditional multi-factor model that captures maturity differences and default risks.2 Boney, Comer, and Kelly (2009) develop a model based on Sharpe’s (1992) quadratic programming technique to examine the market timing ability of U.S. high-quality bond fund managers. They report that managers generally fail to achieve abnormal returns either through timing between cash and bonds or across bond maturities, and confirm neutral performance. Du, Huang, and Blanchfield (2009) find that high-quality corporate-bond mutual funds underperform their multifactor benchmark. Chen, Ferson, and Peters (2010) adjust Treynor and Mazuy’s (1966) classical market timing model for nonlinearity and conclude that U.S. bond funds’ managers achieve a slightly positive timing performance during the period 1962–2007. This performance does not, however, offset their management fees. Alternatively, Clare, Sherman, and Thomas (2016) develop an asset class-based performance measure to assess the timing ability of a sample of US, UK, and Canadian balanced funds. Their findings suggest little evidence of asset class timing in all markets. In particular, they report that less than 4% of Canadian multi-class fund managers have fixed-income timing abilities. Li, Luo, and Tee (2017) find evidence that managers of fixed-income oriented hedge funds have liquidity timing skills. Moreover, long only funds show joint liquidity timing of both equity and bonds. Moneta (2015) reports that generally bond fund managers do not have timing abilities with the exception of multi-sectors funds when they shift the credit quality of their portfolios. Goldstein, Jiang, and Ng (2017) show that fund flows chase bond funds performance. They demonstrate that flows are sensitive to bad performance especially for funds holding illiquid assets when total market illiquidity is high.

The regime-switching approach introduced by Hamilton (1989) is an econometric methodology that infers the latent drivers of an observed economic vector. This model is able to capture time-series variance in dynamic markets and has been widely used in stock market, interest rates, and portfolio asset allocation analyses. The Markov switching model is very flexible in the sense that specifications, such as mean, variance, and autoregressive terms, can be assumed state dependent, either individually or all together, depending on the purpose of the estimation. For example, Nielsen and Olesen (2000) use two state regimes to explain Danish stock returns. Hardy (2001) adopts a similar model for the S&P 500 and the TSE 300 indices returns. In addition, the literature on relating economic variables to latent regimes is vast. Ang and Bekaert (2002) and Bansal and Tauchen (2004) relate changes in interest rates to different latent economic regimes. Elliott and Timmermann (2005) and Maheu, McCurdy, and Song (2012) argue that there are four regimes corresponding to the four economic states of bull, bear, bull rally, and bear rally. Guidolin and Timmermann, 2007, Guidolin and Timmermann, 2008 rely on regime-switching models to infer optimal asset allocation decisions under different regimes. Siu (2012) develops a regime-switching approach to study the asset allocation problem of a member of a defined contribution (DC) pension fund using backward stochastic differential equations.

There is very little academic research on mutual fund performance evaluation that incorporates an unobservable regime approach. Ferson and Qian (2005) use a multi-factor benchmark model that incorporates a discrete state-like dummy variable to gauge the unobservable regime to find that interest rate term structure is the most informative instrument. Using this time-varying model on a large U.S. mutual fund sample (grouped by style) shows better manager performance than classical approaches, as the return is approximately equal to the cost of mutual fund fees. Instead of estimating the state by a regime-switching model, Ferson and Qian measure state changes using a dummy variable defined by the average mean-to-variability ratio of the last 60 months' return. However, this approach fails to capture the most recent stochastic movement in the underlying states which is most obvious when there is a jump or crash in the market. Glode (2011) develops a theoretical model based on the asset pricing kernel framework to empirically show that U.S. equity mutual funds perform better during economic downturns and that investors are willing to pay higher fund fees for this recession insurance. This theoretical model has been tested by Fink, Raatz, and Weigert (2015) in sixteen international mutual funds markets. Their results show little support for the hypothesis that mutual funds outperform during recessions and that funds with high recession alphas can charge higher fees to investors. Kosowski (2011) examines the asymmetric performance of domestic U.S. equity funds using a two-state multivariate regime-switching model. He demonstrates that U.S. mutual fund managers generally have state dependent loadings on market risk factors, which he interprets as evidence of market timing ability. Moreover, U.S. mutual funds perform better during recessions. Turtle and Zhang (2012) measure the performance of U.S. domestic and global mutual funds, and suggest that either a one-factor or a two-factor regime-switching model with fixed transition probabilities is the most parsimonious specification.

This paper has two major objectives designed to complement and extend the mutual funds’ performance literature using conditional regime-switching models. The first major objective is to assess the performance of Canadian fixed-income funds using various specifications that rely on latent regime variables. First, we augment the multifactor benchmark models with non-linearity in the market risk factors to account for fund managers who adopt different investment strategies for bull and bear markets. Second, because a fund’s exposure to market risks depend on the realization of a state variable, performance is based on the joint distribution of regime and fund returns. Thus, fund performance is estimated conditionally on market trends in different episodes.

The second major objective of this paper is to develop more precise performance measures using multivariate models that incorporate a multi-class series to account for cross-correlation of mutual fund returns. In all of our tests, the timing ability measure is not limited to the differential in loadings between states as in Kosowski (2011) but we also rely on the usual Treynor-Mazuy estimates in the presence of state conditioning.

The first major finding of this paper is that more than one state variable is necessary to explain the return dynamics of Canadian fixed-income mutual funds. Specifically, there are two distinct regimes that can be identified with a turning point during the mid-eighties. This change corresponds to the increase of the Canadian bond index from its low values in the early 1980s when interest rates peaked, to its current high value. Other fixed-income funds results show latent state variables that mimic the behaviour of general economic activity. We demonstrate that the multivariate regime-switching model is superior to univariate models given the dynamic market conditions and the correlation between fund portfolios.

The second major finding is that the selection performance of Canadian fixed-income fund managers is negative, regime dependent, and deteriorates during recessions. While factor loadings or exposure are state dependent, the Treynor-Mazuy estimates indicate negative timing abilities for Canadian fixed-income fund managers. These results are primarily in the Canadian Inflation Protected Fixed Income funds, Long Term Fixed Income funds, and Money Market funds groups. This evidence contrasts with the conclusions of Kosowski (2011) on U.S. equity funds.

Although previous literature has shed some light on mutual fund performance evaluation especially for equity investments, the depth and breadth of research on fixed-income funds is relatively small in comparison. We believe that fixed-income funds performance evaluation should receive more attention for several reasons. First, investors’ demand for diversified mutual fund investment vehicles in recent years has dramatically increased the number and size of fixed-income funds. Second, although fixed-income funds behave differently from other types of funds, the empirical research that exclusively focuses on fixed-income funds is limited. Third, an interesting finding from earlier literature is that fixed-income fund performance is easier to assess and that the results may be interpreted more intuitively as there are fewer risk factors in the fixed-income market (Elton et al., 1993). Since fixed-income fund managers generally expose their portfolios to fewer market risk factors, the choice of a performance evaluation method is crucial in capturing their dynamic sensitivity to the market risk factors. Fourth, the measures of underlying states using fund return series alone may not be accurate because fund returns heavily rely on only a few factors. However, these prevailing market risk factors can deviate significantly from true states if the factors do not accurately project those states. Therefore, fundamentals of the general economic condition are included to help identify the latent states. Based on this result, we can better infer how managers are making their investment decisions and if they are affected by ongoing economic conditions. Finally, most research on fixed-income fund performance has been conducted on U.S. data with very little work on the Canadian market. Although the U.S. is geographically close to Canada, the underlying assets in these two countries may deviate substantially due to market liquidity, policies, and investment styles. Since many advanced pricing techniques have not been applied to the Canadian market, some of them may generate different inferences.

To our knowledge, we are the first to test fixed-income fund performance using a conditional asset pricing model with a Markov regime-switching approach. Assuming multiple states in market returns, our model is able to capture dramatic variation in long data series and is especially effective at modeling the crash and boom patterns of bond returns. Moreover, we can determine if managers have added value to the portfolio in relation to the underlying regime. Furthermore, we break down the bond fund performance and determine what abilities the fund managers possess under different states. We compare the results to the performance evaluation process based on the original setting and then investigate the implications of any differences. This research contributes to the literature on Canadian bond funds, as well as to the study of performance evaluation under the Markov regime-switching methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces a flexible mutual fund evaluation model that includes a regime-switching approach. Section 3 discusses data collection and our sample selection. Section 4 reports our main empirical results. Finally, section 5 concludes the paper.

This is a research article published in The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance (Volume 69, August 2018, pages 217-231) by Elsevier, authored by Mohamed A. Ayadi, Skander Lazrak, Yusui Liao, and Robert Welch. The paper examines the performance of Canadian fixed-income mutual funds using Markovian regime-switching models over the period 1980-2011.

**Key Objectives:** The study has two major goals: (1) assess the performance of Canadian fixed-income funds using latent regime variable specifications, and (2) develop more precise performance measures using multivariate models that account for cross-correlation of mutual fund returns.

**Methodology:** The authors use univariate and multivariate Markovian regime-switching models, extending traditional linear unconditional multifactor models (Ross 1976; Sharpe 1964) by incorporating non-linearity in market risk factors. They use a sample of 895 surviving and non-surviving fixed-income funds from the Fundata database, including 403 Canadian Fixed Income funds (CFI), 17 Canadian Inflation Protected Fixed Income funds (CIPFI), 11 Canadian Long Term Fixed Income funds (CLTFI), 270 Canadian Money Market funds (CMM), 121 Canadian Short Term Fixed Income funds (CSTFI), and 73 High Yield Fixed Income funds (HYFI).

**Key Findings:**
- Fund returns are well described by two distinct volatility-related bull and bear regimes
- The selection performance of Canadian fixed-income fund managers is negative, regime dependent, and deteriorates during recessions
- Mixed results on timing ability, with poor performance for Canadian Inflation Protected Fixed Income funds, Long Term Fixed Income funds, and Money Market funds groups
- The multivariate regime-switching model is superior to univariate models given dynamic market conditions and fund portfolios' cross-correlations
- More than one state variable is necessary to explain the return dynamics of Canadian fixed-income mutual funds, with a turning point in the mid-1980s corresponding to the rise in the Canadian bond index from low values when interest rates peaked

**Literature Context:** The paper extends prior research on bond fund performance, including work by Cornell and Green (1991), Elton, Gruber, and Blake (1993, 1995), Moneta (2015), Ayadi and Kryzanowski (2011), and Kosowski (2011). The regime-switching approach draws on Hamilton (1989). The authors claim to be the first to test fixed-income fund performance using a conditional asset pricing model with a Markov regime-switching approach.

**Other Details:** The article has 37 references, is cited by 6 other works, and has 27 Mendeley readers. JEL classifications: C24, C34, G12. Keywords: Performance evaluation, Markovian regime-switching models, Selection and timing abilities, Fixed-income mutual funds.

Track records by themselves are typically too short to distinguish skill from chance. Moreover, what shows up as alpha may instead be an artifact of a mis-specified benchmark. The consequences of poor performance evaluation are significant. Investment managers are needlessly fired, and perhaps more often, unjustifiably hired. And the transaction costs associated with this turnover substantially and unnecessarily dilute investor savings. Another, more subtle, cost of unnecessary turnover exists. If managers operate at different levels of risk, then in the absence of reliable information, switching managers into and out of a portfolio is riskier than maintaining a constant exposure to them. We are thus quite fortunate that Wayne Ferson and Meijun Qian have revisited the critically important topic of conditional performance evaluation.
Unlike the conventional approach to performance evaluation, which assumes that investment styles and economic states remain constant, this methodology compares a fund’s returns with the returns of a dynamic strategy that matches the fund’s time-varying risk exposures. It thus controls for a variety of biases that might lead an investor to mistakenly shift between managers. And as a nod to the more cynically inclined, conditional performance evaluation prevents managers from gaming less refined performance benchmarks. Although the methodology is quite sophisticated, Ferson and Qian present the topic in a style that is accessible to practitioners, and they provide sufficient detail to facilitate implementation of their models. Yet, they do not bend to simplicity. Even the most quantitatively advanced scholars will be satisfied with their rigor and their comprehensive review of the extant literature.
Ferson and Qian present a compelling case for conditional performance evaluation, both conceptually and empirically. Managers who are truly confi-dent of their skill should be eager to have it rendered transparent by conditional performance evaluation. And investors should be equally eager to move from a murky system that confounds alpha with shifting economic states to one that shines a light on true skill—or the lack thereof.
