## (c) SPIVA (S&P Indices Versus Active) Scorecard Methodology

### Overview

SPIVA is "a long-running scorecard published by S&P Dow Jones Indices. It compares how active funds perform against relevant S&P benchmarks around the globe." Published semi-annually, it measures the percentage of actively-managed funds that outperform their market index benchmarks over specific periods of time, net of fees, across large cap, mid cap, small cap, international, and fixed income categories. [12][18][11]

The SPIVA U.S. Scorecard is "the definitive report on the active vs. passive fund management debate in the U.S." [17] Two main reports exist: SPIVA Scorecards (active fund performance vs. benchmarks) and SPIVA Persistence Scorecards (whether outperformance persists, testing skill vs. luck). [15]

### Methodology Principles

SPIVA's methodology stands out due to four key principles: no survivorship bias (includes funds that disappeared during the period), asset-weighted returns (larger funds carry more weight), like-for-like comparisons (matching funds to appropriate benchmarks by style and category), and style consistency checks (tracking how well funds stick to their stated investment approach). [12]

The official methodology principles listed in the SPIVA report include: [17]
- **Survivorship Bias Correction**: accounts for the entire opportunity set including liquidated/merged funds
- **Apples-to-Apples Comparison**: measures funds against appropriate category benchmarks
- **Asset-Weighted Returns**: shows both equal- and asset-weighted averages
- **Style Consistency**: measures style drift across time horizons
- **Data Cleaning**: avoids double-counting share classes, excludes index funds and leveraged/inverse products

Fund data comes from the CRSP Survivor-Bias-Free US Mutual Fund Database, with classifications based on the Lipper fund classification system. [17]

### Key Findings

- Over any 15-year period, approximately 85-90% of actively managed equity funds underperform the S&P 500 on a net-of-fees basis. Underperformance rates are lower over 1-year periods but increase consistently as the time horizon extends. [11]
- 79% of all large-cap U.S. equity funds underperformed their indexes in 2025 (across 22 equity categories), worse than the 65% rate in 2024 and the fourth-worst year for active large-cap managers in the 25-year SPIVA history. [14][17]
- After 15 years, there were "no categories in which the majority of active managers outperformed" across domestic, international equities, and fixed income. [14]
- Nearly 64% of domestic stock funds and almost two-thirds of international equity funds were shuttered or merged over 20 years. [14]
- US Large Cap Funds underperformance: 60.9% (1 year), 79.8% (3 years), 86.6% (5 years), 92.2% (15 years) vs. S&P 500. Australian General Equity Funds: 76.5% (1 year), 69.3% (3 years), 77.6% (5 years), 85.4% (15 years). In every category with a 10-year history, 75% or more of funds underperformed their benchmark. [15]
- Among U.S. domestic funds (year-end 2018): 68.83% underperformed over 1 year, rising to 81.49% over 3 years, 88.13% over 5 years, 84.49% over 10 years, and 88.97% over 15 years. Large-cap: 64.49% underperforming the S&P 500 over 1 year and 91.62% over 15 years. Small-cap core: 87.55% over 1 year and 97.44% over 15 years. Emerging markets: 78.10% over 1 year and 96.15% over 15 years. High yield fixed income: 75.60% over 1 year and 99.15% over 15 years. [18]
- 2025 SPIVA U.S. Scorecard details: The S&P 500 returned +18% in 2025; 55% of mid-cap and 41% of small-cap funds underperformed; 63% of International funds and 76% of Global funds underperformed; 53% of Emerging Markets funds underperformed; 70% cross-category average underperformance for fixed income (82% of General Investment-Grade and 76% of High Yield funds underperformed); Emerging Market Debt was the sole bright spot with only 31% underperforming. [17]
- Persistence findings: none of 2020's top-quartile large-cap funds remained in the top quartile for the next two years; only 5% of above-median large-cap active funds remained above median in succeeding years; 0% chance of a top-half performer as of Dec 2018 still being a top-half performer by Dec 2022. [15]
- "Our very first SPIVA Scorecard reported that most active managers had underperformed a benchmark appropriate to their investment style over a full market cycle. Our most recent SPIVA update reports more or less the same thing." — Craig Lazzara, Managing Director, S&P Dow Jones Indices. [15]
- SPIVA's conclusions are "robust across geographies": most institutional managers underperform most of the time; underperformance tends to rise with longer observation periods; good performance tends not to persist. [15]

### Critiques of SPIVA Methodology

A 40-page study sponsored by the Investment Adviser Association's Active Managers Council — "How the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard Understates the Performance of Actively Managed Mutual Funds" by Professors K.J. Martijn Cremers (University of Notre Dame), Jon Fulkerson (University of Dayton), and Timothy B. Riley (University of Arkansas) — argues SPIVA "consistently and substantially" understates the performance of actively managed mutual funds. [13][16]

Three major methodological changes proposed: (1) don't automatically classify funds that exit the sample as underperformers — incorporate their pre-exit performance ("if you don't survive, then you automatically underperform" is the rule they modify); (2) weight results by fund assets rather than giving all funds equal weight; (3) compare active funds to investable passive funds (index mutual funds) rather than hypothetical benchmarks. [13][16]

Results after the three changes: U.S. equity underperformance dropped from 92% to 55% of assets underperforming (probability of outperformance for a given dollar invested over 20 years "approximated a coin flip"); fixed income underperformance dropped from 71% of funds over 10 years to 37%. In fixed income, 86% of assets in high yield bond funds outperformed over five years ending 2024 vs. SPIVA's reported 46%; in domestic equity, 43% of assets outperformed vs. SPIVA's 15%. [13][16]

S&P Dow Jones Indices defended its methodology, stating SPIVA measures the proportion of funds that underperform (not assets), providing a clear view of manager performance independent of fund size, and that the fundamental claim of active management is beating the market, not outperforming a basket of index funds. [16]

Critiques of the IAA study (Neil Bathon, FUSE Research Network): taxes (high turnover funds generate greater capital gains taxes) should be factored in; some concentrated funds within broad categories shouldn't be compared to broad-based indexes; weighting by assets can be misleading since funds may generate outsized returns in early years that are difficult to replicate later. [16]

### Limitations of SPIVA

SPIVA measures relative performance against a benchmark net of fees but does not address absolute risk-adjusted returns or drawdown considerations. A strategy underperforming the S&P 500 by 2% annually while producing only half the maximum drawdown could create substantially more wealth for investors who cannot endure full-market drawdowns. [11] SPIVA data has been the primary empirical support for the shift toward passive index investing. [11]

## (d) Performance Attribution Techniques

### Brinson-Type Return Attribution

The Brinson attribution model is "the most widely used framework in institutional investment management for answering the question every portfolio review demands: why did a portfolio outperform or underperform its benchmark?" It decomposes a portfolio's active return (portfolio return minus benchmark return) into three effects: allocation, selection, and interaction. [20]

Two primary variants: [20][50][51][52]
- **Brinson-Fachler (BF, 1985)**: measures allocation relative to overall benchmark return. Allocation Effect = (Portfolio Weight − Benchmark Weight) × (Benchmark Return − Total Benchmark Return). Selection Effect = Benchmark Weight × (Portfolio Return − Benchmark Return). Interaction Effect = (Portfolio Weight − Benchmark Weight) × (Portfolio Return − Benchmark Return). [20][50][24]
- **Brinson-Hood-Beebower (BHB, 1986)**: uses a different allocation baseline; calculates allocation effect by multiplying the difference in portfolio and benchmark weights by the benchmark return per sector. Selection and interaction formulas are identical in both variants. [20][22]

The BHB model "creates allocation effect (A) and selection effect (S) portfolios. The interaction effect (I) bridges the gap between A + S and active return." The Brinson-Fachler (1985) model folds the interaction term into the selection term (per one CFA study note). [52]

The model requires beginning-of-period weights, arithmetic single-period returns, same currency/classification scheme, and categories that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive. The standard model is holdings-based (buy-and-hold assumption), while transaction-based attribution captures intra-period trades but requires complete trade-level data. [20]

The R Journal "pa" package (Yang Lu, Williams College and David Kane, Harvard University, September 2013) implements the BHB model and a regression-based analysis. Formulas: Allocation effect = Σ(W_Pj − W_Bj) × R_Bj; Selection effect = Σ W_Bj × (R_Pj − R_Bj); Interaction effect = R_active − R_allocation − R_selection. Demonstrated using MSCI Barra's Global Equity Model II (GEM2) data. A noted limitation: "it is very hard to expand the analysis beyond two categories due to the curse of dimensionality." [23]

A worked example (US large-cap equity manager benchmarked to Russell 1000, five GICS sectors) produced portfolio return 1.478%, benchmark 1.206%, active return 0.272% (27.2 bps): selection +16.9 bps, interaction +7.4 bps, allocation +2.9 bps. The BF same-sign rule: underweighting an underperforming sector produces a positive allocation effect. [20]

Wikipedia's example: portfolio returned 4.60% vs. benchmark 2.40% (220 bps outperformance) decomposed into asset allocation (+0.40%), stock selection (+1.40%), and interaction (+0.40%). Valid benchmarks must be: unambiguous, investable, measurable, appropriate, reflective of current investment opinions, specified in advance, and owned. [21]

Common mistakes: confusing BHB and BF allocation effects, applying single-period formulas to multi-period data (requiring linking methods like Carino, Menchero, or GRAP), using end-of-period weights, using non-exhaustive categories, ignoring trading/reconciliation residuals, and confusing attribution with contribution analysis. [20]

Limitations: sensitivity to classification scheme, holdings-based approach ignoring intra-period trading, no risk adjustment, designed for single-manager/single-benchmark contexts, multi-period linking methodology choices, and not well-suited for fixed-income, derivatives-heavy, long/short, or absolute-return mandates. [20]

Two types of attribution: **Relative attribution** (reconciles to excess return = portfolio return minus benchmark return) and **Absolute attribution**/"contribution" (focuses on total return). Top-down managers make allocation decisions based on macro analysis; bottom-up managers focus on security selection. [22]

The Hierarchical Attribution Model (Stephen Campisi, "Balanced Portfolio Attribution," Journal of Performance Measurement) decomposes total effect into two components: Allocation Effect = (Portfolio Weight − Benchmark Weight) × (Benchmark Return − Total Benchmark Return); Selection Effect = Portfolio Weight × (Portfolio Return − Benchmark Return). It rescales weights within a given asset class and links a security's return to underlying risk drivers via time-series regression, scaling contributions by systematic risk exposure (beta). [50]

Historical development of attribution (Wikipedia): 1966 Peter Dietz established time-weighted rate of return; 1968 Bank Administration Institute proposed common pension fund comparison methods; 1972 Eugene Fama decomposed returns into "selectivity" and "timing"; 1985-1986 Brinson and Fachler (1985) and Brinson, Hood, and Beebower (1986) introduced foundational models ("arithmetic attribution" models underpinning Morningstar's methodology); Bacon (2002) proposed geometric excess return to solve multi-period compounding issues (popular in Europe/UK). [21]

Other models: Karnosky-Singer (extends BF to incorporate currency effects for global portfolios), Frongello (flexible, allows multiple factors and sub-asset classes), Wagner-Tito (1977, fixed income attribution replacing market return with duration risk), currency attribution (Allen 1991; Ankrim and Hensel 1992-94; Karnosky and Singer 1994). [21][51]

### Factor Attribution (BARRA/Carhart-style)

Returns-based attribution (developed after the 1970s) requires time-series return data rather than holdings data: 1988-1992 William Sharpe proposed a 12-factor model for style benchmarks; 1993 Fama-French three-factor model (market, size, value); 1997 Carhart four-factor model added momentum. [21]

Factor-based attribution is used when detailed portfolio holdings breakdowns are unavailable; it involves correlating portfolio returns with relevant factor returns. Fixed income factors (e.g., Aa spread) and equity factors (e.g., value vs. growth) typically differ. [52]

"Risk-based performance attribution decomposes performance based on risk factors/exposures, useful for complex portfolios like hedge funds, and should not be confused with risk attribution (which decomposes total portfolio risk)." [21]

### Risk Attribution / Risk Decomposition

The Barra model provides risk decomposition via the formula: risk = X'FX + Δ, where X is the matrix of factor exposures, F is the factor return variance-covariance matrix, and Δ is the diagonal matrix of specific risk variance. Risk attribution uses the x-sigma-rho formula (per GEM3 technical appendices). [43][41]

Factor and risk decomposition applications include: performance attribution (decomposing returns into factor-driven and alpha components), portfolio construction (targeting specific factor loadings), risk decomposition (understanding factor exposure risks), and alpha measurement. [28]

## (e) Academic Performance Evaluation Literature

### Jensen's Alpha (1968)

Jensen's Alpha, developed by economist Michael Jensen in 1968, measures whether a portfolio manager generated returns above or below what CAPM predicted given systematic risk. Formula: αp = Rp – [Rf + βp(Rm – Rf)], or rearranged: αp = (Rp – Rf) – βp(Rm – Rf). In practice, alpha is more rigorously estimated as the intercept from a regression of portfolio excess returns on market excess returns, producing a t-statistic for significance. [27]

Interpretation: positive alpha = outperformed CAPM expectation; alpha = 0 = matched expectation; negative alpha = underperformed. Alpha is only meaningful if statistically significant (t-statistic above 2.0). Most actively managed large-cap funds deliver negative alpha after fees (per SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2024). [27]

Calculation steps: (1) determine portfolio return using total return including dividends (time-weighted returns standard); (2) estimate beta via regression (36–60 month window using monthly returns is standard); (3) select risk-free rate matching the evaluation horizon; (4) choose market benchmark matching the portfolio's universe; (5) apply the formula. [27]

Limitations: built entirely on CAPM assumptions; single-factor model (ignores size, value, momentum factors); backward-looking; beta instability; CAPM assumes efficient markets, rational investors, no transaction costs, unlimited borrowing at the risk-free rate. Should be combined with Sharpe Ratio, Treynor Ratio, and Information Ratio for comprehensive assessment. [27]

### Treynor Ratio

The Treynor Ratio is a beta-based ratio (risk-adjusted performance measure using systematic risk), in contrast to the Sharpe Ratio (total risk) and Information Ratio (active return divided by tracking error, measuring consistency of outperformance — benchmark-relative, not CAPM-based). [27][52]

### CAPM

CAPM (1964, Sharpe/Lintner): single-factor model using only market sensitivity (beta). Formula: E(Ri) = Rf + βi × (E(Rm) − Rf). Explains ~70% of stock return variation. Limitation: misses size effect and value premium. [25]

### Fama-French Three-Factor Model (1993)

The Fama-French model extends CAPM by adding size and value factors. The three-factor model captures roughly 90% of the variation in diversified portfolio returns (versus CAPM's ~70%). [28][25]

Formula: E(Ri) − Rf = βi(Rm − Rf) + si(SMB) + hi(HML). [28]

- **Market Factor (Rm−Rf)**: same as CAPM; broad systematic risk.
- **SMB (Small Minus Big)**: size factor — small-cap minus large-cap returns. Historical US premium of roughly 2-3% per year, though inconsistent across decades. Economic rationale: smaller companies carry more risk.
- **HML (High Minus Low)**: value factor — high book-to-market (value) minus low book-to-market (growth). Historical US premium of roughly 3-5% annually. Two competing explanations: risk-based (Fama's view) and behavioural (investors overreact to bad news). [28][25]

### Carhart Four-Factor Model (1997)

The Carhart Four-Factor Model, proposed by Mark Carhart in 1997, extends the Fama-French Three-Factor Model by adding a momentum (WML/UMD/MOM) factor: [25][26][28]

Formula: E(Ri) − Rf = αi + βi(Rm − Rf) + si(SMB) + hi(HML) + wi(WML) + εi. Explains ~92-95% of return variation. [25]

- **WML (Winners Minus Losers / momentum)**: constructed by sorting stocks on prior 12-month returns (skipping the most recent month to avoid short-term reversal — the "12-1-1" approach standard since Jegadeesh & Titman 1993) and taking the spread between top and bottom 30%. [25][26][28]
- Momentum premium is substantial (~6-8% annually gross) but carries severe tail risk (e.g., 2009 momentum crash lost roughly 40% of factor value). [28][25]
- Carhart found mutual fund performance persistence was almost entirely explained by momentum. [28]
- The regression intercept is Jensen's alpha, representing performance beyond factor exposures. A significant positive alpha (t-statistic above 2.0) signals genuine manager skill; alpha of +0.001 per month is roughly +1.2% annualized. Adjusted R-squared above 0.90 is typical for diversified equity funds. [26]
- Example output (120 monthly observations): Carhart alpha 0.003203 per period (≈3.9% annualized), t=3.87; factor loadings MKT-RF=1.123, SMB=0.314, HML=-0.122, MOM=0.205; R-squared 0.9633. [26]
- Limitations: static factor loadings assumed; requires 36-60 months of data for reliable estimates; no accounting for dynamic factor timing; missing later-discovered factors (profitability, investment, low volatility, quality); momentum crashes not predicted; transaction costs ignored. [25][26]
- Portfolio attribution example: portfolio returning 15% with 4% risk-free rate (11% excess): factor contributions totaled 9.95% (Market 8.40%, SMB 0.50%, HML 0.15%, WML 0.90%) and genuine alpha was only 1.05%. [25]

### Fama-French Five-Factor Model (2015)

Formula: E(Ri) − Rf = βi(Rm − Rf) + si(SMB) + hi(HML) + ri(RMW) + ci(CMA). [28]

- **RMW (Robust Minus Weak)**: profitability factor — difference between firms with high and low operating profitability. Premium of roughly 3-4% annually. Operating profitability defined as revenue minus COGS, minus SG&A, minus interest expense, divided by book equity. [28]
- **CMA (Conservative Minus Aggressive)**: investment factor — difference between firms that invest conservatively (low asset growth) and aggressively (high asset growth). Premium of roughly 2-3% per year. [28]
- Key finding: HML becomes largely redundant in the five-factor model — the value premium is substantially absorbed by RMW and CMA. [28]
- Five-factor model typically explains 90-95% of return variation for diversified portfolios, but only 30-60% for individual stocks. [28]

Criticisms of the Fama-French framework: data mining (the "factor zoo" problem); premiums may not persist; mixed international evidence; no momentum factor (deliberate exclusion by Fama, who argues momentum is short-lived and microstructure-driven); theoretical weakness; regime sensitivity (factor loadings aren't stable). [28]

Data sources: Kenneth French maintains a free public data library at Dartmouth College (mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library.html), including monthly/daily factor returns, US data back to 1926. [28]

### NBIM (Norway Sovereign Wealth Fund) Factor-Adjusted Return Methodology

Norges Bank Investment Management's "Factor and risk-adjusted returns 2022" report uses: the Fama and French (2015) global five-factor model (MKT, SMB, HML, RMW, CMA) for equity portfolios; a two-factor model (duration-adjusted default premium and term premium) for fixed income per Hallerbach and Houweling (2011); and a seven-factor combined model for the total fund per Dahlquist et al. (2015). Data spans January 1998 to December 2022. Main equity factors sourced from Kenneth French's data library; fixed-income factors constructed from Barclays data; AQR factors (Quality Minus Junk, Betting Against Beta) used for robustness tests. [29]

Key regression results: Equity asset class annualized alpha of 0.29% since 1999 (t=1.90); fixed-income asset class alpha of 0.19% since 1998 (t=0.73); equity management entity alpha of 0.35% since 1999 (t=2.27); fixed-income management alpha of 0.17% since 1998 (t=0.67). Before vs. after management costs for equity: alpha drops from 0.47% to 0.35% when costs are accounted for. "Throughout the analysis, we use the global five-factor model of Fama and French (2015) in Equation (1.1) as our main model for portfolio composites that hold only listed equities." [29]

### Other Performance Measures

- **Sharpe Ratio**: excess return per unit of total risk. [52]
- **Information Ratio**: active return per unit of tracking error. [52]
- **Sortino Ratio**: uses semi-deviation with a Minimum Acceptable Return (MAR). [52]
- Downside risk measures: VaR, Expected Shortfall (cVaR), Semi-standard Deviation. Measures are typically computed using monthly returns and annualized by multiplying by √12. [52]
- Statistical significance: t-statistic formula (sample mean / sample standard deviation × √N); a t-statistic of 2 roughly translates to 95% probability the true mean is positive. A portfolio with 10% return and 20% standard deviation requires over 16 years for t-statistic to exceed 2. CUSUM (Cumulative SUM) is a Statistical Process Control scheme that identifies underperforming managers in about 3.5 years (vs. 16 years via t-statistic). [52]

---

## (f) Institutional Allocator Frameworks: Benchmarking and Manager Evaluation

### CFA Institute Investment Manager Selection Framework

The CFA Institute learning module "Investment Manager Selection" (2026 CFA Program Level III) emphasizes that "Evaluating an investment manager is a complex and detailed process that encompasses a great deal more than analyzing investment returns." It requires both quantitative and qualitative due diligence. [37]

Key quantitative considerations: Type I errors (hiring/retaining a manager who subsequently underperforms) versus Type II errors (not hiring/firing a manager who subsequently outperforms); returns-based style analysis (RBSA) as a top-down imprecise tool versus holdings-based style analysis (HBSA) as a bottom-up approach allowing current risk factor estimation; capture ratios measuring return asymmetry; maximum drawdown and drawdown duration. [37]

Qualitative considerations: evaluating a manager's investment philosophy, investment decision-making process, and behavioral factors affecting investment team decisions. Also covers pooled investment vehicles vs. separate accounts, types of contracts, and the three basic forms of performance-based fees. Management fees lower realized return without affecting standard deviation; performance fees also lower realized standard deviation. [37]

Manager selection involves a reasonableness test (comparing active managers vs. passive vehicles like S&P 500 ETFs using SPIVA reports), evaluating the investment process, ensuring reasonable fee structures (including clawback provisions for performance fees), and ongoing performance monitoring with statistical process control. [52]

### AIMA Due Diligence Questionnaires

AIMA has been publishing DDQs for more than 20 years; the first AIMA DDQ (for investors conducting due diligence on hedge fund managers) was published in 1997. "It was a response to requests from investors for a standardised set of questions. Since then, the DDQs have gone on to become the industry-standard template." AIMA's 2,100 corporate members manage $2.5 trillion. [33][31]

"Standardised questions help investors compare like-for-like when they receive responses from multiple managers. Managers like standardised questions because it reduces the amount of work they have to do and helps them reassure investors that they are all receiving the same information." [33]

The DDQ is "the primary structured information exchange between a private equity fund and the institutional investors considering allocating capital to it" (in PE context). It differs from an RFP in that it is a risk assessment evaluating a specific party against defined criteria. [30]

AIMA DDQ structure is modular, covering: (1) Basic Setup Modules (firm background, ownership, governance, personnel, regulatory status); (2) Fund Type Modules (open-end vs. closed-end, managed accounts, platform providers, sub-advisory relationships — covering liquidity, redemptions, capital calls, valuation, reporting, fees); (3) Strategy Modules (hedge fund strategy, private credit, private markets, leverage, counterparty exposure, liquidity risk); (4) Operations and Risk Modules (risk management, operational controls, outsourcing, technology, AML, valuation policies, business continuity); (5) Data Requests and Supporting Information (performance data, risk reports, policies, org charts, compliance documents). [31]

The AIMA DDQ "has become the industry standard for hedge fund operational due diligence." It includes modules covering firm ownership/governance, investment strategy, risk management, operational processes, compliance/regulatory disclosures, technology/cybersecurity controls, and business continuity planning. [32]

Three industry bodies publish standardized DDQ frameworks: AIMA (hedge funds and alternatives), ILPA (private equity, focusing on governance and alignment), and PRI (ESG-focused). [30] Other industry DDQ templates include: AFG (French asset management), Diversity Project D&I, EDCI (ESG Data Convergence Initiative), IAA (Investment Adviser Association — fiduciary duties and compliance), ICI Distributor, ILPA DDQ, ILPA Fee Template (standardized fee and expense reporting), INREV (non-listed real estate), InvestEurope, NCREIF PERA (real estate performance reporting), PLSA Voting Template, SBAI (Standards Board for Alternative Investments), TCFD Reporting. [34]

### SBAI (Standards Board for Alternative Investments)

SBAI, formerly the Hedge Fund Standards Board (HFSB), is "an international standard-setting body for the alternative investment industry." Founded in June 2007 as the Hedge Fund Working Group by leading alternative investment managers including Marshall Wace, Cheyne Capital Management, Man Group, and CQS; formally established as a nonprofit in January 2008. Headquartered in London at Somerset House. By 2016, membership had grown to nearly 200 hedge fund managers and institutional investors with total AUM of $3 trillion. In 2014, SBAI became an affiliate member of IOSCO; in 2016 established a mutual observer relationship with the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds. Renamed from HFSB to SBAI in September 2017. [45]

SBAI's Alternative Investment Standards "address key areas of industry practice including: Disclosure, Valuation, Risk Management, Fund Governance, and Shareholder Conduct." [49]

Standards structure: [49]
- Disclosure (Standards 1-4): areas managers are expected to disclose to investors
- Valuation (Standards 5-8): segregation of functions in valuation, handling/disclosure of hard-to-value assets, and disclosure
- Risk Management (Standards 9-20): risk framework with governance structure and control processes, including limits
- Fund Governance (Standards 21-22)
- Shareholder Conduct (Standards 23-28)

"Asset manager signatories sign up on a 'comply-or-explain' basis and disclose their conformity to investors upon request." The Standards were created by asset managers and institutional investors and are updated through public consultation. Standards 2026 available in PDF and XLS; translated into Chinese and Japanese. [49]

"Risk management processes and controls are a vital part of the investor due diligence process and the proper functioning of an asset manager." [47]

In April 2026, SBAI published new and updated valuation standards for alternative fund managers, adding 20 new sub-standards within the existing Valuation Standards framework addressing: engagement with external valuation service providers, selection/appointment/engagement with auditors, manager-led secondaries and related-party transactions, valuation methodology, financial statements, valuation process evaluation, and liquidity considerations. SBAI Chair Jane Buchan: "Sound valuation practices sit at the heart of trust in investment decision-making." SBAI is an alliance of over 150 alternative asset managers and over 100 institutional investors. [48]

### Cambridge Associates Manager Evaluation Process

Cambridge Associates (CA) serves institutional investors including endowments, foundations, healthcare systems, pensions, private clients, governments, and insurance companies. As of December 31, 2022: 50 years of investment innovation, 280+ senior investment professionals globally (averaging 18 years of experience), ~5,000 manager meetings per year (five-year average 2018-2022), 11 global offices, 600+ fee/terms/access concessions secured for clients since 2016. [35]

The iterative research process: (1) gathering historical data and preliminary analysis, (2) initial meetings evaluating investment strategy and team, (3) on-site diligence meetings including business risk reviews, (4) additional analysis of returns and holdings, and (5) ongoing monitoring. Fund analysis continues for several quarters before any recommendation. [35]

Manager evaluation criteria cover organization, alignment, strategy, performance, market environment, and fees & terms. CA looks for sustainable competitive advantage, team cohesion, GP commitment, transparency, LP-friendly terms, and competitive fees based on alpha rather than beta. [35]

"To know managers well so that we can represent them well in considering them for portfolios. We start by collecting data and materials. Then, if appropriate, we meet to conduct an in-depth analysis and perform risk reviews—all before recommending any manager to a client." [38]

Post-COVID due diligence adaptations (Ashby Hatch, Head of Global Investment Research): formalized agendas with deep single-topic calls; increased team presence required; enhanced reference calls and use of industry networks/back channels; higher expectations for documented information; "trust but verify" approach including outreach to service providers; Investment Committees require documentation of how conviction was developed. "We will not lower the bar on our process or on what constitutes a high-quality investment opportunity." Due diligence is "more than a checklist." [36]

### Due Diligence Questionnaire Details

Typical PE DDQs contain 100-300 questions in 8-15 sections; large LPs may send 400+ questions; AIMA full DDQ runs over 100 pages. [30]

Eight core sections of a PE DDQ: (1) Firm overview and organizational structure; (2) Investment strategy and process; (3) Team, governance, and key personnel (key-person risk is dominant in smaller/emerging managers); (4) Risk management (market risk, leverage, valuation policy, liquidity); (5) Operations, compliance, and legal (service providers, cybersecurity, regulatory status); (6) ESG and responsible investment; (7) Track record and performance (gross/net IRR, MOIC, DPI, RVPI, attribution); (8) Fees, terms, and alignment of interests (management fee, carried interest, hurdle rate, waterfall, co-investment rights, GP commitment). [30]

LP review criteria: internal consistency, evidence over claims, consistency over time, risk management specificity, team transparency, track record depth, ESG with substance, and operational proof. Generic statements and unsupported claims are red flags. [30]

AIMA DDQ response framework (9 sections): Firm Overview; Investment Strategy and Performance (philosophy, capacity management with soft-close trigger at ~80% of capacity, performance attribution); Risk Management (CRO reporting independently, position/leverage/liquidity limits, stress testing against 2008 and 2020 events); Technology/AI Governance/Cybersecurity; Operations/Service Providers/Cash Controls (dual signatory requirements, daily trade reconciliation, shadow accounting, valuation oversight); Fee Structure (management fee, performance fee, high-water mark, side letters); Compliance and Conflicts (personal trading pre-clearance, soft dollar arrangements, regulatory history); Business Continuity (multi-cloud redundancy, RTO, remote operations with MFA); ESG and Regulatory Framework (ESG integration, EU SFDR Article 6/8/9 classification). [32]

## 5.4. Reverse Stress Testing

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **No:**  60697.BCS. 28747 | **Date(g):**  23/11/2011  | **Date(h):**  27/12/1432 | **Status:**  In-Force |

Reverse stress testing is used to identify and assess the stress scenarios most likely to cause a bank’s current business plan to become unviable. A reverse stress test starts with a specified outcome that challenges the viability of the bank. The analysis would then work backward (reverse engineered) to identify a scenario or combination of scenarios that could bring about such a specified outcome. The ultimate objective of reverse stress testing is to enable the banks to fully explore the vulnerabilities of their current business plan, take decisions that better integrate business and capital planning, and improve their contingency planning.

Banks are required to reverse stress test their business plan to failure i.e. the point at which the bank becomes unable to carry out its business activities due to the lack of market confidence. While doing this, they must identify a range of adverse circumstances which would cause their business plan to become unviable and assess the likelihood that such events could crystallize. In case the reverse stress testing reveal a risk of business failure that is inconsistent with the bank’s risk appetite or tolerance, it must take effective remedial measures to prevent or mitigate that risk. Banks should also document the entire process of reverse stress testing as a part of their stress testing framework.

args.summary: This webpage is from the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) Rulebook, specifically section 5.4 on Reverse Stress Testing under the Stress Testing rules for the banking sector. The document (No: 60697.BCS. 28747, dated 23/11/2011 / 27/12/1432 Hijri, Status: In-Force) defines reverse stress testing as a methodology used to identify stress scenarios most likely to cause a bank's current business plan to become unviable. The process starts with a specified outcome that challenges bank viability and works backward (reverse engineered) to identify scenarios that could bring about that outcome. The ultimate objective is to enable banks to fully explore vulnerabilities in their business plans, better integrate business and capital planning, and improve contingency planning. Banks are required to reverse stress test their business plan to the point of failure (where the bank becomes unable to carry out business activities due to lack of market confidence), identify a range of adverse circumstances that would render their business plan unviable, and assess the likelihood of such events crystallizing. If reverse stress testing reveals a risk of business failure inconsistent with the bank's risk appetite or tolerance, the bank must take effective remedial measures to prevent or mitigate that risk. Banks must also document the entire reverse stress testing process as part of their stress testing framework. The page is part of the broader chapter on Methodologies and Techniques (section 5), preceded by 5.3 Financial Models and followed by section 6 on Selection of Scenarios.

# The Bank of England’s approach to stress testing the UK banking system

### Contents

## Executive summary

This publication sets out the Bank’s approach to stress testing the UK banking system from 2025 onwards.

The Bank of England’s (the Bank’s) updated approach to stress testing the UK banking system is designed to support the statutory objectives of the Financial Policy Committee (FPC) and the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA). It takes into account that the level of capital in the banking system has increased materially since the global financial crisis, the changing nature of risks the banking sector faces, and the need to be effective, proportionate and efficient in pursuit of the FPC’s and PRA’s objectives.

The updated approach combines the predictability of regular stress testing to risks from the financial cycle – which has played an important role in determining the capitalisation of both the banking system and individual banks – with the adaptability the Bank has been using over recent years to explore different risks. It sits within the Bank’s broader framework for assessing financial stability and the safety and soundness of individual banks. The updated approach has benefitted from engagement with participating banks, academics and other stakeholders. It has three key components, as summarised in Figure 1.

First, the Bank expects to carry out a Bank Capital Stress Test every other year. This will be a test of risks related to the financial cycle in which the largest and most systemic UK banks participate, and will be used to inform the setting of capital buffers for the banking system and individual banks. This is a reduced frequency relative to that of the annual cyclical scenario exercises under the previous approach.

The scenario used in this test will be severe but plausible, vary with the state of the financial cycle and typically be countercyclical. The results of the test will be informed by the Bank of England’s and participating banks’ estimates of the impact of the stress scenario. The Bank expects to publish the results at an aggregate and bank-specific level and to use them to inform the setting of capital buffers for the banking system and individual participating banks, as well as to inform broader understanding of risks.

This biennial approach represents a reduced frequency for full cyclical stress tests compared to the annual cyclical scenario tests used for similar purposes under the previous approach set out in 2015. In updating its approach, and reflecting both the build-up of bank capital since the global financial crisis and the need to be proportionate in pursuit of the FPC’s and PRA’s objectives, the Bank has judged that it can now better support those objectives by undertaking a capital-setting exercise informed by both banks’ and the Bank’s estimates every other year instead of annually.

This change in approach represents a material efficiency gain in the Bank’s overall approach to stress testing the banking system, ensures the burden placed on participating banks is proportionate, and supports the UK banking sector’s competitiveness and growth. It will create space to assess and address a wider set of risks to help respond to an evolving risk environment. The approach will also support participating banks in addressing risks identified through stress testing and enhancing their risk management capabilities. It maintains predictability for the purposes of setting individual banks’ capital buffers.

Participation in this stress test will be based on an assessment of a bank’s share of lending to the UK real economy, other measures of its systemic importance, and the test’s overall coverage of the banking sector’s lending to the UK real economy. The Bank will give at least 12 months’ notice to any new bank it decides to include in this exercise to ensure that it has sufficient time to prepare for its participation.

Alongside the Bank Capital Stress Test, the Bank will deliver insights into the resilience of non-systemic banks to the FPC and Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC) by utilising existing stress testing and supervisory assessment tools for these banks. The Bank will also continue to gain reassurance on the resilience of UK-based branches and investment bank subsidiaries of foreign banks through engagement with the home supervisory authorities.

Second, in the intervening years the Bank expects to use stress testing when appropriate to supplement its assessment of the resilience of the banking system to risks related to the financial cycle. This will be done in a way that is less burdensome for banks than Bank Capital Stress Tests, for example through desk-based exercises.

In forming their assessment of the resilience of the banking system and individual banks within it to cyclical risks, the FPC and PRC consider a broad range of inputs from financial stability and supervisory analysis and intelligence. In alternate years, these can be supplemented through stress testing in a number of ways that are less burdensome for banks than a Bank Capital Stress Test.

Such exercises could be carried out at different levels of granularity or with multiple scenarios, allowing more adaptability in the Bank’s approach to assessing risks and vulnerabilities, and meeting the FPC’s and PRC’s needs in a proportionate way. For example, they could include desk-based exercises which rely primarily on the Bank’s own estimates of the impact of stress scenarios. Or they could include targeted exercises capturing how specific vulnerabilities or aspects of banks’ business models – rather than their whole balance sheets – could evolve under adverse scenarios. They could also include assessments of resilience to cyclical risks based on information in banks’ own stress tests carried out as part of their Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Processes (ICAAPs). The results of these exercises of cyclical risks are not expected to be published beyond an aggregate level.

Third, the Bank will continue to use exploratory exercises as a means of assessing other risks, including structural and emerging risks that are not closely linked to the financial cycle. When deciding on the timing of these exercises the Bank will take into account the risk environment and the sequencing and timing of the stress tests described above.

Stress test exercises based on exploratory scenarios not closely linked to the financial cycle have proven a successful part of the Bank’s approach to stress testing over the past decade (eg the 2021 climate biennial exploratory scenario). The Bank intends to continue to undertake such exploratory stress tests to explore a wide range of risks – including structural and emerging risks – that might threaten financial stability or the safety and soundness of individual banks.

While some of these exercises could be desk-based, stress tests of emerging or structural risks which have had limited previous assessment typically benefit from participation by banks (as well as other financial institutions where relevant). Banks have given positive feedback on their participation in past exercises and how they have helped them identify and address vulnerabilities.

The timing of such exploratory exercises will be informed by the FPC’s and PRC’s assessment of such risks, and, in line with the approach the Bank has taken to past tests, these exercises will be designed under their guidance. As it has done with such tests in the past, when deciding on timing of these exercises the Bank will take into account the sequencing and timing of other stress-test exercises. The Bank will engage with relevant firms to ensure appropriate notice is provided to allow time to prepare for participation, and will ensure the volume and complexity of submissions is proportionate.

Participation in these exercises will depend on the relevance of banks’ business models to the scenario and whether it is proportionate for those banks. The exercises could be focused on the banking sector, or banks could be invited to participate in exercises involving the broader financial system, such as the 2024 system-wide exploratory scenario.

The results of these exercises are likely to be published at an aggregate level and will be used to inform financial stability and supervisory assessment, wider policy, and banks’ risk management.

The Bank’s approach to stress testing the UK banking system will be used to provide a range of insights within its broader framework for financial stability and safety and soundness.

It is important for stress testing to continue to deliver insights beyond point estimates of resilience. This could include the impact of alternative assumptions and risks, the propensity of the banking system to amplify shocks in the real economy or financial system, and the business models and risk management capabilities of banks. To broaden the range of insights, the Bank will embed further the use of sensitivity and supplementary analysis into banking system stress tests as appropriate. The Bank will ensure appropriate notice is provided to participants if such analysis requires their input.

There is scope for synergies between the different banking system stress tests the Bank undertakes. For example, a desk-based stress test might allow initial exploration of a risk or sensitivity which could subsequently be incorporated into the scenario for a Bank Capital Stress Test. Alternatively, a Bank Capital Stress Test may reveal a vulnerability that could become the focus of an exploratory or targeted exercise.

All stress tests have limitations, as they cannot capture and address resilience to every risk to the banking system, and there is uncertainty around results given the limitations of modelling and assumptions. In part reflecting that, the Bank will continue to ensure that banking system stress tests are used within its broader framework for financial stability and safety and soundness, including: regular macroprudential and supervisory analysis of the banking system; supervisory intelligence and analysis of banks’ ICAAPs; and assessment of risks in other parts of the financial system including stress tests of other financial sectors.

A key strength of the Bank’s approach to stress testing over the past decade has been how it has been adapted to assess vulnerabilities to changing risks, for example, during the Covid-19 (Covid) pandemic. As such the Bank considers it important to be able to adapt the approach set out in this publication as the risk environment and the costs and benefits of stress test design choices evolve. The Bank will continue to be mindful of the potential burden on banks before making changes to the approach.

# Reverse stress testing – Simplified guide

A typical [stress test creates a scenario and evaluates how a bank would fare](https://financetrainingcourse.com/education/2016/03/bank-stress-test-evolution/) under it. In comparison to reverse stress testing, we use conventional stress tests to assure shareholders, regulators and customers that the capital on the bank balance sheet is sufficient to weather a given storm.

A reverse stress test starts with the failure of a bank. That is the desired or modeled event. The end state.  We assume that an unexpected challenge strikes and we don’t survive as a bank. We then identify the exact sequence of events – scenarios and probabilities that would lead to our modeled event – the failure of the bank. And work through possible responses today that can help us avoid that end state.

![Reverse stress testing - The difference between reverse stress test and conventional stress test](https://financetrainingcourse.com/education/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/reverse-stress-testing.png)

The reverse stress test helps answers three important questions.

The third question is the most important one. Ideally, a reverse stress test should highlight weaknesses in exposures, the balance sheet, processes, models and/or concentrations. The right answer to the third question focus on addressing specific weaknesses identified by the reverse stress test.

## 1. Who wants a reverse stress test?

### a. Regulators

Bank regulators now require a reverse stress test as part of the stress testing process as well as regulatory reporting. The overall capital adequacy (ICAAP) and internal liquidity adequacy assessment process (ILAAP – EU, EBA and BOE) now include reverse stress testing.

In the late 80’s and early 90’s tracking a daily Value at Risk (VaR) target account was presumed to be sufficient to reduce risk levels at a bank, whether we looked at market or credit risk. The inherent failings of VaR models were adequately highlighted first with the LTCM collapse in August 1998. Then, by the break down of VaR based risk systems during the 2008-2009 financial crisis.

But the financial crisis also highlighted a few other failings:

Post 2008, Regulators have increasingly favored tools such as reverse stress tests. They are a better fit for their needs. Especially when it comes to involving boards in the risk management process.  Free from the challenges of calibration with real world probabilities, such a tool may serve the important needs of highlighting weaknesses in bank balance sheets ahead of a crisis.

#### b. Executive Teams & Boards

While the shape and form of a crisis would not be as important, the insight provided by reviewing possible routes to failure would more than repay any additional costs incurred by performing the reverse stress test. ***As long as executive teams and bank boards use this opportunity to test and refine their responses to future crisis***.

Quantitative Impact Studies conducted by a number of central banks indicate that there is only marginal cost and effort impact for including the reverse stress test in the stress testing protocol of a bank. While regulators are open to small bank only using qualitative analysis for their reverse stress testing submissions, larger banks are expected to use more quantitative techniques.

Calibration with real world probabilities and rating agency models (1 in 200 years, 1 in 100 years models) is not a requirement for regulatory reverse stress testing. However, [probabilities of shortfall models](https://financetrainingcourse.com/education/2012/06/probability-of-shortfall-and-expected-shortfall-with-or-without-basel-iii-financial-risk-management-training-course-day-three-update/) allow boards to get a stronger sense of balance sheet strength as well as weaknesses. They also make it possible to set risk appetites using a quantitative approach.

## 2. Difference between stress testing and reverse stress testing

Here are a few instances that would clarify the difference between a regular stress test and a reverse stress test.

### a. Stress test examples

A typical market risk stress test would use the worst case market price shock recorded in the history of our applicable financial markets over the last ten years. It would apply this price shock and evaluate the size of the loss the bank would have to book on its balance sheet. We would quote that loss as part of our stress test report. If the worst possible day in the history of our markets would repeat itself, the bank’s investment book would drop 30% in value in a single day. The objective is to see how much damage a shock can do and that is it.

Typically if we are heavily invested in equities and equity markets go down, bond prices rally as capital moves from riskier equity securities to relatively safer government and treasury bonds.  And if for some extreme reason equity and bonds market both go down, the safer (perceived to be) currencies should rally. Depending on which market the run is occurring in that safe currency could be the US dollar, the Japanese Yen or the Swiss Franc. While a flight to safety test may already be in use at a bank, it would stop once the data set reaches its final threshold.

### b. Reverse stress test examples

On the other hand, a reverse stress test would use a range of flight to safety scenarios to identify the specific one that would kill the bank. ***No action on part of management at the point of crisis would be able to deflect.***

A reverse stress test would begin with a simple assumption. Our entire stock of capital is wiped out because of a market price event or a combination of such events. With our current book of positions, by how much would markets move for such an event to happen? What would be the probability of such a move? Is there anything we could do to survive such a shock when it occurs? Is there anything we can do now to avoid that specific version of the future? A reverse stress test could be based on actual historical data. For instance, the collapse of market prices in October 1987 (Black Monday) or the financial stocks and debt markets meltdown of 2008-2009.

## 3. A reverse stress test for credit and liquidity risk?

The concept applied to credit risk uses a similar framework. Our entire account of capital is wiped out because of provisions recorded on overdue and non-performing loans. With our current book of advances, what proportion of loans would need to default to make such an event possible? Over what time?  Is there a single relationship, a sector, a sub segment that can sink us all by itself? What combination of events, economic or otherwise would lead to such a situation? (The recessionary credit crunch of 2001-2001 and the major credit lockdown between 2008-2010).

### a. **Key questions to consider and model**

### b. Liquidity risk

While each of these shocks and scenarios sound implausible by themselves to kill a healthy bank, there is one factor that can very easily scale up a minor shock in prices or credit portfolios into a system wide melt down.

***What if, the real shock that leads to such an event is neither linked to market or credit risk but is linked to liquidity drying up.***

Liquidity problems may arise due to:

Liquidity can dry up for many reasons. The biggest is fear triggered by a name crisis involving our bank or a country crisis involving our economy. Both instances trigger chain reactions that can push the strongest of institutions into insolvency. And it doesn’t take much to push a bank into receivership with the right conditions.

**Banks don’t fail because their balance sheets are fragile. They are fragile to begin with given the leverage a typical financial institution needs as part of its business model**. But that leverage is counterbalanced by market confidence. Once you remove market faith in your ability to survive, the strongest balance sheet transforms into a house of cards.

![Liquidity-Risk-Run-On-The-Bank](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20670%20432'%3E%3C/svg%3E)
![Liquidity-Risk-Run-On-The-Bank](https://financetrainingcourse.com/education/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Liquidity-Risk-Run-On-The-Bank.jpg)

A simple reverse stress test for liquidity would begin with a run on the bank and would end with analysis and recommendation on the steps needed to take to shore up liquidity today if a run did materialize at some point in the future.

### c. Funding choices & ALM Gaps

In the past as part of our training workshops on ALM and Stress Testing, we have also used funding choices and **[simulating asset liability management gaps to drive banks all the way into insolvency](https://financetrainingcourse.com/education/why-does-bank-regulation-failcapital-adequacy-risk/)** as well as bankruptcy.

## 4. The key to building a reverse stress test

The key to building a reverse stress test is understanding that ***it won’t be a single shock that would undo our bank***. It would take a combination of factors to sink our ship. Liquidity can make the biggest holes in our hull. Once that happens, a trigger event in financial markets or in our credit portfolio or an accounting scandal would be sufficient to drive us to a point where the market or regulator would take preventive actions.

### a. Reverse stress testing factors

While a name crises are one possible source or starting point for reverse stress testing, the three other big ones are:

### b. Modeling the factors

Modeling broader economic weakness is always a challenge. However, credit portfolios tend to behave in well recognized cycles when hit by recessionary shocks. Certain economic segments remain neutral while others weaken significantly (airlines, hospitality, construction, building materials). Liquidity and cash are hoarded and forced sale value of pledged collateral falls. Customer delay payments but if their core business is strong and the bank is willing to work with them, everyone can ride the cycle.

![The reverse stress testing cycle for a market driven credit crunch](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20886%20512'%3E%3C/svg%3E)
![The reverse stress testing cycle for a market driven credit crunch](https://financetrainingcourse.com/education/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Reverse-stress-testing-credit-cycle.png)

But the modeling exercise will vary. For instance, modeling the impact of falling oil prices on construction and real estate development in Dubai is a different exercise from modeling the impact of the same shock on refining complexes, down stream petrochemical manufacturers in China or shipping industry and the Baltic Dry Index in Singapore.

### c. Consider broader applications

We also have to understand that the reverse stress test is not just for regulatory consumption. Here is what the FSA has to say about the intent behind the stress test as part of their FAQ on reverse stress testing.

**We are asking firms to identify those events (or confluences of events) that would lead to their business model failing after currently available management actions had been taken.**

**This will enable firms to identify those management actions that would not be sufficiently effective in their current state of development and/or would not currently be possible.**

**Given this knowledge, firms should then consider:**

## 5. What is bank failure?

There is also the failure threshold argument that needs to be considered. Market participants and regulators don’t wait till the entire stock of capital is gone before reacting to a bank in difficulty. They react on a preemptive basis while they (counterparties) can still get their money out and regulators can still salvage the bank’s balance sheet. The only way you can ensure that you are paid out in full is if you are the first one out of the gates.

This means the definition of bank failure is not bankruptcy or even insolvency. It could be set as high as the inability to transact regular business under normal conditions. It’s the same definition that the FSA points to in their FAQ’s on reverse stress testing.

## 6. FSA’s guidance on bank failure and expectations

The “FSA Reverse Stress Testing Surgeries – FAQ” answers a number of key questions addressed by a regulator on expectations as well as methodologies. Here are two important extracts from the document.

### a. On Bank Failure

**Firms may start to develop scenarios that lead to the business model failing by considering the cause, consequence or impact (financial or otherwise) of one or more events that lead to the failure of the firm. Firms should note that ’failure’ is not necessarily identified with the point at which the capital and/or liquidity of the firm is exhausted.****For example, it may be the point at which:**

**Firms might consider any one of these as a starting point from which to develop the scenarios. (This may be contrasted with a real-world failure, where the sequence of cause-consequence impact occurs in that distinct order.)**

And

### b. **On Expectations from the process**

The reverse stress-tests that cause a firm’s business model to fail are those where prospective management actions would not be sufficient to prevent such a failure.

Having identified such scenarios, we ask firms to think about ways in which they might strengthen their business models now to mitigate the risks posed by the scenarios.

This strengthening may include enhancing the impact that prospective management actions would have, or putting in place the necessary conditions for taking new management actions that could avert business model failure

args.summary:
This article from FinanceTrainingCourse.com provides a simplified guide to reverse stress testing in banking. It contrasts reverse stress testing with conventional stress testing: a typical stress test creates a scenario and evaluates how a bank would fare under it, while a reverse stress test starts with the assumed failure of the bank as the end state, then works backwards to identify the exact sequence of events, scenarios, and probabilities that would lead to that failure, and what responses could be taken today to avoid it.

The article answers three key questions: (1) What events would cause the bank's business model to fail? (2) What management actions could be taken to prevent this? (3) What can be done now to avoid those events—with the third question being the most important as it should highlight weaknesses in exposures, balance sheets, processes, models, and/or concentrations.

**Who requires reverse stress tests:** Bank regulators now require reverse stress testing as part of the stress testing process and regulatory reporting, including within the capital adequacy (ICAAP) and internal liquidity adequacy assessment process (ILAAP – EU, EBA, and BOE). The article notes that VaR models' inherent failings were highlighted by the LTCM collapse in August 1998 and the 2008-2009 financial crisis, leading regulators post-2008 to favor tools like reverse stress tests, especially for involving boards in risk management. Quantitative Impact Studies by central banks indicate only marginal cost/effort impact from adding reverse stress tests. Smaller banks may use qualitative analysis, while larger banks are expected to use more quantitative techniques. Calibration with real-world probabilities (1-in-200-year, 1-in-100-year models) is not required, but probability of shortfall models allow boards to set risk appetites quantitatively.

**Difference between stress testing and reverse stress testing:** A typical market risk stress test uses the worst-case market price shock from the last ten years and evaluates the resulting loss (e.g., investment book dropping 30% in a single day). A reverse stress test instead uses a range of scenarios (e.g., flight to safety) to identify the specific one that would kill the bank, assuming the entire capital stock is wiped out, then asks: by how much would markets move, what is the probability, and what could be done to survive or avoid that scenario. Reverse stress tests can be based on historical events like Black Monday (October 1987) or the 2008-2009 financial crisis.

**Application to credit and liquidity risk:** For credit risk, the framework assumes the entire capital account is wiped out by provisions on non-performing loans, asking what proportion of loans would need to default, over what time, and whether a single relationship, sector, or sub-segment could sink the bank. For liquidity risk, the article emphasizes that banks don't fail because their balance sheets are fragile—they are fragile due to leverage, but that leverage is counterbalanced by market confidence. Once market faith in survival is removed, the strongest balance sheet becomes a house of cards. A simple liquidity reverse stress test begins with a run on the bank and ends with recommendations on steps to shore up liquidity today.

**Key to building a reverse stress test:** The key understanding is that it won't be a single shock that undoes a bank—it takes a combination of factors. Liquidity can make the biggest holes in the hull; once that happens, a trigger event in financial markets, credit portfolios, or an accounting scandal can drive the bank to where market or regulator intervention occurs. Four major starting points/factors are name crises and three other big ones (economic weakness, market-driven credit crunch, etc.). Modeling economic weakness is challenging, but credit portfolios behave in well-recognized cycles under recessionary shocks (e.g., airlines, hospitality, construction weaken; liquidity is hoarded; collateral forced-sale values fall). Modeling varies by context—for example, falling oil prices affect Dubai construction differently than Chinese petrochemical manufacturers or Singapore shipping/Baltic Dry Index.

**What is bank failure:** The article emphasizes that market participants and regulators don't wait until capital is fully gone—they react preemptively. Bank failure is not bankruptcy or even insolvency; it can be set as high as the inability to transact regular business under normal conditions (the same definition used by the FSA).

**FSA guidance (from "FSA Reverse Stress Testing Surgeries – FAQ"):** Key excerpts include that failure is not necessarily identified with the point where capital/liquidity is exhausted—it may be the point at which the firm cannot meet obligations, loses market confidence, or other preemptive thresholds. Reverse stress tests that cause business model failure are those where prospective management actions would not be sufficient to prevent failure. The FSA asks firms to think about ways to strengthen business models now to mitigate these scenarios, including enhancing the impact of prospective management actions or putting in place conditions for new management actions.
args.key_excerpts: "We are asking firms to identify those events (or confluences of events) that would lead to their business model failing after currently available management actions had been taken. This will enable firms to identify those management actions that would not be sufficiently effective in their current state of development and/or would not currently be possible."
